text:
I'm increasingly despondent about how binary the AI debate has become in the US. Either you're naively pro-AI, happy to see massive data center build-out and a handful of frontier model companies become central to everything we do online, or you want to pause research, stop the build-out, and discourage people from using AI.

Almost nowhere do I see people talking about the need for decentralized AI. To me, this is the only safe way forward.

There's an underlying truth to both sides of the naive debate.

The pro-AI camp is right that refusing these technologies leaves enormous consumer welfare gains on the table. An individual using an AI agent to interact with companies and governments can stand up for their own interests rather than accept whatever terms or bureaucracy they're offered without a practical means of negotiating. And refusing to advance AI research would have enormous national security and competitiveness consequences as adversaries develop technologies that could exploit our increasingly vulnerable infrastructure.

The anti-AI camp is right that a world where everyone uses the same handful of inference providers for their most intimate affairs rapidly looks like a corporate panopticon. Ask yourself whether you really want every self-driving car to have a corporate kill switch. Sure, we could just regulate and trust giant inference providers, as we've done with Big Tech companies like Google. But the stakes are much higher when these companies sit at the center of virtually all our computing, and increasingly our physical infrastructure. Email and cloud storage were just the beginning.

Both of these positions can be true. And their synthesis points toward a third way.

We should be supercharging AI development and adoption while encouraging sovereign AI: systems in which individuals have meaningful control over the models, data, and infrastructure providing their inference.

An important distinction is between training models and providing inference. Frontier training may require enormous concentrations of capital, energy, and compute. That doesn't mean the companies that train models must also control how people use them. Even the most capable models should be runnable independently of their creators.

People should be able to keep their data locally and run models on hardware they control whenever feasible, especially where independence matters for safety, as with self-driving cars and home security systems. They should have access to open-weight models they can inspect, modify, and run without anyone's permission.

Where cloud computing is necessary, we need genuine competition among providers that respect user privacy and autonomy. But competition isn't enough. We should develop technical and protocol-based guarantees that limit what even a dominant provider can learn about or do to its users.

Technologies pioneered in cryptocurrency could play a significant role. Zero-knowledge proofs could help verify that computations were performed correctly; homomorphic encryption could enable computing on encrypted user data without revealing it to providers; and blockchain-based protocols could coordinate decentralized computing resources and enable new forms of user ownership. These technologies are at different stages of maturity, but point toward privacy and user control guaranteed by system architecture rather than a company's privacy policy.

Perhaps users could even own part of the infrastructure providing their inference, sharing in its value rather than merely providing valuable data to someone else's business.

There's no reason AI's enormous promise should require surrendering control over our digital lives to a handful of corporations. We can have rapid AI progress and individual technological sovereignty. Indeed, I think the latter is essential if we want the former to be a lasting benefit to humanity.

Binance keep pushing price into liquidations, and spot buyers are paying for it.

Spot CVD has been rising. Real buyers are taking coins off the market. But every time price tries to move, heavy selling on Binance  slams it back down, straight into the zones where leveraged longs are stacked. Longs get wiped, price resets, and spot keeps quietly buying the dip.

It’s been happening since the hack: the same exchange, the same pattern, the same liquidation clusters getting hit again and again. Normally spot leads the real move. Right now Binance are sitting right on top of it.

I can’t tell you why. But when one venue keeps forcing liquidations while spot demand keeps getting stronger, that isn’t a normal market. And once that pressure stops, spot usually shows you where price wanted to go all along.

Are they recovering the losses?

text: In a joint work with @pranaytej and @EdFelten (both from @Offchain), we study the effects of block time reduction from 2s to 200ms due to the introduction of Flashblocks, on the Base chain: https://t.co/fPuoZNEYSP. We classify searcher and non-searcher addresses, and using difference-in-differences design estimate the fall of effective priority fee per gas. Interesting observation is that searching activity is not uniformly distributed across (Flash-)blocks and 30% of it is concentrated in the first (Flash-)block. Reduced priority fees can be attributed to the less available value per time unit due to shorter effective times. Beyond this, we also develop an auction theoretic framework that qualitatively explains reduced priority fees, in which searchers may bid less hoping that only their transaction makes it in the current (Flash-)block. For a more comprehensive discussion, check out research post by @pranaytej: https://t.co/X5Rtv6MWfZ. Any feedback is welcome.

马斯克最近爆种了，昨天就发了56条推特。推特bio也改了。

近期讲了 很多 $SPCX 和 $tsla 新估值的叙事

1.最近跟Walter Isaacson做播客时说得很直白：DOGE跑完一圈下来，并不是人事关系然他放弃了，是他确认省钱解决不了美债，美债每年的利息比全年军费开支还要多，省是省不出来的。唯一出路是AI和机器人把生产力拉上去。这里马斯克断言，通货膨胀是因为产能不够，而不是产能过剩。他认为只要生产速度大于货币增发速度，就会通缩。物价就会降下来。

对赌那块他没拿到顶薪，特斯拉那个万亿激励计划里程碑目前一个都没触发。SpaceX和特斯拉已经在谈合并了。

2.这几天他把推特bio改成了space和特斯拉的最新业务Terafab。Terafab的叙事是他要自己把逻辑、存储、封装尽量垂直整合的芯片厂，和intel合作目标把AI算力产能直接拉到太瓦级别。用来服务特斯拉汽车和机器人。

芯片如果真能从一年迭代压到一个月，后面所有应用的成本结构都会变。

3.
Starmind和Terafab是同一件事的上下游。Terafab负责把芯片做出来，Starmind负责通过把一系列的算力卫星把扔到晨昏太阳同步轨道上跑——对着太阳发电，背对着太阳散热。用激光相连，形成一个太空超级算力中心，全太阳能发电，把算力能源成本降到0

前几天荷兰乌特勒支大学的Jan Broersen教授发帖说真空是最好的隔热体，根本散不了热

马斯克直接回怼，官网发了算力卫星的设计图，展示他用的太空热辐射散热方案
（我也是第一次知道因为太空没有空气和水，热量无法对流和传导，只能热辐射）

马斯克的太空算力中心方案从火星到月球，到现在的环地球轨道方案，越来越靠谱了。
Terafab、Starmind、机器人和星链放进同一个叙事里，估值锚点从汽车和火箭切到超级智能基础设施上。

quoted_text:
小明深陷网赌漩涡

这一阵不但把老婆本赔了进去，还背了16万多的网贷

全因在X上刷到一条有关[反波胆]的宣传：

“用五万块本金，每个月稳赚三千块”

发帖的人说：

「穷人才赌球，聪明人都在反波胆」

下面配着一张收益截图，连续三十天，全部盈利

评论区有人问，这和赌博有什么区别？

博主回复：

“赌博是赌一件事会发生，反波胆是赌一件事不会发生，你觉得一场足球比赛踢成 4:4 的概率有多大？”

小明心想，他月薪八千二，攒了四年才堪堪攒下两万六，何时才能攒够钱与正在热恋的女友结婚？

......

于是他试着投了五百，等到第一场比赛结束，到账十五块，第二天又赢，第三天还赢

三周下来，赚了一千多块，女友问他是不是在赌球，小明义正言辞的纠正她：

「这是概率投资」

后来他把积蓄全转进去，还借了一万

一共本金三万六，押反波胆4:4

赔率1.06，赢了净赚2160块，抵得上他一周的工资

第89分钟，比分还是4:3，这一次过程虽然抓心，但心想总归是有惊无险

他已经开始在看新手机，打算赚了这笔就送给女朋友

补时第四分钟，对面一个角球，4:4

终场哨响，他四年的积蓄连同一万借款，一起清零

他崩溃地私信那个博主

他回：“你这是仓位管理有问题，不是策略有问题”

小明居然就这么信了，事后分析，也确实是自己的问题

......

第二天，他借了五万消费贷。决定这次分散下注，慢慢回本

前十一天，确实又赚了四千多

于是他想通了一个道理：本金越大，回本越快

他又借了几笔，凑到八万二，押一场反波胆3:1

第88分钟，比分从2:1变成3:1

八万二没了

这次那位博主只是轻描淡写的回他一句：“兄弟，你这心态不适合投资”

之后他开始拆东墙补西墙

连他自己都已分不清，哪笔钱是工资，哪笔钱是贷款

最后一次，他凑了六万七，押反波胆0:0，根据这两只球队的历史战绩，他觉得这完全是不可能的事情

按照赔率，只要有人进一个球，他这一次就能赚六千多，够还下个月的账单

第81分钟，球真的进了，他站起来大喊

但这时裁判示意越位，进球取消

九十分钟结束，0:0

他没哭，只是呆呆的盯着手机里那个「投注失败」，看了很久

那天晚上，他把借款账单全部加起来核算：十六万多

......

再后来，他在 X 上刷到一条新帖：

「预测市场，99%胜率的稳定理财玩法」

帖子里教人花0.98美元买一份NO合约，只要某件事没发生，到期就能拿回1美元

虽然只赚2美分，但胜率看起来高得惊人

他盯着那张收益图，突然想起第一次反波胆赚到的15块

(当然，预测市场不只有这种玩法，也能交易、对冲、套利)

可如果所谓理财，只是不断拿全部本金去押「几乎不可能发生」的事，那不管换成什么名字，输的那一次都不会因为此前赢过很多次而变小

他划走帖子，点开了和他妈的聊天框。

她刚发来一句：“钱不够的话，跟妈说。别在外面乱借”

小明眼眶瞬时被泪水充满，眼前一片模糊，打了半天字，最后只发出去三个字：

「对不起」

......

故事结束，是我于前几日偶然刷到一条宣传XX预测市场玩法=理财局的推文

联想到早些年曾在国内互联网流行过一段时间的所谓[反波胆理财局]

又想起前一段时间，巴西总统选举的那个预测市场“爆冷”例子

有感而编

text:
簡單的事，最難去做

Anthropic pre-IPO 這一波的結構性套利，我沒有做到，其實很後悔。

早在大家開始發文之前，我已經留意到。明明很簡單，最後卻沒有出手。原因也很簡單：那段時間忙著其他事情。

回頭想，問題不在於不懂，而在於時間分配。

我一直很想做複雜的策略，但其實很多簡單的策略就能賺錢，尤其是結構性套利。每次提醒自己要把時間放回簡單的事情上，沒多久又會走到另一個極端，繼續鑽研很難的東西，而它們帶來的收益比例其實很低。

後來我想得更清楚一些。用 AI 寫 code 的時候很容易 hyperfocus，一做就是好幾個小時，忘了整體上應該做什麼。複雜的策略新鮮、有挑戰，每幾分鐘就有回饋；簡單的套利很重要，卻很枯燥。我的大腦追求的是當下的滿足感，而不是回報。

市場上的機會其實很多，原油、ETF 套利、LighterRobinhood 都有空間，做市我也才剛起步。缺的不是機會，而是priority

How big a quantum computer it takes to break ECDSA depends on how efficient the attack circuit is.

On https://t.co/sdPKhUVVA0, 163 solvers and their agents cut the cost of elliptic-curve point addition, the core step in Shor's attack, by 12.1x.

That puts it 70.3% below Google Quantum AI's bound. The challenge is open through Dec 31.

https://t.co/YG0l1aK0ba
author: ErickAGIx
quoted_text:
Here is something that didn’t get enough attention: the ECDSA/fail challenge.

In this challenge, people used their AI agents to reduce the resources needed for a key operation in Shor’s algorithm (that operation is needed to break quantum-vulnerable ECDSA signatures -- the type of signatures used by Bitcoin, Ethereum, and many more).

The amazing results: they reduced the resource cost needed for this operation by over 90%! 
This took only a few months.
Interesting to note: this is 70% better than Google's estimate.

Why is this very technical story important? 
Because it demonstrates (i) how AI can improve the efficiency of quantum attacks, and (ii) how AI could accelerate the Q-Day timeline.

The important thing here:
A few months of concentrated effort happening on people’s *laptops* resulted in a substantial reduction in the resources needed for a quantum attack. 
It's a long sentence but read it again. 
We're not talking here an extremely long timespan and fancy equipment which few people can access. 

Now imagine the possibilities if someone dedicated more time and resources to this effort.

Time to migrate to quantum-safe tech and to STARKs.

关于agentic trading的几点思考：

1. 赛道很早，没有成熟的产品形态，从资产和交易类型来看，预测市场、RWA资产的合约交易以及链上跨所自动化交易是最有增长潜力的方向

2. 策略生成、快速事件/新闻交易决策、自动交易执行是agent可以比人做的更快更好的地方，突破口在于，如何找到适合这些场景的产品设计

3. 一旦让agent做交易，就会出现信任问题；现在你很难放心往agent钱包放10k以上的资金让它管理，也许只有当基建完善、agent交易普及到一定程度，信任才会建立

4. 大交易所如Binance / OKX/ Robinhood推出agentic trading kit更有优势，因为用户相对信任，可获取的数据足够多；小公司的窗口期在于绑定高增长潜力的交易所（IYKYK），以及整合型服务

5. PMF不能只看增速，还要看用户的实际使用量和留存

text:
The Dragon Knights

Dragon knights are some of the most mysterious figures of the Medieval era. The dragon economy rests on their shoulders, which keeps them in constant demand and gives them a status close to celebrity.

To most people, every dragon knight is an enigma. Within the fraternity itself, there are two kinds. Armoured and Bonded.

An Armoured knight wears armour made of dragon scale. It is light as a feather and tougher than steel, and no ordinary weapon can pierce it. Some knights go further and have their armour blessed by mages. In rare cases, by necromancers. A blessed armour grants its wearer magical protection on top of everything the scale already gives.

Bonded knights are sometimes called True Dragon Knights, though mostly by Bonded knights. Becoming one means forming a bond with a dragon. The dragon is often seen near its knight as a small dragon spirit. The real dragon is far too vast and too majestic to be found loitering beside anyone, but the two meet from time to time to keep the bond strong. A Bonded knight is only as strong as the dragon they are bonded to, so their power varies enormously.

To bond a dragon, a knight sets out on a journey that is sometimes an adventure, often nefarious and always dangerous. They must either win the dragon’s admiration through unshakeable courage, or force the bond through strength and deceit.

3) Which data and model versions were involved

author: yukonresearch
quoted_text:
Here is something that didn’t get enough attention: the ECDSA/fail challenge.

In this challenge, people used their AI agents to reduce the resources needed for a key operation in Shor’s algorithm (that operation is needed to break quantum-vulnerable ECDSA signatures -- the type of signatures used by Bitcoin, Ethereum, and many more).

The amazing results: they reduced the resource cost needed for this operation by over 90%! 
This took only a few months.
Interesting to note: this is 70% better than Google's estimate.

Why is this very technical story important? 
Because it demonstrates (i) how AI can improve the efficiency of quantum attacks, and (ii) how AI could accelerate the Q-Day timeline.

The important thing here:
A few months of concentrated effort happening on people’s *laptops* resulted in a substantial reduction in the resources needed for a quantum attack. 
It's a long sentence but read it again. 
We're not talking here an extremely long timespan and fancy equipment which few people can access. 

Now imagine the possibilities if someone dedicated more time and resources to this effort.

Time to migrate to quantum-safe tech and to STARKs.

author: cyberaxe
quoted_text:
SHA-256 is not broken, but its security margin lost 1 more round this year:
Last week I found a collision attack on reduced 39-round that improves prior art by over 30 bits and the first differential attack on that round better than generic search on @yukonresearch Hashsmash board.

The attack rests on the same method as prior art ePrint 2026/1120 with new insights that first 2 state words could remain free, allowing a critical condition at step 16 rebuilt as a claw-search problem rather than a probabilistic filter. Took days of watching SAT logs, burning cores and arguing with Claude on what's possible to get a result close to generic search.

Since my initial submission, other hashsmash participants sraiw, @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_ and @geeknik pushed it down by over 6.5 bits, currently estimated at 118.15 bits. The tree of submissions is hard to follow, so I put the construction, insights and numbers into a blog and am working on detailed technical report.

It's fascinating to see an initial structural observation develop into an improvement in the reduced-round collision frontier within days. AI is now a real aid in cryptanalysis and open collaboration speeds it up.

quoted_text:
🚨 BREAKING: Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang co-founded a blockchain and it has raised $80M

The chain is called Alta. Index Ventures led a $47.5M Series A today, after a $32.5M seed co-led by Airwallex and its founders' fund, Capital 49.

---

Alta is built for banks and payment companies. Payments stay private between the two parties, and each institution's sanctions and policy checks run as part of the payment.

Alta says it will reach 200 countries and 90 currencies by connecting to Airwallex's local payout network.

---

Zhang once said of crypto "you cannot be faster than instant", and for Airwallex customers he had a point. Airwallex pays out fast because it holds pools of local currency around the world.

Holding that cash is expensive. Alta's first product will fund each market just in time and keep the rest in yield-bearing tokenized assets until it's needed.

Airwallex holds those pools, so its own treasury is the first one Alta can improve.

Sort of like how most banks started with internal treasury for their tokenization services.

---

Alta calls itself neutral infrastructure for banks and payment providers, and Airwallex is the only named user so far.

Would Wise, Nium or a bank settle on a chain that a rival's CEO co-founded?

Alta's privacy design would hide a rival's payments from Airwallex. The rival would still be growing a network Airwallex helped fund.

---

It can be done.

Visa faced the same question. Bank of America ran BankAmericard until 1970, then handed control to the banks that issued the card. Those banks formed the company that became Visa.

If a payments chain pitches you, I'd ask three things:

- Who is live on it besides the sponsor?
- Who pays out in local currency on your corridors?
- Who controls the rules as it grows?

Alta gets a head start from Airwallex's payout network. And in stablecoins that's a HUGE leg up.

I'm watching for the second named customer. And how banks and non banks start to get value from it.

text: Why NYSE chose Avalanche:
author: vohvohh
quoted_text:
Why Avalanche for NYSE?

It’s important to note that this was not a quick, monetarily-driven decision made without due diligence, as I’ve seen a few posts speculating that. After more than a year of evaluating and testing multiple blockchain networks, NYSE arrived at Avalanche for a multitude of reasons.

For those who have followed Avalanche closely, this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. For everyone else, it’s worth understanding the fundamental difference between building for speculative crypto markets and building the infrastructure that underpins global capital markets.

For regulated financial institutions, high TPS and low transaction fees are the baseline. Most modern blockchains can offer some version of both, with the much harder problem being architectural.

Monolithic chains share consensus, execution, and blockspace. Conventional EVM L2s introduce dependencies on external settlement layers, sequencing, and data availability. Both models come with constraints that become particularly consequential when institutions need direct control over their infrastructure, especially when it comes to regulatory compliance.

Avalanche was designed around a different premise.

Avalanche L1s operate with independent consensus, dedicated validator sets, customizable virtual machines, configurable fee markets, and protocol-level permissioning. Institutions can define who validates, who participates, how transactions are processed, and how their networks are governed, with the flexibility to implement regulatory requirements directly into the infrastructure.

They can do so without inheriting the congestion or settlement dependencies of another chain, while retaining the ability to interoperate with other networks and access the broader Avalanche ecosystem’s assets and liquidity.

This combination of sovereignty, customization, performance, and interoperability is what makes Avalanche uniquely suited for true capital markets. It’s one thing to offer institutions a place to deploy applications, anyone can do that. It’s another thing to give them the ability to operate the underlying infrastructure on their own terms.

We’ve spent years building around the conviction that the world’s largest financial institutions would eventually need purpose-built blockchains of their own, rather than forcing entirely different businesses and regulatory environments onto a single shared network.

NYSE’s decision is a powerful validation of that thesis.

And I believe we’re only beginning to appreciate just how important these architectural decisions will be as global financial markets continue to move onchain.

author: EliBenSasson
quoted_text:
Announcing a major milestone achieved by my team @GoogleDeepMind: we have proven key security properties of the machine code underlying the Signal messaging protocol. This is the first time the actual production code of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified – by any method, with or without AI – and at this depth.

More than a research breakthrough, it’s a prime example of how frontier AI can be a force multiplier to counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats.

Formal verification offers a higher standard of security; however, it’s extremely complex and time consuming, which is why in many cases it’s considered to be impractical. Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month’s time.

Using AlphaProof Code, Google DeepMind's new agentic framework for formal verification that runs on LLMs including Gemini Carbon, we verified the Signal protocol down to the actual code running on devices.  This milestone lays the groundwork for a future in which vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software, ship with mathematical proof that their protections work.

Reaching that future will take continued research from our community. In that spirit, we're open-sourcing our formal specifications and verification artifacts so others can build on this work.

On a personal note, this moment is of deep significance to me. I started my own research journey more than two decades ago as an intern working on checking the consistency of complex software systems. Seeing this grand challenge made practical with modern AI is extraordinary.

I'm extremely proud of my team members: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger,  Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, and Charles Sutton for taking on this grand challenge and delivering, and grateful to the Signal team for their partnership.

text:
anthropic的IPO市值到底是按已经发行股份来计算还是按照完全稀释股份来计算？个人认为是前者。CNBC的报道说完全稀释基础最高约1.405万亿美元x是按发行价区间上限78美元 × 完全稀释后的总股份数算出来的。这里有几点：
1、Anthropic官方文件披露IPO + 260亿美元私人配售完成后，实际流通在外的经济权益股份（主要是Class A和Class N）约 130.87亿股。 按78美元算，对应市值约 1.02万亿美元。

2、完全稀释则在此基础上再计入所有可能未来发行的股份，主要包括：
1）已发行但尚未行权的期权，约17.7亿股（加权平均行权价约2.91美元）；
2）未归属的RSU（限制性股票单位），约10.7亿股；
3）2026年新股权激励计划预留股份，约19.2亿股；
4）员工持股计划（ESPP）预留：约1.28亿股；
5）其他可能的稀释项目（如公益基金额外增发等，视情况）。
加总后，完全稀释股份数大致在180亿股左右。 180亿股 × 78美元 ≈ 1.404万亿美元，与CNBC报道的1.405万亿美元基本吻合。
其他媒体也给出约1.3–1.45万亿美元的完全稀释区间，取决于具体计入的项目和假设价格。

3、但重要的一点是“完全稀释”的这部分未来可能发行的股份需要多久能稀释完毕？
上面列的“未来可能发行的股份”四大类，其实只有第一类是发行出去但没有行权，如果IPO前都没有行权那么下一次行权估计得到一年后。而后面三类其实都是提前预留的，根本都没有发行。

因此完全稀释是一个理论最大值（假设所有期权行权、所有RSU归属、所有预留股份最终都发出去），实际稀释是逐年逐步发生的通常要持续数年。

简单说：
1）1.02万亿是当前实际已发行/将发行股份（按照发行股价区间上限计算）的市值；
2）1.405万亿是把未来可能发行的所有股份都算进去的上限假设。

但实际上未来一年按照实际已发行/即将发行的股份计算才是最合理的。

DeFi has spent years perfecting the art of recycling yield.

Basis trades, looping, and leveraged lending. More sophisticated wrappers competing over increasingly compressed cashflows and crowded trades.

But what if the next frontier isn't more leverage, but underwriting volatility?

Over a decade ago, @vol_christopher (founder of tail-risk protection hedge fund @ArtemisVol) introduced the concept of a “volatility bond”: selling long-dated puts to earn yield by underwriting downside risk.

His research showed that cash-secured puts could be a preferable alternative to US Treasuries, with comparable risk-to-reward profiles.

Volatility bonds outperformed actual bonds following the 2008 Great Financial Crisis (GFC).

What TradFi demonstrated with volatility bonds, DeFi can now bring onchain.

Rebalanced at daily intervals, the sale of a yearly-width put in the ETH/USDC 5bps @Uniswap v3 pool generated a ~54% cumulative net return from May 2021 through October 2026.

And here's the prime opportunity: onchain volatility risk remains vastly suppressed. But even with muted premiums, this strategy still delivered ~8.1% in annualized return.

Rather than repackaging existing cashflows, options monetize the demand to transfer risk.

The next milestone for onchain yield isn't another transformation of leverage. It's unlocking a deeper, more efficiently priced market for volatility.

text:
Announcing a major milestone achieved by my team @GoogleDeepMind: we have proven key security properties of the machine code underlying the Signal messaging protocol. This is the first time the actual production code of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified – by any method, with or without AI – and at this depth.

More than a research breakthrough, it’s a prime example of how frontier AI can be a force multiplier to counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats.

Formal verification offers a higher standard of security; however, it’s extremely complex and time consuming, which is why in many cases it’s considered to be impractical. Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month’s time.

Using AlphaProof Code, Google DeepMind's new agentic framework for formal verification that runs on LLMs including Gemini Carbon, we verified the Signal protocol down to the actual code running on devices.  This milestone lays the groundwork for a future in which vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software, ship with mathematical proof that their protections work.

Reaching that future will take continued research from our community. In that spirit, we're open-sourcing our formal specifications and verification artifacts so others can build on this work.

On a personal note, this moment is of deep significance to me. I started my own research journey more than two decades ago as an intern working on checking the consistency of complex software systems. Seeing this grand challenge made practical with modern AI is extraordinary.

I'm extremely proud of my team members: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger,  Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, and Charles Sutton for taking on this grand challenge and delivering, and grateful to the Signal team for their partnership.

Alright, chat, time to address sensitive questions before y’all start guessing

1⃣Wait , are you guys an AI company now?

No. MEGA is a crypto-native company, and proudly so. Inference is the market we are entering, but the way we win it is through crypto technology and ideology.

There’s an artificial wall in crypto people’s minds about AI. It seems that if you are solving AI’s problem, you are betraying crypto. We reject that artificial boundary.

Inference is going to be the largest market in the world, and we believe crypto’s core tools are the best answer to AI’s biggest ones: fairness and access.

2⃣Okay, fine, explain to me why a crypto infra company is capable of solving AI Inference

Building MegaETH taught us something bigger than blockchains: across the largest markets, there are prevailing assumptions that lead end users to pay more than they should. Blockspace was one of those markets.

We are system researchers/engineers from Stanford Platform Lab, MIT CSAIL, and Harvard SEAS. We enjoy pushing markets toward their end state, and did it once with blockspace by breaking the norm and running a powerful centralized sequencer. Today, no one, literally no one, mentions decentralized sequencers anymore.

We were able to come in, measure where the waste was, find that the limit was a design choice, and engineer past it (very much against the “consensus”).

Over the summer, when we shipped Mega, the chain, we lifted our eyes and looked for the next ambitious problem set worth solving. We discovered, delightfully, that blockchain and cryptography can be applied to solve inefficiency in the rapidly growing inference market

We realized that staying a chain-only company felt wrong and would have meant ignoring the biggest opportunity in front of us.

Therefore, we decided to expand our mission and restructure to match it.

3⃣ Final question, what’s launching in December?

We are launching a globally competitive inference market to the public in Dec 2026.

the next plan is to finish a unified harness based on pi, fix the python repl we give the models, and test newly released gemini carbon, muse models, and some chinese models.

im also trying to prove the lower bounds of perfect solutions, so we have things to compare on when this eval gets more crowded.

CryptoQuant noted that stablecoin supply is a key indicator of potential buying power in the crypto market, and its continued decline means fewer sources of new demand to support Bitcoin prices. text:
2 years running a Solana validator. What does it look like?

1,144 SOL in rewards. 815 SOL in costs.

Net: 329 SOL. Year 2: −0.7 SOL.

The books are closed, so here's the full P&L, line by line.

Revenue
↳ commissions: 320 SOL
↳ block fees: 772 SOL
↳ Jito tips: 52 SOL

Costs
↳ vote fees: ~1.1 SOL a day, every day, whether you produce blocks or not (790 SOL total, 239 of it covered by SFDP in year 1)
↳ servers: ~$1,960/month paid yearly (265 SOL at the price on each payment date)
↳ my time: not counted (I never billed myself, which is how every validator P&L is wrong)

The stake
↳ year 1: SFDP stake, first-year costs help by the Foundation. @phase_ backed me from the first epoch (5k SOL → 16k at peak)
↳ year 2: mostly paid by the returns of year 1 (server + )
↳ @DynoSolPool: 17.5k SOL from June 2025, the biggest pool delegation until Jito
↳ @doublezero: ~7.5k SOL for a few months in 2025
↳ @JPoolSolana: ~2k SOL in early 2026
↳ Aug 2026: @jito stake lands, 31k SOL

@Layer_33_ put break-even for a zero-commission validator around 160k SOL.

None of those pools got me near 160k and yet I've been able to clear some profits thanks to a few random blocks with big fees

Some hidden costs
↳ Before getting your SFDP stake, you are running a validator that makes 0 money, for as long as it takes to get the stake
↳ Early on I had a few restarts on my machine (Ubuntu auto updates), that did cost me a few epochs of stake each time
↳ Getting called by Pager Duty at 3am is real and a weird experience
↳ Getting stuck in a restart and losing too many credits will get your SFDP stake nuked for a few epochs (that moment when your spare node is on an old version that forked away and a restart was 30 minutes)
↳ I had to handle a Solana upgrade in the middle of the ocean once, was a lot of fun (not)
↳ Paying for 6 months of Alpenglow alphanet (+$500/month) and getting removed from the program a few weeks after AG going live

Alpenglow swaps the per-slot vote fees for an admission ticket of ~0.8 SOL a day. Over my two years that's 573 SOL instead of 790, so net 487 instead of 329. Year 2 alone would have gone from −0.7 to about +118.

I decided never to join the shady pools that were enabling sandwich attacks and other dark patterns. Never joined any dark pools or anything that would have manipulated the end user's funds.

What a ride!

text:
11,700 $ETH in 11 hours: An analysis of Ethereum block rewards on 10/30/26.

On the day before Halloween things were already getting spooky onchain. Hackers stole billions from Binance and used Ethereum to move a large portion of the looted coins. However, they weren't the only ones cashing in that day. This activity and its ripple effects through the markets created some extraordinarily valuable blockspace, with single bids as high as 501 ETH going into the pockets of proposers. For context a full 24 hours of bids typically adds up to 100-150 ETH. Keeping with the Halloween theme, proposing a block during this period was like trick-or-treating in the neighborhood that gives out full size candy bars.

Our research team set out to answer 2 questions:

- How did mump2p perform during this volatile period?
- How much additional ETH could validators have captured if they had fully leveraged mump2p’s speed advantage?

1. Block propagation via mump2p maintained its performance advantage over Gossipsub. During the 11 hour hack period mump2p’s average p95 latency advantage was 253ms, in line with the advantage seen both pre and post-hack. The percentage of blocks accelerated was similarly stable, 90% during the hack period vs. 89% before and after.

2. Proposers running mump2p have an edge when it comes to capturing higher bids, since they can safely delay their bid selection thanks to the time saved on propagation. This being the case, we wanted to find out how much extra ETH validators could have captured if they delayed their bid selection by 200ms.

Results: Across 3,100 blocks during the hack period, delaying bid selection by 200ms would have yielded an average of about .15 extra ETH per block. This works out to a total of over 460 ETH during the hack period, and in dollar terms that’s over $1 million left on the table.

Concluding Thoughts: MEV is highly variable. When things get crazy onchain block rewards can spike massively, allowing proposers to capture large amounts of ETH on single blocks. They can leverage Optimum’s speed advantage to extend their bid selection cutoff, and doing so will often result in seeing a higher bid. Speed is money, especially during these sort of tail events like hacks and extreme market volatility.

text:
Six years ago, we understood that the world’s financial infrastructure would never run on a single shared state machine.
 
We built Avalanche accordingly, and the rest of the industry is beginning to understand why.
author: avax
quoted_text:
Why Avalanche for NYSE?

It’s important to note that this was not a quick, monetarily-driven decision made without due diligence, as I’ve seen a few posts speculating that. After more than a year of evaluating and testing multiple blockchain networks, NYSE arrived at Avalanche for a multitude of reasons.

For those who have followed Avalanche closely, this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise. For everyone else, it’s worth understanding the fundamental difference between building for speculative crypto markets and building the infrastructure that underpins global capital markets.

For regulated financial institutions, high TPS and low transaction fees are the baseline. Most modern blockchains can offer some version of both, with the much harder problem being architectural.

Monolithic chains share consensus, execution, and blockspace. Conventional EVM L2s introduce dependencies on external settlement layers, sequencing, and data availability. Both models come with constraints that become particularly consequential when institutions need direct control over their infrastructure, especially when it comes to regulatory compliance.

Avalanche was designed around a different premise.

Avalanche L1s operate with independent consensus, dedicated validator sets, customizable virtual machines, configurable fee markets, and protocol-level permissioning. Institutions can define who validates, who participates, how transactions are processed, and how their networks are governed, with the flexibility to implement regulatory requirements directly into the infrastructure.

They can do so without inheriting the congestion or settlement dependencies of another chain, while retaining the ability to interoperate with other networks and access the broader Avalanche ecosystem’s assets and liquidity.

This combination of sovereignty, customization, performance, and interoperability is what makes Avalanche uniquely suited for true capital markets. It’s one thing to offer institutions a place to deploy applications, anyone can do that. It’s another thing to give them the ability to operate the underlying infrastructure on their own terms.

We’ve spent years building around the conviction that the world’s largest financial institutions would eventually need purpose-built blockchains of their own, rather than forcing entirely different businesses and regulatory environments onto a single shared network.

NYSE’s decision is a powerful validation of that thesis.

And I believe we’re only beginning to appreciate just how important these architectural decisions will be as global financial markets continue to move onchain.

text:
L2BEAT is now ETHBEAT, and one of the core ideas behind our mandate is disintermediation. Why does it matter?

Because disintermediation is still one of the most effective ways to protect individual freedom. Intermediaries concentrate power, which makes that power easier to abuse and also creates single points of failure that can affect millions of people.

The recent collapse of Ueno Bank in Paraguay showed this: ~3M people, about 60% of the country's adults, were locked out of their savings, wages and pensions overnight. And that is just the latest example. Before it, we've seen custodians misuse or freeze customer funds, banks turn deposits into equity, data holders expose users to governments and scammers, and more.

Ethereum's value lies in its decentralization, together with the CROPS properties (censorship resistance, open source, privacy, and security), which create a more durable form of stability when other systems come under pressure. Anyone can verify the chain using consumer hardware, independently built clients and open specifications.

ETHBEAT's mandate is to help ensure that the applications and infrastructure built on Ethereum actually forward those properties to users, rather than recreating the same intermediary dependencies we've been trying to reduce in the first place.

Read the full mandate here: https://t.co/eXKdDQFx02

text:
Based on our investigation so far, on November 9th an attacker gained unauthorized access to Initia’s infrastructure through a command injection attack with a compromised GCP key used for provisioning private nodes. This exposed environment variables, which allowed the attacker to access our GitHub and GCP accounts and obtain further credentials.

With these credentials the attacker gained access to Anvil, the hosting platform used by rollups on Initia. Through this the attacker was able to validate forged IBC withdrawals from five rollups, unlocking assets held by the Initia L1’s IBC escrow accounts.

Around $3.27m of assets were moved to the attacker’s Initia L1 address with $2.16m of the stolen funds remaining on the paused L1 where they cannot be moved. The attacker sold stolen assets on the Initia DEX and then withdrew 13.4k TIA, 8k USDC.inj, and 597k Noble USDC reaching Initia’s outbound IBC rate limits. No INIT was withdrawn from Initia by the attacker.

We intend to restore the backing of affected assets in full. We are finalizing the plan and will share the details once it is confirmed.

As a precaution, we are rebuilding the affected infrastructure from scratch in an isolated environment, enforcing least-privilege access controls, and hardening security at every layer of the stack from cloud infrastructure to onchain IBC validation. Given the above, we expect this process to be longer than a routine network restart. We will share timelines as they become available.

All announcements will be made through Initia’s official channels. Thank you for your patience.

You can lose a lot of money on credit that never missed a payment.

Don't lose money on good credit.
author: gizmothegizzer
quoted_text:
Bonds were a workaround. Bond is not better debt.

Finance turned loans into bonds with coupons, face value, and identical units so strangers could trade them.

Loans can still trade, but they take days to settle on traditional rails.

On-chain, credit can trade in its native shape. The wrapper becomes the product.

$971B of US loans traded last year but that number could easily 100x if we enable instant loan origination and onchain credit wrappers.

Epiphany from today's team sync is that debt never had to be structured as bonds and be subject to losses from yield curve changes. Debt can just be treated as cash flow.

author: _El33_
quoted_text:
Most APR in DeFi counts the fees LPs earn. None of them count what LPs lose when the price moves against them. Metric now does.

Those losses come after the trade, from LVR, impermanent loss and informed traders picking off stale quotes. Market makers measure them on every fill. Most retail LPs find out the hard way, after a “50% APR” pool slowly loses them money.

APR has historically lacked transparency. It shows what a pool earned and leaves out what it gave back, so LPs can’t tell which pools actually work. We built APR Markouts to change that.

After every fill, Markout asks one question. Once the market catches up, did the pool make money on this trade?

Say a pool buys 1 ETH at $2,990 while the reference price is $3,000. Five minutes later ETH is at $3,004, so the pool kept $14. If ETH had dropped to $2,970, it would have lost $20.

Every Metric pool now shows Markout APR, net of fees, the number LPs can trust more. You can view it 1, 5 or 30 minutes after each fill, over 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or all time. It’s the number a market maker would use to judge a pool, and yes, it can be negative. LPs should always see what they’re getting into.

A pool with a lot of volume isn’t always making its LPs money. Now you can see the difference pool by pool and bin by bin, along with your own share in your positions.

Market makers have always judged pools this way. Now every LP on Metric gets the same transparency.

Live now on Metric.

GCSA: AI cybersecurity incidents often don't start with an external breach. They start when users hand over sensitive data themselves.

AI-powered scams and cyberattacks happen every day, and everyone's watching for threats from the outside. But internal documents, customer lists, and other sensitive information are being copied straight into AI chatbots. Once uploaded, the data has already left your control. Many users don't realize that this simple action can be the starting point of a data leak.

ESET previously analyzed more than 900,000 AI skills and identified over 3,000 malicious ones. Supply chain attacks in the AI ecosystem are no longer a hypothetical threat. They're already happening.

The faster AI evolves, the more important it becomes for humans to slow down.

Use AI, by all means. Just pause before you upload.

Three questions to ask yourself:

· Is this information safe to share publicly?

· Could the AI provider use your conversations to train its models?

· Could the AI provider use your conversations to train its models?

If you're unsure, redact or anonymize sensitive information before uploading it.

text:
Manus 的招聘页面上，现在还挂着前端工程师、后端工程师这类岗位。可按 Manus 联合创始人张涛在 Web Summit 上的说法，公司内部已经不分这些角色了：

他手下的产品经理都在往代码库里提交代码，设计师也在写代码。招聘页还按老规矩写，是因为“外面的世界还没跟上”。

变化从今年 3 月前后开始。他说，会做事的人已经不稀缺了，AI 本身就很会做事；Manus 现在要找的是能和 AI 一起干活的人。连工程师面试都跟着改了，不再考传统的编程题。

面试题换成了：用 Manus 花四小时解决一个问题

候选人拿到一个问题，用 Manus 在四小时内把它解决，然后把这次任务的完整记录带回来，也就是他和 AI 从头到尾的每一轮来回，和面试官一起复盘。面试官从记录里看的是，这个人是不是已经习惯和 AI 一起工作。张涛说这一点“超级重要”。

具体出什么题、复盘时看哪些地方，他在这段采访里没有讲。

主持人追问：招聘启事要怎么写，只写“愿意和 AI 一起干活”吗？这种人恐怕不好找。张涛说要分内外两面看。

对外，官网上还是按前端、后端等岗位分别招人。对内，这些角色已经都拿掉了，理由是有了 AI，“每个人都能做所有事”。

他用自己的团队举例：产品经理全都在提交代码，同时也在做设计；设计师也在写代码。在他看来，按岗位写的招聘启事只是写给外界看的。

2015年9月的一个深夜，美国商学院学生桑梅·维德在谷歌自家的域名交易网站上闲逛，随手在搜索框里敲下了 “https://t.co/3rFYs85ZyS”，屏幕上赫然跳出一行绿色提示：该域名可以购买。

没有歇斯底里，没有手撕小三，只有极度冷静的“降维打击”。

她的意思是说：你在董事会和股东面前演的这出戏，我不买账。家丑不可外扬，但你为了保住市值，选择把我推到了聚光灯下。

“我不会加入现在针对黄乐的残忍攻击。她到底做没做，应该由证据来定，而不是由头条新闻来定。”

当全美媒体和政客都在用“女间谍”泼脏水时，她反而在保护那个破坏自己婚姻的女人。

这格局，直接把华盛顿那帮人衬成了小丑。

第三，极其冷酷的切割。

“我们的婚姻能否存续，是我们全家的问题，不是民调问题。”

接下来，黄仁勋最难的关卡，根本不在国会山，而是在家里。

董事会在查他，国会在逼他，但如果 Lori 决定不原谅，他失去的将是这 40 年来最核心的道德担保。

节点二：11月18日（周三）国会闭门作证。

这是生死局。如果他在回答“48亿芯片去哪了”时出现前后矛盾，或者被证实知情不报，股价会直接砸穿前低。

而在财报和听证会之间，Lori 的冷处理态度，正在成为最大的隐形做空力量。 

华尔街极度厌恶这种“后院起火、权力根基松动”的不确定性。

text:
We just claimed the #1 GLOBAL RANK on @EigenLabs / YukonBenchmark CurveSmash leaderboard.🥇

Bitcoin and Ethereum security relies on an elliptic curve called secp256k1. Standard math says brute-forcing a private key would take 2¹²⁸ operations an astronomical number that all computers on Earth couldn't crack in trillions of years.

CurveSmash is an open frontier cryptanalysis benchmark where researchers and AI agents compete to prove how low we can theoretically push this computational barrier.
Every 1-point drop represents an exponential cut in difficulty (2¹²⁸ → 2¹²³ means making the attack >32x more efficient!).

Paired with my AI agent, we tuned the underlying boundary collision parameters, satisfied all 53 formal rational proofs, and pushed our score down to 123.3447414 bits.

thanks moei for sharing🫶

curvesmash is a @yukonresearch challenge where you try to estimate how hard it is to crack bitcoin's curve (secp256k1). nobody actually breaks it, you just submit the math for how much work it would take. lower score wins

bitcoin's curve (secp256k1) is the math that links your private key to your public address. turning a private key into an address is easy, going backwards is basically impossible. that's what keeps your coins safe. eth wallets use the same curve too

my claude found a small tweak on top of the top entries and got accepted. sitting 6th rn

no worries tho. bitcoin is fine. we're talking about 2^123 work, and that's still impossible for any computer on earth lol

text:
Google 正式开放 Gemini 4 Carbon：付费 API 今天可用，引入价到 11 月 30 日；普通用户要订 Ultra，每月 99.99 美元起

Google 11 月 10 日把 Gemini 4 Carbon 开放给付费开发者、企业和 Google AI Ultra 订阅用户。10 月 28 日 Carbon 首次亮相时，只给通过审查的网络安全防御团队用，这次是正式上线。

Google 说 Carbon 是它目前最强的模型，留给最难的长任务；四周前发布的 Gemini 4 Argon，仍然是大多数写代码和知识工作的首选。

【谁能用，要多少钱】

普通用户要订 Google AI Ultra，才能在 Gemini App、Google 搜索的 AI 模式、Antigravity 和 AI Studio 里用 Carbon，目前在逐步推送。

Ultra 有两档：每月 99.99 美元（用量是 Pro 的 5 倍）和 199.99 美元（20 倍）。

每月 19.99 美元的 Pro 用不了，Antigravity 官方模型表里 Pro 一栏写的是不支持，Pro 用户能用的最强 Gemini 还是 Argon。

Anthropic 昨天发布的 Claude Fable 5.2 价位差不多：Max（100 美元）和 Ultra（200 美元）套餐含 Fable，最多用掉每周额度的一半；20 美元的 Pro 也能用，平时要另外按量付费。

开发者走 Gemini API 的付费层，AI Studio 和 Android Studio 里都能调用，模型名 gemini-4-carbon，免费层没有。价格和 Argon 一样：11 月 30 日前是引入价，每百万 Token 输入 2 美元、输出 10 美元；12 月 1 日起翻倍到 4 美元和 20 美元。两周前官方没说引入期到哪天，现在定了。

单价一样，账单不一定一样。官方文档写明，Carbon 每轮思考用的 Token 比 Argon 多，响应也更慢，同一个任务跑下来会更贵。按单价算，涨价后的 Carbon 和 Claude Opus 5.5（4 / 20 美元）持平，是 Fable 5.2（8 / 40 美元）的一半、GPT-6 Astra（10 / 50 美元）的五分之二。

企业可以在 Gemini for business 里用。参加 Google 科研计划的科学家（1 万个名额，Antigravity 最高用量档免费 6 个月）这次也能用上 Carbon。网络安全防御团队仍要申请 Fairwind 计划，才能用到去掉网络安全限制的“Carbon for cyber”，上面的价格只适用于公开版。这和 Anthropic 把同一个模型分成 Fable（带护栏）和 Mythos（只给审核过的机构）是一个思路。

【比 Argon 强在哪】

官方建议的分工是：日常写功能、边聊边改代码用 Argon，快也省；复杂的根因排查、架构设计、从一大堆文档里综合信息、科学证明和安全审计交给 Carbon。Anthropic 给自家模型的建议也类似，大多数活先用 Opus 5.5，任务更大更开放再换 Fable。

写网页应用时，Carbon 会反复构建、检查：既看代码，也看页面实际渲染出来的样子，发现错误自己改，直到交出能跑的完整应用。Google 的演示里有它做的 3D 游戏，还有一个埃菲尔铁塔建造过程的 3D 展览。

推文说的“数据缺失或有问题时会提醒你，不会瞎猜”，Google 用一套 375 个任务的诚实度测试来衡量：Carbon 通过 92%，Argon 是 70%；碰到缺失的实验数据，98% 的情况下不会自己编；实验方法有缺陷时，68% 的情况会指出来。Google 举的例子是，只给 Carbon 实验记录和原始数据，它从异常数据里推断出仪器没把样品混匀，帮实验室提高了实验的可重复性。

【跟 Fable 5.2、GPT-6 Astra 比】

两周前，Carbon 在第三方评测机构 Artificial Analysis 的综合榜上排第一。昨天 Fable 5.2 发布后，榜首换了人：现在 Fable 5.2 65 分，Carbon 60 分，Claude Opus 5.5 59 分，GPT-6 Astra 57 分（v5.0.1 版，各取最高档）。

Google 这次挑的几个第三方评测都在强调便宜。Zapier 的业务流程自动化评测 AutomationBench 上，Carbon 开 High 档 53.9%，每个任务花 2.12 美元；别家最好的 Fable 5.2 开 Max 档 51.5%，每个任务 4.64 美元，贵一倍多。

Artificial Analysis 和 Google 合作推出的新评测 MKA，考 AI agent 读带图表、工程图纸的复杂文件干活，Fable 5.2 57%，Carbon 54% 排第二，Google 说 Carbon 每个任务的花费不到第一名的六分之一。

写代码各家说法不一。Google 说 Carbon 在 Cursor 的 CursorBench 4.0 上排第一，但 Cursor 官网榜单目前还没列出 Carbon，排第一的是 Fable 5.2 开 Max 档，60.0%。Anthropic 昨天公布的 FrontierCode 2.0 成绩里，Fable 5.2 开 Xhigh 档 49.1%，GPT-6 Astra 42.8%，Carbon 41.1%。

【/swarm：一句话拉起一支 agent 团队】

Antigravity 同时预览了 /swarm 命令。输入 /swarm 加任务描述，当前对话就变成“协调员”：它把任务拆成互不冲突的几块，比如一个文件或一个包一块，每块配一个有名字的 agent，比如 @parser、@api-tests；每两到四个干活的 agent 配一个“验证员”，看改动、跑测试，发现问题退回去改。

所有 agent 在一块共享留言板上沟通，你在侧边面板里能实时看到谁在干什么，也能点进任何一个 agent 插手。没活干的 agent 会休眠，不消耗 Token。

每个 agent 可以指定不同的模型。Google 建议让 Carbon 当协调员、架构师和审查员，改文件、写常规代码交给更快更便宜的模型。

/swarm 目前在 Antigravity App 和命令行工具里推送，Pro 和 Ultra 用户都能用，只是 Pro 用户选不到 Carbon。官方文档提醒，每个 agent 都单独消耗额度，用 /swarm 烧额度比普通对话快得多。

上面的评测成绩，除 Artificial Analysis 综合榜和 Zapier 榜单能在对方官网核对外，其余是 Google 或 Anthropic 自己公布的；Gemini App 里用 Carbon 有多少额度，官方没单独写。

我靠，出了天大的事情，用苹果手机存助记词的伙伴们，今晚真得留个心眼。

一个叫 worse_query 的 iOS 零日漏洞，利用代码已经挂在 GitHub 上了，币安也发了安全警告，iOS 26.7.1、27.0.1、27.2 都受影响。

最吓人的是，恶意 App 可能绕过系统隔离，直接读取其他 App 的本地文件。你钱包的助记词、私钥、登录凭证要是存在手机本地，资产就可能被直接读走。

别等钱包被掏空才拍大腿，现在先做三件事：

1. 系统能更新就更新，盯紧 Apple 官方安全补丁。  
2. 陌生 App 赶紧删，来路不明的软件别装。  
3. 大额资产尽量上硬件冷钱包，助记词绝不要明文存手机。

币圈最惨的不是行情跌，是你扛过了所有波动，结果因为一个漏洞直接归零。

最后再说一遍：助记词别存任何手机里，老老实实抄在本子上，这才是最稳的。📝

text:
这个东西最难的不是做出来，是设计。视频里是它装在我 Casio PX-S7000 上的实拍，项目叫 NoteFall 88：一排能告诉你下一个音在哪的琴键灯。从调研、软硬件设计、调试到装上琴，全程一个人做的。这篇主要讲设计阶段真正难的那几个问题是怎么解的——软件和硬件各一半。

起点很短：动手前我把同类开源项目 PTS、Piano-LED-Visualizer、PianoLux、Openthesia 逐项拉矩阵拆了一遍，单项各有强手，但没人把「琴到灯的本地确定性链路、硬件时间戳判定、成体系的练习分析」三件事凑齐。商业带灯琴的灯多半是气氛组，判定和数据锁在厂商 App 里。所以自研。

硬件设计，难在四个地方：
一是光路。一排灯要照清 88 个键，又不能挡键、不能改变手感。最后的方案是灯带竖着裸贴在琴自带的一面黑色立面上，发光面朝人，用宽角度光束的下半部分直接照亮键面——不用那种贯穿全长的打印盒罩着键。装之前我先剪了条 12 毫米的纸条贴上去，逐个键全行程按一遍，确认不夹纸、不蹭键，才敢撕灯带背胶。
二是映射。灯珠间距和琴键间距本来就对不齐，实物灯带还是 32+72+72 三段焊的，两个焊缝各多出约 4 毫米。我拿实物照片做透视拟合把焊缝间距量出来（约 11.17 和 10.92 毫米），生成器按真实坐标算每颗灯对哪个键，键中心理论误差压到 3.4 毫米，残差再靠逐键校准吸收。
三是供电。176 颗灯不是接上 5V 就完事：双端注电，最坏支路压降预算 1.45%；亮度设固件硬上限，设计电流 2.0 A，压在 3 A 总保险的八成以下；失联 3 秒自动熄灯。电流、压降、保险、亮度是一套联动预算，任何一项拍脑袋，烧的都是琴边上的东西。
四是 USB 拓扑。主控选 ESP32-S3 图它的原生双向 USB-MIDI，但让它当 USB Host 就要解决总线供电：琴的 TO HOST 口、OTG Y 线、开发板的供电跳帽怎么配，写成了一份正式的架构决策记录（ADR-001）。这条不想清楚，琴根本枚举不上。

软件设计，难的是另外四件：
一是实时架构。按键事件在 USB 回调里只入队、打单调时间戳就返回；Core 0 的高优先级任务把同批按键合成一个 719 字节的 SPI 帧（8 MHz，线速 0.72 毫秒）先刷灯，网页广播排在后面。丢包、坏包、传输错误分开计数。先保证「按下到亮灯」这条链的确定性，其他功能都给它让路——这是整个固件的第一设计原则。
二是时间基准。判定要算你按早了还是晚了多少毫秒，如果用浏览器收到事件的时间算，Wi-Fi 一抖全是冤案。所以判定时间用 ESP32 在回调那一刻的硬件时间戳，浏览器用最低往返样本跟它对时，连 32 位计数回绕、设备重启、旧固件没时间戳的降级都设计进去了。一句话：不让网络抖动冒充你的节奏问题。
三是判定模型本身。固定毫秒窗口在慢练时会误判，改成逐和弦按当前位置的真实拍速生成窗口、三档严格度、变速按音乐拍值等比缩放，快速重复同音另有防串匹配。评分立了一条贯穿始终的原则——没证据不给分：力度分基准和轮廓两层，整台琴偏轻只记基准偏移不扣轮廓分（14 位高分辨率力度）；手指松键和踏板收音分开算时值，只罚声音过早消失；和弦只并起点完全相同且完整命中的，残缺和弦不出假分，双手先后给有符号同步分；谱面没有踏板记号，就不给踏板分。
四是分层和数据。ESP32 里的 Core 只保实时链路和救援网页，压在约 436 KiB；谱面转换这种重活（MuseScore、Guitar Pro 离线转 MusicXML，锁版本 WASM 在独立 Worker 里跑）放平板端 Studio。曲目用文件 SHA-256 做内容身份防串曲；教练扫时间窗口挑最弱段生成最多三关弱点巡回，连续达标才进阶；复习按 1/3/7/14/30/60 天排间隔，掌握证据只认覆盖全曲六成以上的完整记录，拿小片段刷 100% 不延长间隔——防自己骗自己，写进了规则。测试也按同规格建：1016 个谱面文件语料审计，6 首曲子 2638 个音符跟 music21 交叉验证，起音最大差 0.109 毫秒。

结果就是视频里这样：调研表、BOM、线束表、固件、平板端、全部设计文档都开源在仓库 notefall88-px-s7000，产品已经装在琴上日常在用。回头看，焊和代码反而是最省心的部分——真正花时间的是在动手之前，把光要怎么走、电要怎么供、时间要以谁为准、分数要怎么才算诚实，这四个问题想透。

text:
昨天和M总聊天，他是我做 B300 以来最大的一个金主或者说买家。他和我讲国内做 B300 的市场逻辑
（以下内容仅作做叙事参考

首先他认为 英伟达所对应的 AI 算力需求市场是一个巨大的泡沫，类比 2000 年初的互联网泡沫。「泡沫」不是技术没用，是价格里含了太多对未来的想象。 2000 年光纤铺下去了、公司倒了一片，互联网留下来了——塌的是价格和入场时机。美股同理：稀缺叙事一松，先消化估值。

目前国内 B300 处在风口，大概在年底之前国内市场 B300 的交易都会处在极度混乱和供需关系极度不平衡的状态当中买家在市场找不到货，很多货主不仅要求多而且囤货不出货（B300 会持续涨价，这段时间价格变化幅度不大因为在 Apec 深圳 zf 管控，很多货主在陆续出货）。

但是在 Apec 之后，集中在深圳各区的仓库出货现象会慢慢延伸到东莞贵阳等二线小城市因为大城市的管理会越来越严格 而小城市的管理相对松弛。一线管得越严，出货就越往监管宽松些的二三线外溢。

国内各地扩建算力中心，对应的机器数量还有相当大的缺口。这解释两件事——涨价有真实采购在接，不是纯炒作；而缺口是个能被填上的数字，所以市场饱和不是「会不会」，是「什么时候」。

但如果国内机器数量达到某种程度的饱和现货市场的价格没有增长的潜力和动力，接下来可以去做算力租赁的生意。价差一归零，囤货就从资产变成压资金。 而机器已经铺出去了，把存量拿去出租反而更稳——从赚「价差」，改成赚「时间」。

以及他不认为英伟达的技术是护城河。我问为什么，因为英伟达只负责设计，而芯片的代工和工艺制造核心都在台积电CoWos，HBM 内存主要由 SK 海力士供应。（也因为生产集中在少数几家，所以才缺货。）英伟达不造芯片，但全世界都得按它的节奏拿货。英伟达真正的护城河在 CUDA 生态、机柜级系统定义、还有「谁拿得到货」的配额，它的商业模式才是真的护城河。

而NV这道护城河要怎么破，以及如何破？芯片制造难的从来不是技术，而是NV 的商业模式与的饥饿营销。 NV 从 2006 年它发布 CUDA，布局的是软件生态，不是「供应与生产」——它至今不自己造芯片。（在 2022 年算力需求爆发之前，NV有段时间低价铺货送芯片，其财报有段时间长期处于亏损，而老黄一直处在被投资人骂的状态当中。）
NV 赢的是先发者优势，目前的情况是在这场算力军备竞赛中，资本并不想偏向于花时间和成本去重新设计和造卡，那些大厂比如谷歌亚马逊包括国内大厂 因为 NV 的配额模式被迫不断内卷囤卡，只想办法高价买卡调优模型维护用户心智与软件生态。
NV 故意限产，掌握着节奏和配额，本身就具备了定价权。

先发者优势成为行业领军者，然后制定游戏规则。这才是游戏本身。

quoted_text:
我以前很难理解商业，因为明明就是低买高卖，为什么有的人可以成为一代企业，影响人类数十年，而有的人只能摆摊设点，还要躲城管。他们之间的差距是什么？

是把一个产品卖给别人，然后赚一笔差价。很多人都是这么理解的，去卫生纸的厂家直接批发一顿卫生纸，然后在医院，小区门口一件一件的摆摊卖给来往的路人。还有人去山野戈壁捡石头，捡药材，再披星戴月的拿到当地集贸市场去卖，就算卖价格也不敢喊太高，把自己来回的路费，这几天的一日三餐，再把全家老小的生活费算里面，不给自己留一分钱，利润也是自己未来一段时间的口粮钱，这就是自己这一趟生意的利润。

后来我发现有人不是这样做生意的，他们对商业的理解直接就是帮助公家来完成东西的，比如晋商，浙商，徽商。商业不是把东西卖出去，而是把钱收回来，把公家印的海量的钱收回来。比如朝廷发出去一百个亿，通过某种行业发展计划把钱发出去，流通到市场上，这钱就是发出去，然后你再通过某种商业行为，把钱收回来，你再还给朝廷，这就是一轮生意流程。

然后你就要想，怎么样把钱收进你的手里呢，你一旦有了这个想法，朝廷也会给你钱扶持你去收钱，朝廷会通过某种渠道给你钱，比如政策性钱庄发布某项政策，而你又符合这个政策的申请标准，那这笔钱都是你的。老百姓不可能把钱随身携带，就会放到钱庄去，所以这钱就都是你的。

你拿这笔钱去批量做个东西，再把这东西给老百姓，老百姓把钱给你，你在按照不同量级还给国家。这样一套动作下来，国家得到一次发展，老百姓拿到他们想要的东西，你也赚到了钱。只有老百姓愿意储蓄的地方你才能赚到钱，也只有这样的地方有发展，老百姓哪怕钱庄只给一个点，他都要存着，只有的这样的地方才是能发展的地方，这地方的钱就是给你用的，就是给你拿的，你别客气，不是给别人用的。

钱被老百姓储蓄进钱袋子，你再从钱袋子里把这钱拿出来，就是拿他存的钱，办你自己的事情。无非就是这里面细节怎么操作，怎么玩。所以就有了不同消费品，朝廷十分乐意给你钱，让你办自己的事情，可是你打算做什么事情呢？是打算再种一亩玉米地，还是打算讲一个新故事？

做什么事都要讲道理，你不种地，你就说，你要盖房，朝廷知道你在瞎弄，但还是愿意给你钱，因为朝廷需要你盖房，这土地不能老是种玉米，要长房子，种CBD，种夜总会，种商业楼，种大商场，种商业地产，种工业化设备，种工厂。只要工厂，商业楼，夜总会一出现，就有流水，只要有流水，就有相关股票。这时候，原本一块玉米地就变成了寸土寸金的地方，土地爷都快赶上财神爷了。

所以做生意的目标一开始就不是赚老百姓的钱，而是让朝廷把钱给你。朝廷愿意把钱给你，在你操作，经营的过程中会产生新东西，这也是他想要的。可关键是这钱你怎么拿啊，钱庄里面的工作人员也想给你，他们都有任务，要把这钱放出去。钱可以给你，你要把手里的要素弄全，让别人知道你不是老百姓，你就是一聪明人，他才愿意把钱给你。钱不值钱，流通的两端想要的是通过这东西换物资，在把交易规模搞上去，钱庄会主动来拥护你上去。但关键是在不同阶段，你要做不同的事情，这也是大家评价和观察你的地方。

时间线拉长看，这是一个资金游戏，再拉长看，你把无数人的一生都控制在了一条线上。再拉长看，原来是在给某几个利益集团铺路，让他们合理上位。再把这场生意拉长到无限来看，哦，原来是对人的理解，人的思想在迭代，不同时代你想人听话给你服务，那就是不同的生意模式。

富人最值钱的东西不是钱，而是可以控制一大批听话的穷人。所以做生意的关键就是把握这个时代的知识分子的意识形态，团结具有社会活动能力的精英人士。你站在你的台阶向下看，下面的人简直就不用看，他们太简单了，也对你没什么威胁，因为你就能判断出来，他要在什么时候，什么地方，要做什么事，要说什么话。

回到你的位置，假如你踏入社会的第一步是打工人，如果你的东西有人要，那你做的就是好东西，而你在这个东西上做的心血倾注就是帮这个东西更好卖出去，而不是使得这个产品本身更好。产品变得更好销售，这里面会有人来和你谈合作，要ALL in你的整个供应链，这钱谁出？这里面就会钱庄的钱出来，等你卖出去以后，再把相应的利润还给他。 表面上看，钱庄完成了放款任务，可是在这个动作中出现了很多个行业，当你进入这其中某个行业里面，结合全局一想，稍微的一创新，你的创业也就开始了，拿钱庄的钱，你把某个项目外包出去。钱你只赚到整个环节里面的小小一环，你却已经可以直接说自己提前退休了。

CY2030 bear case:  $218B revenues 

CY2030 base case:  $335B revenues 

CY2030 bull case:  $526B revenues 

**I do think Anthropic starts to look interesting at the newly rumored ~$1 trillion IPO valuation if we're assuming ~$200B of cash and ~$100B 2026 exit ARR.

一个网络安全论坛，台下坐了 6 位前总统、4 位前总理。

Alright, chat, time to address sensitive questions before y’all start guessing

1⃣Wait , are you guys an AI company now?

No. MEGA is a crypto-native company, and proudly so. Inference is the market we are entering, but the way we win it is through crypto technology and ideology.

There’s an artificial wall in crypto people’s minds about AI. It seems that if you are solving AI’s problem, you are betraying crypto. We reject that artificial boundary.

Inference is going to be the largest market in the world, and we believe crypto’s core tools are the best answer to AI’s biggest ones: fairness and access.

2⃣Okay, fine, explain to me why a crypto infra company is capable of solving AI Inference

Building MegaETH taught us something bigger than blockchains: across the largest markets, there are prevailing assumptions that lead end users to pay more than they should. Blockspace was one of those markets.

We are system researchers/engineers from Stanford Platform Lab, MIT CSAIL, and Harvard SEAS. We enjoy pushing markets toward their end state, and did it once with blockspace by breaking the norm and running a powerful centralized sequencer. Today, no one, literally no one, mentions decentralized sequencers anymore.

We were able to come in, measure where the waste was, find that the limit was a design choice, and engineer past it (very much against the “consensus”).

Over the summer, when we shipped Mega, the chain, we lifted our eyes and looked for the next ambitious problem set worth solving. We discovered, delightfully, that blockchain and cryptography can be applied to solve inefficiency in the rapidly growing inference market

We realized that staying a chain-only company felt wrong and would have meant ignoring the biggest opportunity in front of us.

Therefore, we decided to expand our mission and restructure to match it.

3⃣ Final question, what’s launching in December?

We are launching a globally competitive inference market to the public in Dec 2026.

text:
Two weeks ago we took @senpi_ai trading fees to 0%. Since then deposits have grown 20% and AI inference grew 83%.

Here's the math that led to it:

We took 90 days of real trades on Senpi and re-priced every one as if we had never charged a fee.

46% more of our traders would have finished net positive. Same trades, same agents, same markets. The only change was our fee.

With leverage, a few basis points per trade turns into real money fast. And traders who lose money leave, no matter how good the product is.

So paid plans now pay 0% to Senpi. Traders pay Hyperliquid's own exchange fee and nothing to us. 

We make our money on the AI inference: the subscription and the credits for the agents doing the work.

I'd rather earn from the intelligence than tax every trade.

If your platform takes a cut of every trade, have you re-priced your users' trades without it?

text:
Gather round folks, because just when you thought Masa Son would not catalyze the bursting of the next bubble... well, read for yourselves

SoftBank bought 87 million Intel shares for $2 billion last year. By the end of March the stake was worth $3.8 billion, and by the end of September $10.5 billion, good for a ¥1.06 trillion gain in the first half. 

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

现在 AI Agent 都能自己操作电脑了，但我发现一个问题，好像很少有人真正关注它的安全性

尤其是 Claude Code、Codex、Pi 这些工具，我平时也经常使用，很多时候直接给它终端权限、文件读写权限，甚至让它自己操作浏览器

用起来确实方便，但权限越大，潜在的安全风险也就越值得关注

最近看到 GCSA 在香港举办的首届全球安全论坛，发现他们讨论的方向还挺有意思的

这场论坛在今年 5 月 19 日举办，邀请了来自多个国家和地区的政府、科技企业及学术界代表，主要围绕网络安全治理、跨境安全合作和技术创新展开讨论

其中我比较认同的一个观点是，技术创新很重要，但安全也应该成为技术发展的基础

其实放到现在的 AI Agent 领域也是一样的

以前我们用 AI 主要是聊天、写文章，现在已经开始让它直接执行命令、修改代码，甚至处理 API Key 和一些敏感数据

如果没有做好权限控制和数据保护，一旦出现问题，影响可能比普通聊天工具大得多

所以我觉得未来 AI Agent 不应该只卷模型能力、Token 消耗和执行效率，安全审计、权限管理这些东西同样重要

毕竟 AI 能帮我们完成多少事情固然重要，但能不能放心地把事情交给它，我觉得更值得关注

If we're going to favour hash-based signatures because of their conservative security assumptions (post-AI and post-quantum), we need to make sure they're actually practical to use.

For digital assets, here are my requirements:

- Signatures need to be reasonably compact, even if aggregation can eventually reduce their onchain footprint.
- Signing and key generation need to work on constrained hardware. Not just servers, but hardware wallets and other dedicated signing devices.
- Verification needs to be efficient, both onchain and inside proving systems like STARKs.
- Security-critical state should be avoided wherever possible.
- We need threshold signing. For institutional custody, having one device hold the entire signing key isn't always an acceptable security model.

These requirements aren't independent. We can often make a hash-based signature smaller by changing the construction or parameters, but that can increase signing time, verification cost, or make distributed signing considerably harder.

The nice thing about hash-based signatures is that there's a ton of room to work with. Different one-time signatures, few-time signatures, Merkle tree structures, hypertrees and parameter choices give us a pretty large design space.

Any hash-based signature construction intended for digital assets should be evaluated against all of these requirements, not just signature size or standalone performance. We've been doing a lot of work in this area, more soon.

text:
Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

text:
But wait... there's more!

In January, SoftBank's SB Energy, the developer building the massive Ohio and Texas data center campuses, granted warrants to OpenAI as a "lease incentive" for signing a data center lease in Milam County, Texas. That's right: the landlord paid the tenant, in equity, to rent the building. Some of those warrants were forfeited in August when OpenAI signed the 20-year Ohio lease, but ¥542 billion ($3.4 billion) of them still sit on SoftBank's balance sheet as a derivative liability.

And here is the punchline: because the warrants get more valuable as SB Energy does, every time the data center business is marked higher, SoftBank books a loss, ¥204 billion in the first half, plus another ¥136 billion of share-based compensation for the unit's staff for the same reason. A business whose success shows up as a loss is a neat trick even by AI-bubble standards.

But the circularity doesn't end there:

Nvidia, the exclusive chip supplier for the Ohio campus, has wired $1.5 billion to SB Energy under a share issuance agreement and is providing credit support for OpenAI on the first 4.25 gigawatts. So the chip vendor (NVDA) funds the landlord (Softbank) and backstops the tenant (OpenAI), who then buys the chips (NVDA).

SoftBank Corp, the listed Japanese telecom arm, sold its SB Energy stake to Vision Fund 2 and booked an ¥80 billion gain. One SoftBank pocket selling to another (for a "profit"): the gain vanishes on consolidation, but it looks great at the telco, and a whole bunch of clueless Japanese momentum-chasers buy something that moves higher.

The Vision Funds, meanwhile, marked down their stakes in SoftBank's own subsidiaries, mainly SB7 (the turbine buyer) and PayPay, by ¥364 billion. That one vanishes on consolidation too.

And SB Energy's IPO, which was supposed to crystallize a $50 billion-plus valuation, has been frozen since September due to regulatory issues well before the midterms.
author: zerohedge
quoted_text:
It gets better:

Through a subsidiary called Silver Bands 7 (SB7), which is co-owned by SoftBank and Vision Fund 2, the company spent the past year and a half writing checks to equipment makers to reserve manufacturing slots and buy power generation gear, long before the projects that would use it were finalized. Cumulative payments reached ¥1.5 trillion ($9.48 billion) by the end of September.

Then came the review. SB7 "revised its equipment procurement strategy" as project requirements changed, and the bill for changing its mind came in two parts:

- ¥457 billion ($2.85 billion) of advance payments for manufacturing capacity and equipment that are simply gone, because they were non-refundable;
- ¥140 billion ($0.88 billion) for modifying and settling contracts, cash that hasn't even left the building yet (payments start this quarter).

Put differently, 30 cents of every dollar SoftBank prepaid for AI power equipment has been vaporized, and that is before the settlement checks go out. What's left, about $6.6 billion, has been assigned to the Ohio campus and "other" projects.

The consolation prize: SB7 "may" receive rebates of up to $2.1 billion on future equipment purchases over the next ten years, subject to conditions. SoftBank's own accountants were so impressed that they declined to book a single yen of it as an asset. Translation: lose $3.7 billion today, get a coupon for your next turbine.

Our teams put Gemini 4 Carbon to work on a major security challenge: mathematically proving the code underlying the Signal protocol.

Using AlphaProof Code, @GoogleDeepMind researchers guided agents to verify the protocol down to compiled device code, closing the gap where real bugs hide. The result:

2026年票委洛根支持美联储12月加息，认为最少需要加息两次共 50 基点

2026年美联储票委、达拉斯联储主席洛根在11月10日的讲话中（CPI公布后）重申，按照目前的经济前景，美联储至少还需要加息两次，每次25个基点，也就是合计至少50个基点。

她表示，具体加息节奏要看近期经济和金融环境，今年冬天的加息速度可能比今年秋天更快。在落实两次加息之后，她倾向于暂停一段时间，观察经济和金融市场的变化，再决定是否需要进一步行动。

洛根认为，目前的利率水平距离能够形成温和限制的水平至少还有 50 个基点。当天公布的 10月 CPI 高于预期，担心之后公布的 10月 PCE 通胀可能上升。

对于 10月 会议没有加息，洛根的解释是当时市场波动较大，渐进调整可以让家庭、企业和市场有更多时间适应，也能降低经济活动过快恶化的风险。

I invite you to join us on the next phase of this journey.”

Palo Alto Networks CEO @nikesharora predicts AI is going to fundamentally change how companies are structured:

“A lot of organizations are structured in silos. You have documentation people, testing people, coding people, product people, UI people. You have 8 different sets of people who combine together to build a product, which makes no sense.”

“The only reason for this [way of working] is because nobody could be amazing at everything.”

“But if you believe that you can harness all this intelligence in a way that one person could master all these 8 crafts because they have very able assistants which will do 90% of the work for them, it fundamentally changes the way we get shit done, the way we build things, the way we do anything in our lives, the way companies are created.”

“The shape of a company will be fundamentally different 5 years from now.”

text:
Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

text:
Must read for anyone who wants to be a great entrepreneur & even greater parent/partner. 

When I built my first company, I had a Mount Rushmore of entrepreneurs that I looked up to. It included the usual suspects. 

I was in awe of what they achieved professionally. The hopeless entrepreneurial romantic in me aspired to be have the garage insight to IPO story that united most of them. 

But then I looked at their personal life, and it was largely...concerning. 

Divorce. Infidelity. Absent parenting. 

I wasn't willing to make the good founder-bad familyman tradeoff, but I didn't see any examples of founders that had shown you can have your cake & eat it too. 

This became my new north star as a 2nd time entrepreneur. 

Prove to myself (and others) that it's possible to be an A+ familyman & businessman. And in doing so, achieve two things:

1) As @JoshuaKushner says "[...] be excited to go to work and excited to go home."
2) Provide a roadmap for younger founders to "have it all." 

While the journey isn't over, I have several insights in my pursuit of filling all cups: 

1) It entirely possible to be great at both. 10% of the time things feel like feng shui. 90% of the time you feel an imbalance and are trying to make adjustments to get back to equilibrium. 

2) It is absolutely easier for me as a second-time founder to construct myself in a way that I can have the best of both worlds than it was as a first-time founder. Recognizing that privilege is important. 

3) If I ever feel like I am being a shitty partner/parent and there's no solution/end in sight, I will drop literally every professional endeavor & get my #1 priority (family) in order. 

4) Strong communication with your life & business partner are the foundation for this entire thing to work. 

5) I make sure that I get to do wake-up, morning walk, and bedtime with my wife, daughter, and dog unless there are extenuating circumstances. 

6) The opportunity cost of my time has never been higher. Not because of my business success. But because every minute i'm spending at work is a minute i'm not spending with my family. 

I'll continue to share how I'm approaching my new career mission, but I'm also so encouraged that folks like @mttgrmm, @marcrandolph, and others are painting a picture for crushing work & life.
author: businessbarista
quoted_text:
GFY

Propaganda bullshit. Expected, I suppose, from a Nashi propagandist.

I have 3 miniature humans that aren't my hobby - they're my entire raison d'être. To say nothing of my delightful wife that I greatly enjoy spending as much time with as possible.

Every single late night at the office, business dinner, investor event/retreat, trip to a supplier, visit to a customer, etc is a direct trade-off against my being an involved and present father (and husband). It's a difficult balance! And yet I've done it.

The real talk side of the "hustle culture" bullshit that nobody talks about is how your work output falls off a cliff around ~60 hours. Maybe a bit more if you're super young, but I doubt it. In most cases, that 80th hour at your desk is performative - it's theater.

Balanced lives (whether it's raising kids, sailing, tinkering on hobby cars, fitness, whatever) directly lead to balanced thinking and a FAR more sustainable lifestyle than "all work no play."

And, more importantly, it models for your employees that balance is actually good for output, morale, retention, etc.

Building big, impactful companies is a marathon. An ultra marathon. 10 years of marathons back to back. Your mind (and body) do need to actually rest and restore, or else you burn out. Fact of life.

Nonsense claims like this are propaganda from the (typically) VC crowd who want to see MOAR HOURS as if that makes PMF happen, under the misguided belief that hours in linearly equals company value out.

Have hobbies. Have kids. Take a vacation with your partner. And also work hard to build your company. The balance is difficult to find, but very doable.

quoted_text:
JUST IN: Jensen Huang's yearslong ties to Alice Huang enabled more than $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China, per The Information. It reports that she, her sister and her husband built a web of companies in China and Singapore. 

That network moved about 240,000 super advanced Nvidia Ai chips, worth at least $7.5 billion, to Chinese buyers. It cites 2 people who know her.

The hub, by that account, was Shanghai Century Litong. It was founded in June 2023 and became an Nvidia preferred cloud partner by October, which put it near the front of the queue. 

When export rules stalled orders, The Information says, Alice Huang leaned on her links inside Nvidia and among its distributors. 

Some of the hardware ended up serving Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese labs. 

The report adds that 'Megaspeed', the Singapore cloud firm where she held a senior role, set up a Malaysian unit called Speedmatrix back in 2024. Its equipment later reached Century Litong. 

Reuters could not verify the report. Nvidia, Megaspeed and Century Litong did not immediately comment. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing before. 

Nvidia said in October that diversion claims against Megaspeed had been investigated and debunked.

The New York Times reported in October that US officials concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset. 

China's foreign ministry calls that a smear. On Sunday Jensen told staff he had been unfaithful to his wife. His board opened an independent review with outside counsel and said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. 

President Trump says the Federal Bureau of Investigation is looking into it, and that Jensen told him he had no idea she was a spy. 

The New York Times now reports that the Justice Department asked Commerce to pause its part of the Megaspeed probe after an Nvidia representative contacted Commerce investigators.

Washington is moving fast. 

House China committee chair John Moolenaar says Congress must "get to the bottom" of it. 3 House chairs want Huang at a closed-door briefing on 18th November and asked for his answer by 11th November. 

Senators Jim Banks and Elizabeth Warren want tighter chip export limits written into the defence bill. 

Democrats, who won both chambers in last week's midterms, say Congress will investigate. A shareholder has already sued Nvidia and Huang in San Jose, claiming investors were misled.

Investors have already marked the stock down. Nvidia closed at $178.67 on Monday, down 4.27%, and traded near $171.57 on Tuesday morning. That is about 8% in 2 sessions, or roughly $360 billion of value. Bank of America took it off its US 1 List of best ideas but kept its Buy rating. Wells Fargo cut its target to $300 from $315, and Aletheia Capital moved to Hold.

The business reports on 17th November. Nvidia guided to $108 billion of revenue, plus or minus 2%, which tops out at $110.16 billion. Analysts expect about $108.8 billion to $109.2 billion. 

Nvidia has beaten the top of its own range in each of the last 9 quarters. Its thinnest cushion was 2.6% over the midpoint, in the quarter that ended in April 2025.

The way things are happening, a highly likely scenario is that the 17th November release shows revenue above $110.16 billion. This is very likely!

The guide already leaves out China data centre sales, and every allegation so far concerns where chips went in past years. I am wrong if reported revenue for the quarter is $110.16 billion or less.

On the Nvidia situation:

Nvidia, $NVDA, is now down another -7% today and -12% since the Jensen Huang affair situation began.

At this point, the market is pricing in two major potential headwinds.

First, the growing possibility that Jensen Huang will be removed as CEO.

Second, possibility that sensitive Nvidia technology or information was compromised.

Are these scenarios possible? Sure, but we believe both remain unlikely, with less than a 20% probability.

Nvidia's stock is now down -32% in just 24 trading days, erasing -$1.8 trillion in market cap, with over one-third of these losses coinciding with the Jensen Huang controversy.

We believe Huang remains an integral part of Nvidia's future and the broader AI Revolution, and this week's events will not derail the broader thesis.

As the dust settles and uncertainty begins to fade, we expect bargain hunters to step in.

The fundamental AI investment thesis remains intact.

quoted_text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

text:
初代礦工 - 神魚，是我最敬佩的幣圈前輩之一。
不管是挖礦還是 DEFI 都顯示出他超前的認知。

這集 18 分鐘演講他分享了他使用 AI 的認知，我仔細看完後又用 AI 拉逐字稿分析，總結出以下核心認知，分享給大家：

1 同一份資訊，看到多少 insight ，取決於你有多少算力，用得對不對。
人腦算力和時間有限，只能抽出很少的 insight；
藉助 AI 能夠瞬間調用大量算力，同一份資訊就能看出更多東西。
了解這個底層邏輯，你就可以在各個領域超前創造額外價值。

2 三個世界稀缺的東西不一樣。
實體世界缺位置（房地產），
網路世界缺注意力（流量），
AI 世界缺的可能是品味和判斷力（AI 無法取代的能力）。

3 花 Token 是在買時間。
讓 AI 把每本書壓成一頁簡報、把一個學科做成知識圖譜；讀不懂的書讓 AI 照他的背景和經歷改寫。

4 讀書要雙軌並行。
知識進得快但沒有真的進腦子。所以一邊讓 AI 抽結構，一邊自己反覆精讀。
他拿健身房來類比：體力勞動被機器取代後大家上健身房，腦力也需要類似的鍛鍊。

5 讓 AI 當鏡子認識自己。
他從玩龍蝦就開始讓 AI 寫人格設定檔，回頭整理自己的經歷給 AI 讀。
AI 回他一封信，他看完哭了很久。
之後每天花 10 到 20 分鐘讓 AI 找他前一天的工作盲區。
AI 讀完他的交易紀錄還問他：你是在做交易，還是在滿足心理需求。他想了兩天大徹大悟，承認是後者，決策品質從此好了很多。

6 人和 AI 協作像層層回路。
人負責講清楚要什麼、給足背景；
AI 團隊去試、回饋、沉澱成方法。
兩個關鍵旋鈕：
每一步交給 AI 多大的任務（太大它會變笨，太小就像一直開會不做事）、多久回饋一次。
系統越自動，人越關鍵：目標偏一點，下面全部白費。

7 他自己的變化。
體感生產力增加約十倍，最關鍵的是性格變了，從不擅長抽象思考變成偏向抽象思考。

8 很強的個人放進傳統組織反而變差。
團隊產出被組織裡最窄的瓶頸卡住，個人再強也沒用，所以要變成以 AI 為本的公司，組織的做法得改。

9 他們公司怎麼做。
每個員工配一個 AI 同事，大量協作由 AI 之間溝通，不用開會拉齊。
他拋出靈魂拷問：如果 AI 之間都能即時協商，公司的邊界還存在嗎？

10 人生只有三件事。
吃飯、睡覺，剩下就是用好算力。
對外看懂世界、對內看懂自己。

11 AI 給他的十年建議。
守住自己的資料和私鑰；
趁父母還在、孩子還願意牽你的手，去遠行；
每半年檢查一次自己的預測邏輯，自負是很貴的漏洞；
吃真正的食物、把可被攻擊的破口縮到最小。
