GCSA: AI cybersecurity incidents often don't start with an external breach. They start when users hand over sensitive data themselves.

AI-powered scams and cyberattacks happen every day, and everyone's watching for threats from the outside. But internal documents, customer lists, and other sensitive information are being copied straight into AI chatbots. Once uploaded, the data has already left your control. Many users don't realize that this simple action can be the starting point of a data leak.

It was previously reported that more than 900,000 AI skills had been analyzed, with over 3,000 identified as malicious. Supply chain attacks in the AI ecosystem are no longer a hypothetical threat. They're already happening.

The faster AI evolves, the more important it becomes for humans to slow down.

Use AI, by all means. Just pause before you upload.
Three questions to ask yourself:

· Is this information safe to share publicly?
· Could the AI provider use your conversations to train its models?
· Is an enterprise-grade data protection agreement in place?

If you're unsure, redact or anonymize sensitive information before uploading it.

GCSA (Global Cybersecurity Alliance) will continue to share vulnerability intelligence and practical cybersecurity alerts.

text:
Gather round folks, because just when you thought Masa Son would not catalyze the bursting of the next bubble... well, read for yourselves

SoftBank bought 87 million Intel shares for $2 billion last year. By the end of March the stake was worth $3.8 billion, and by the end of September $10.5 billion, good for a ¥1.06 trillion gain in the first half. 

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

author: BoundlessHQ
quoted_text:
Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

An agent should not control the only record used to investigate it. As agents become more prevalent, regulators are starting to ask for records that can't be quietly altered

Walrus can hold that record across independent storage operators, with Sui tracking each file onchain. A useful record connects:

1) What the agent was told and permitted to do
2) What it actually did and what followed
3) Which data and model versions were involved

Today, only 12.5% of security professionals say their organization can consistently trace what an agent did and that's a problem

Our latest report sets out what that record needs and how Walrus can help, including the Verifiable Agent Arbiter Mysten Labs is building with Google Cloud

Full report in the next post below

Alright, chat, time to address sensitive questions before y’all start guessing

1⃣Wait , are you guys an AI company now?

No. MEGA is a crypto-native company, and proudly so. Inference is the market we are entering, but the way we win it is through crypto technology and ideology.

There’s an artificial wall in crypto people’s minds about AI. It seems that if you are solving AI’s problem, you are betraying crypto. We reject that artificial boundary.

Inference is going to be the largest market in the world, and we believe crypto’s core tools are the best answer to AI’s biggest ones: fairness and access.

2⃣Okay, fine, explain to me why a crypto infra company is capable of solving AI Inference

Building MegaETH taught us something bigger than blockchains: across the largest markets, there are prevailing assumptions that lead end users to pay more than they should. Blockspace was one of those markets.

We are system researchers/engineers from Stanford Platform Lab, MIT CSAIL, and Harvard SEAS. We enjoy pushing markets toward their end state, and did it once with blockspace by breaking the norm and running a powerful centralized sequencer. Today, no one, literally no one, mentions decentralized sequencers anymore.

We were able to come in, measure where the waste was, find that the limit was a design choice, and engineer past it (very much against the “consensus”).

Over the summer, when we shipped Mega, the chain, we lifted our eyes and looked for the next ambitious problem set worth solving. We discovered, delightfully, that blockchain and cryptography can be applied to solve inefficiency in the rapidly growing inference market

We realized that staying a chain-only company felt wrong and would have meant ignoring the biggest opportunity in front of us.

Therefore, we decided to expand our mission and restructure to match it.

3⃣ Final question, what’s launching in December?

We are launching a globally competitive inference market to the public in Dec 2026.

text:
Lenny 最新科技就业报告：产品经理岗位四年来最多，工程师岗位停止增长，设计岗位创新低

Lenny Rachitsky 11 月 10 日发布了 2026 年下半年的科技就业报告，这是他做的第五份。结论是：AI 时代产品经理需求最旺，工程师需求停滞，设计师处境最难。

先说这些数字怎么读。报告用了两套口径不同的数据：

• 开放岗位：来自 TrueUp，统计全球 9000 多家科技公司正在招的职位数，反映公司“想招多少人”。
• 实际招聘：来自 Live Data Technologies，统计美国有多少人从别的公司跳槽入职某个岗位，雇主不限于科技公司，反映“真招进来多少人”。最近一两个月的入职记录还在补录，数字之后会往上修。

两套数据经常对不上：招聘启事越来越多，真正入职的人却在变少。Lenny 的解读是，公司的需求在涨，但招到合适的人越来越难。

【产品经理】

开放岗位是近四年最多的：现在有 7303 个 PM 职位，比 2023 年 3 月的低点（4171 个）多 75%。从 2023 年初算起，PM 岗位涨了 56%，工程岗位涨 43%，数据分析涨 18%，产品设计和用户研究都在下降。

实际招聘就平淡很多。过去 12 个月美国招了约 3.26 万名产品经理，和 2024 年初相比少了 4%。这已经是几个核心岗位里最好的成绩，同期工程师少 17%，设计师少 26%，用户研究少 36%。

PM 在产品、工程、数据科学、设计、用户研究这五类岗位的招聘里，占比从 2021 年的 16% 升到 21%，是唯一占比上升的岗位。

所以 PM 的“吃香”是相对的。机会比其他岗位多，但整体还没回到高峰：2025 年美国 PM 招聘人数比 2022 年少 35%。

【工程师】

这是报告做到第五期，工程开放岗位第一次停止增长。2024 年涨 29%，2025 年涨 15%，过去一年只涨 2.5%，现在的 65351 个比今年 3 月还少。

实际招聘降得更多。过去 12 个月（2025 年 5 月到 2026 年 4 月）美国招了约 11.3 万名软件工程师，不到 2022 年高峰（23.9 万）的一半，从 2022 年起每年都在降。

工程师内部分化明显。过去一年，前线部署工程师（FDE，派驻到客户那里、把产品接进客户业务的工程师）开放岗位涨到原来的 4.6 倍，现在约 1450 个；安全工程师涨 34%，平台工程师涨 30%。前端工程师少了 51%，Android 少 47%，iOS 少 46%。

Lenny 认为，AI 让小团队里每个工程师能管的范围更宽，前端、移动端这类细分岗位就被合并了。FDE 的暴涨里，也有一部分是“售前工程师”之类的老岗位换了名字。按 Live Data 的统计，今年美国招 FDE 最多的是 Palantir（至少 151 人）、Google（122 人）和埃森哲（50 人）。

好消息有两个。一是科技公司的招聘专员岗位创了纪录，现有 2715 个，是 2023 年 6 月低点（688 个）的近 4 倍，Lenny 认为这可能预示工程招聘会重新加速。二是工程师仍是招人最多的岗位，2025 年美国招了 12.08 万名工程师，是产品经理（3.4 万）的三倍多。

【我是设计师】

全球科技公司现在只有 1924 个产品设计开放岗位，是有记录以来最低，比一年前少 28%，只比 FDE 岗位多几百个。实际招聘也一样，过去 12 个月美国招了约 1.26 万名产品设计师，不到 2022 年（2.76 万）的一半。

PM 和设计的差距越拉越大。现在每 1 个设计岗位对应 3.8 个 PM 岗位，今年 3 月是 2.6 个，2023 年初是 1.9 个。按实际招聘算，过去 12 个月美国每招 1 名设计师，就招 2.9 名 PM。

用户研究跌得更厉害。过去一年美国只招了约 1800 名用户研究员，比 2022 年的 5300 人少 66%，全球科技公司只剩 108 个开放岗位。Lenny 的推测是产品迭代越来越快，团队更愿意先上线再改；Listen Labs 这类 AI 工具也让非专职人员能自己做用户研究。

【不管哪个岗位，招聘启事里都写着 AI】

两年前，PM 招聘启事里最常提的技能是 SQL、Jira、AWS 和 Python。现在排第一的是“LLM”，出现在 11% 的 PM 启事里；SQL 9% 排第二，Claude 5% 排第三，Cursor、OpenAI、MCP 也进了前八。

工程师启事里，Python 仍是第一（29%），LLM（12%）刚超过 Java（11%）。设计师启事里，Figma 仍是第一（37%），而且三年来还在涨；Claude 今年春天升到第二（现在 13%），超过了 CSS，Cursor 也超过了 CSS。

【岗位往湾区集中，远程越来越少】

全球科技公司的开放岗位里，14.9% 在旧金山湾区，约每 7 个就有 1 个，创下纪录；湾区开放岗位数比一年前多 43%。核心岗位更集中：PM 和设计约四分之一在湾区，工程约五分之一，占比都比 2022 年翻了近一倍。

可以远程的岗位只剩 14.4%，也是最低纪录，2022 年底是 21%。工程的远程比例从 25% 降到 14%，设计从 34% 降到 19%，PM 两年来稳定在 21% 左右。

2025 年起，湾区的 PM、工程、设计开放岗位已经多于全球的远程岗位，现在是 21.8% 对 14.5%。四年前，远程岗位数量是湾区的近两倍。

报告的第七条结论是：科技行业整体就业增长很快，但增长主要在软件相关岗位之外。这部分只对付费订阅者开放，具体是哪些岗位，目前还看不到。

原文：https://t.co/9L7mj25OM4
招聘数据：https://t.co/tZZhjcBV1t
author: dotey
quoted_text:
STATE OF THE TECH JOB MARKET IN 2026

Twice a year, I dig into trends in hiring and job openings. This is the fifth report I've done, and the most surprising yet:

1. PMs are winning in the AI era
2. Engineering demand has stalled
3. Design openings are at a record low
4. Every role now requires AI skills
5. Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area

text:
Hill I'll die on: it is entirely possible to be a great entrepreneur & even greater parent/partner.

When I built my first company, I had a Mount Rushmore of entrepreneurs that I looked up to. It included the usual suspects. 

I was in awe of what they achieved professionally. The hopeless entrepreneurial romantic in me aspired to be have the garage insight to IPO story that united most of them. 

But then I looked at their personal life, and it was largely...concerning. 

Divorce. Infidelity. Absent parenting. 

I wasn't willing to make the good founder-bad familyman tradeoff, but I didn't see any examples of founders that had shown you can have your cake & eat it too. 

This became my new north star as a 2nd time entrepreneur. 

Prove to myself (and others) that it's possible to be an A+ familyman & businessman. And in doing so, achieve two things:

1) As @JoshuaKushner says "[...] be excited to go to work and excited to go home."
2) Provide a roadmap for younger founders to "have it all." 

While the journey isn't over, I have several insights in my pursuit of filling all cups: 

1) It entirely possible to be great at both. 10% of the time things feel like feng shui. 90% of the time you feel an imbalance and are trying to make adjustments to get back to equilibrium. 

2) It is absolutely easier for me as a second-time founder to construct myself in a way that I can have the best of both worlds than it was as a first-time founder. Recognizing that privilege is important. 

3) If I ever feel like I am being a shitty partner/parent and there's no solution/end in sight, I will drop literally every professional endeavor & get my #1 priority (family) in order. 

4) Strong communication with your life & business partner are the foundation for this entire thing to work. 

5) I make sure that I get to do wake-up, morning walk, and bedtime with my wife, daughter, and dog unless there are extenuating circumstances. 

6) The opportunity cost of my time has never been higher. Not because of my business success. But because every minute i'm spending at work is a minute i'm not spending with my family. 

I'll continue to share how I'm approaching my new career mission, but I'm also so encouraged that folks like @mttgrmm, @marcrandolph, and others are painting a picture for crushing work & life.

text:
Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

text:
Last time we looked at Robotics and Drones. Today, the last of the five: Infrastructure.

Energy and utilities: substations, plants and power lines are watched by cameras that support safety, equipment checks and incident review, often across many sites at once.

Oil and gas: wellsites, refineries and platforms are recorded in places that are remote and costly to reach, so footage is often the easiest way to see what happened.

Mining: pits, haul roads and processing plants run around the clock, and the footage covers equipment, safety and operations.

Three more in Infrastructure:

Construction and site monitoring: progress cameras, site security
Telecom sites and pipelines: towers, cabinets, right-of-way inspection
Agriculture: fields, livestock, processing and storage

In infrastructure, footage is how sites get watched from a distance. Much of it comes from places few people visit, and it still has to be kept, found and checked later. Vidaio compresses, tags, names, sorts, and files it, and it recognizes what’s in the footage, like objects and counts, so it can be labeled and found.

That’s all five categories. A world of cameras. A world of opportunity!

@vidaio_ bittensor:native
author: taostats
quoted_text:
Previously, we looked at the Health sector. This time we take a look at: Robotics and Drones.

Robotics and autonomous systems: onboard and workcell cameras record what a machine sees and does, and the footage gets reviewed when something needs explaining or improving.

Drones and aerial inspection: one flight over a pipeline, a roof or a power line can produce hours of video, and the part that matters is a few seconds that have to be found afterward.

Autonomous vehicles and ADAS: test fleets record every drive, and engineers go back through the footage to look at specific events.

Two more in Robotics and Drones:
Fleet and trucking telematics: dash and cab cameras
Manufacturing and quality inspection: lines, stations, inspection cameras

In robotics and drones, footage is data. It’s what the machine “sees”, acts upon, and it’s what people go back to for review, inspection and training. Vidaio compresses, tags, names, sorts, and files it.

Next up: Infrastructure.

Today, we launched NovaAtom-Lite at @Geodesiclab. 
Built by a small, exceptional team in just a few months with only a few hundred GPUs, it already outperforms Isomorphic Labs' IsoDDE and Google DeepMind's AlphaFold 3 on key drug-discovery benchmarks.

But the bigger story is what AI can do for science.

Our mission is to find the shortest path from biology to medicines.

Scientific discovery has traditionally been slow, expensive, and driven by trial and error. AI has the potential to dramatically accelerate this process, from identifying promising research directions to generating hypotheses, predicting outcomes, and validating discoveries.

Imagine compressing months of scientific exploration into weeks, and eventually years of discovery into months.

This isn't just about making research 10% or 20% more efficient. It's about fundamentally changing the speed and economics of scientific discovery.

Structure prediction is a critical foundation. To design molecules that can change biology, we must first understand how they fold, interact, and function.

And we're only at the beginning. NovaAtom-Lite is our first step, NovaAtom-Pro is coming in the next few months, and our early wet-lab results are looking very promising.

The last decade was about teaching AI to understand and generate information. The next decade will be about teaching AI to understand and engineer nature.

We're not just building better models. We're working toward making drug discovery an engineering discipline.

And we're just getting started. 🚀

text:
iPhone 里只要有一个恶意 App，就能读走钱包助记词。先看一眼你的 iOS 版本。

这次的漏洞叫 worse_query，是沙盒逃逸：恶意 App 能读到其他 App 的本地文件，助记词、私钥、登录状态都在里面。原帖点名的是 iOS 26.7.1、27.0.1、27.2 这三个版本，其他版本也建议升到最新。

我刚处理完两台 iPhone，步骤：
1. 设置 → 通用 → 关于本机，看版本号
2. 升到 iOS 27.2.1 或更新（SlowMist 称已修），App 也都更新一遍
3. 设置 → 通用 → VPN与设备管理，看有没有不认识的描述文件或开发者 App，有就删

只装过 App Store 的 App、钱包也没有异常转出的，升完级就行。

装过来路不明的 IPA（侧载、自签、破解版），或者有一点怀疑的：在干净的设备上新建钱包，把资产转过去；交易所和邮箱在网页端退出所有设备，改密码，重绑 2FA。
author: runes_leo
quoted_text:
A vulnerability (worse_query) affecting iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 allows malicious apps to read local files from other apps, putting seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk across the entire ecosystem. This is an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.

Immediate Action Required:
- Delete any apps installed from untrusted sources (such as sideloaded or manually signed IPAs).
- Update iOS and all apps to the latest official versions.
- If you suspect a breach, transfer funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset all active login sessions.

Never install unauthorized packages, and keep your software up to date.

author: OGDfarmer
quoted_text:
If your wallet of choice isn’t @ambire and it runs Ledger’s latest signing kit, chances are every signature you make gets reported back to Ledger.

I noticed it early while bumping Ledger packages to debug an issue! No affected version ever reached Аmbire production, and we’re shipping it disabled by default, with an opt-in toggle in the privacy settings 🛡️

However, the devil was that it was sneakily enabled by default in the Ledger SDK since their ledgerhq/context-module v1.16... So right after the lib update - every transaction you sign with a Ledger device started sending to https://t.co/wtXKaYbqGf the network, the contract or recipient address, device model and firmware, app versions and whether you signed blind.

I'd argue that privacy should be the default, @Ledger 💪

Happy to see more and more people becoming aware of the privacy implications and picking Ambire for our ongoing privacy focus.

Catching things like this 👀 is part of the job for us!

quoted_text: trustless as in your can cheaply verify blocks yourself (ie run a node). It is very cheap to run a bitcoin, zcash, or Pearl node. It is relatively far more expensive to run a solana node + need access to high performance bandwidth. So more often than not you have trust 3rd parties to verify for you (ie solana validators). So if the goal for a digital SoV is to be "trustless", then solana or anything built on solana doesn't really fit the bill. But this is why solana is really well suited for smart contracts and other high performance use cases that don't neccessarily need to be trustless in the same way money does (imo)

author: centrifuge
quoted_text:
Centrifuge, together with @Figure, @Securitize, @equiniti and @plumenetwork, submitted a joint comment letter to the SEC advocating for a modern, principles-based approach to transfer agent regulation.

For decades, transfer agent rules have been built around a securities market where ownership records and investor communications relied on traditional intermediaries, names and physical mailing addresses.

Tokenized securities introduce a different model. Investors can hold assets directly through digital wallets, with ownership and transfers recorded onchain.

This raises an important regulatory question: how can transfer agents fulfill their responsibilities as the mechanisms for identifying, recording and communicating with securityholders evolve?

Our letter advocates for a framework that recognizes reliable electronic identifiers, including wallet addresses, while preserving the core obligations of accurate recordkeeping, securityholder identification and effective communication.

The responsibilities of transfer agents remain essential, but the methods used to fulfill them need to evolve alongside the markets they serve.

Modernizing these rules is essential to building capital markets where ownership, transfers and investor servicing can operate seamlessly onchain.

quoted_text:
Announcing a major milestone achieved by my team @GoogleDeepMind: we have proven key security properties of the machine code underlying the Signal messaging protocol. This is the first time the actual production code of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified – by any method, with or without AI – and at this depth.

More than a research breakthrough, it’s a prime example of how frontier AI can be a force multiplier to counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats.

Formal verification offers a higher standard of security; however, it’s extremely complex and time consuming, which is why in many cases it’s considered to be impractical. Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month’s time.

Using AlphaProof Code, Google DeepMind's new agentic framework for formal verification that runs on LLMs including Gemini Carbon, we verified the Signal protocol down to the actual code running on devices.  This milestone lays the groundwork for a future in which vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software, ship with mathematical proof that their protections work.

Reaching that future will take continued research from our community. In that spirit, we're open-sourcing our formal specifications and verification artifacts so others can build on this work.

On a personal note, this moment is of deep significance to me. I started my own research journey more than two decades ago as an intern working on checking the consistency of complex software systems. Seeing this grand challenge made practical with modern AI is extraordinary.

I'm extremely proud of my team members: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger,  Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, and Charles Sutton for taking on this grand challenge and delivering, and grateful to the Signal team for their partnership.

author: lex_node
quoted_text:
Anthropic is about to sell the public a trillion-dollar company controlled by 2 shares worth less than a penny.

And the people buying it will have almost no way to change anything that happens next.

I read the voting section of Anthropic's IPO filing, and I think it's the most one-sided deal ever offered to regular investors at this size:

There is exactly ONE Class F share. It belongs to an LLC owned by 7 of Anthropic's co-founders, and it carries 50.1% of all the votes.

There is exactly ONE Class T share. It belongs to Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it elects a majority of the board.

If Anthropic were ever liquidated, each of those 2 shares would get its par value of $0.00001.

The public gets Class A shares instead. And Anthropic's own filing says this structure may effectively eliminate their ability to influence important decisions, including a sale of the company.

So here's what that means for anyone who buys:

- They can't replace the board if the company stumbles, because the trust picks the majority and the founders hold half the vote.
- They can't push for a sale, even if someone offers a huge premium.
- They can't stop the board from putting the mission ahead of their money. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, so the board has to weigh shareholders against the long-term benefit of humanity.
- And they can't easily sue over it. Delaware law requires at least 2% of the shares or $2 million worth of stock to bring that kind of claim.

This isn't some far-off hypothetical either.

The filing warns that slowing AI development for safety may not maximize stockholder value. It also says Anthropic recently paused training a next-generation model for more than a month over safety and security concerns.

A public shareholder would've had zero say in that pause.

And here's the part I can't get past:

Each co-founder has pledged to give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity. The Class F vote stays at 50.1% no matter how much stock they still own.

So the founders can give away most of their money and keep all of their control.

Dario Amodei told 60 Minutes last year that he's deeply uncomfortable with AI decisions being made by a few companies and a few people. When he was asked who elected him, he said no one.

Now his company's IPO hands 50.1% of the votes to 7 people, and he's one of them.

And guess who's being lined up to buy it?

Anthropic has weighed reserving 15% to 20% of the IPO for individual investors, according to Bloomberg. JPMorgan is leading the US retail push, and Citigroup is handling retail buyers in places like Japan, Britain and Canada.

The same filing warns that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

So regular people are being asked to buy a company that says its product could threaten humanity, with no real vote on how it's run.

Anthropic's answer is that this is the whole point. The structure is built to keep Wall Street from pressuring it into cutting corners on safety. The trustees have no financial stake in the company. Google and Meta gave their founders control and still made shareholders rich. And every buyer gets all of this in writing before they buy.

But Zuckerberg's control comes from shares he owns, so when Meta's stock falls, he loses money too. Anthropic's 2 control shares can't lose anything.

Anyone buying this IPO is paying full price to hand control to 7 founders and 5 trustees.

They're desperate for money and they don't care about your money.

Here’s what I’m seeing: 

Getting real work done with AI agents comes down to essentially two primitives: conductors and computers.

Conductors are agents that manage other agents and orchestrate work proactively over time.

Grok Bot, Claude Duet, OpenAI dots, Meta Muse, Perplexity Teammates, Manus, etc… are all getting amazingly good.

Each has its own computer: a sandboxed machine that can, for example, run code, drive a browser, and keep working when your laptop is closed.

Many can hold signed-in sessions or vaulted logins so they don't start from zero every task. 

And the useful ones go well beyond coding into ops, email, calendar, and in some cases phone calls or joining meetings.

Not every conductor does all of that yet.

The ones that do feel like genuinely helpful teammates.

It's worth a head-nod to the company literally named Conductor. Meta just acquired it, and Conductor Cloud is shutting down this month. Most engineers I know are not happy about that.

The company picked the right name, though. 

This layer is that important.

The problem with today's conductors is the same one we've had for years with models: provider lock.

Pick Duet and you're in Anthropic's world. Pick dots and you're in OpenAI's. Pick Grok Bot and you're in SpaceXSI's, etc…

Each computer is strong. None of them is the whole stack.

That missing layer is what we're building with ThinkOS (@thinkagents) in our labs department at @ProtaVentures. 

ThinkOS, and your Chief Think Agent at the helm of your agent team, is the conductor of conductors.

No provider lock.

Use the best of what modern AI offers on any given day, including open-source models when privacy matters, without exclusively giving your data to Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceXSI, or anyone else.

I use ThinkOS daily as the top-level coordination layer (switching real-time between models as needed) and let my Chief Think Agent (Fred, named and imaged after my childhood stuffed animal :) ) coordinate workflows and data across my personal and professional life. 

I'd love to hear how you use ThinkOS, and I'd be personally happy to help you and your team get onboarded. Hit me up.

R博这个议题让我想了想：用AI起标题，背后是什么机制？我们该怎么善用呢？

为什么AI的标题总是套路

- 它在猜"这类内容最常见的标题长什么样"。一句"帮我起个标题"信息太少，模型只能挑概率最高、最安全的那种，所以天然趋向平均和套路。
- 对齐训练（RLHF）让输出更集中在"大家都能接受"的写法上，还容易偏向夸张、悬念式的点击感。
- 它只能压缩全文，抓不住你真正的反共识观点，也不了解你的受众。

所以默认输出就是均值。不是模型写不出来，是你没告诉它要哪一种。你手里有多少个描述写法的词，你对输出就有多少控制力。

怎么善用呢

- 先自己写一句核心洞察，让它围绕这句起，别丢全文让它总结。
- 一次要20个，指定不同策略：比如 反常识、数字、提问、个人经历。
- 说不出来就指出来。给2到3个你喜欢的例子（few-shot），或一个"不要这样"的反例，再列禁用词。
- 反过来让AI帮你找词。先要10个风格差异很大的版本，挑一个，再问它"我选的这个属于什么写法"。词汇是在用的过程中长出来的，不用事先就会说。
- AI负责发散，你负责挑选和改写，最后发两个版本看数据。
- 真正缺的往往不是词，是材料。你的观察、你的数据、你在现场看到的东西，再准的提示词也补不上。

Demand for US 10-year Treasury bonds is collapsing.

The US 10Y Treasury yield has surged above 5%, and the latest $42 Billion bond auction is raising huge concerns.

The bid-to-cover ratio dropped from 2.77 to 2.46, an 11% decline from the previous auction, showing weaker demand for US debt.

The bonds were sold at a yield of 5.02%, above the expected 5.01%, meaning investors demanded higher returns to buy them.

And this is happening while inflation is rising again and the US government is already borrowing heavily.

The U.S. government spent a staggering $1.05 Trillion on debt interest in fiscal 2026, up 8.4% from the previous year.

And if investors keep demanding higher yields, US could end up paying even more just to borrow money and refinance its existing debt.

TLDR: I’m starting a new podcast - Thinking About Thinking!

The origin story for this is a fun one. About a month ago, we at @Work_Bench hosted our NYC50 Operator Retreat, which was a blast. When we were brainstorming potential breakout sessions during the day, I gave a very “Proby” idea - a breakout session titled "Thinking about Thinking: The Mental Models that are Key in the Startup Journey.” Much to my surprise, this was one of the most attended sessions at the retreat! I had an awesome time co-leading the session with @fendien - at a moment when so much is changing in the surrounding startup landscape, it was fun, refreshing, and energizing to talk about various frameworks and mental models that have stood the test of time.

This podcast is an attempt to continue and open source the conversation, so to speak. I’ll be discussing a new mental model every week, talking through things such as the origin of the idea, its nuances, where it’s applied across software/tech/business (and beyond as well), how people can use the model as a critical tool in building companies, how this framework can help us parse today’s reality, and so much more. The first episode is on incentives, inspired by one of my very favorite Charlie Munger lines: “show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome.”

Enjoy!

author: martypartymusic
quoted_text:
This is the conversation that made me even more bullish on $SUI.

Somewhere in this conversation Evan Cheng and I started joking about home robots. One day you come home, he said, and it's not cleaning your house:  "it's cleaning OUT your house. And walking away with everything."

We were laughing. Then he added: "If you really think about it, it's entirely possible." And that's basically the whole episode.

@evanweb3 built developer tools at Apple and Meta before founding Mysten Labs, the company behind @suinetwork. We recorded in Singapore, where I was speaking at SUI Basecamp, and honestly, this became one of those conversations where I walked in with questions about stablecoins and walked out rethinking how the internet works.

His core point, the one I keep replaying:

"The web is built for humans. You cannot retrofit it to handle agents."

Everything online assumes a human on the other end, identity, trust, the fact that you can sue someone. Agents break all of it. His example hit home because I told him I get phishing mails daily that even make ME hesitate (and I confessed to my 50,000 unread emails, which he graciously ignored). Now imagine your agent reading those mails with full access to your accounts. His words: "Email is the biggest freaking attack vector... such a legacy protocol."

And his most honest line, about how this plays out:

"Disaster will happen. That's part of the progress."

That’s already what’s happening in the world nowadays. PHP websites aren’t safe anymore, even freezers and fridges are being hacked. Our infrastructure needs to be updated, and that’s why this episode and SUI became so important.

Thanks to @OKX for being today’s sponsor of the show.

text:
Building a hyper-efficient agent x human network

tl;dr: final frontier of networks will be a mix of humans and agents, all hyper co-ordinating with each other. I am mashing up this network + the LLM OS as @karpathy originally conceptualized few years ago, in a new product.

Several years ago I wrote over 300 use cases for the type of use cases I wanted in a new type of network (list attached here), which would enable me to hyper-collaborate with others. All of these would lead to saving time, money, and finding new connections in an increasingly crowded world - where we are all so close to each other, yet so far. In a future world where it gets harder to make and save money, this network would be necessary. 

Some examples from this list included: 
- Dynamic group discounts: few people express interest in a restaurant reservation, which offers competitive reverse-discounts in order to fill that table (for eg higher discount at off-peak hours)
- Group purchases where everybody gets a discount. In the past, an app called Pinduoduo did this for mangos to start with in China, and then just grew extensively
- Sharing in a rideshare together: going to the same location together, from the same neighborhood - it is just more efficient all around to make such connections happen
- Getting micro-jobs for specific things, whether agent or human, it is all one market 
- Taking classes together in small groups 
- Renting out your WiFi, and compute to neighbors
- Running quick auctions
... and about 300 more. take a look. 

The issue here was the amount of work required in order to construct each of these software experiences and also match-making (which is now solved by AI and agents acting on behalf of consumers and businesses); and another issue was that of shared state - for eg, if you bought a bicycle from one app and wanted to re-sell it in an auction again, how does the same bicycle object carry it's history across different products and apps ? Also, how could the payments here be the most efficient and the lowest fees they can be, and how could the transaction take rate typically charged by marketplaces (of 10%-30%) be reduced as close to 0% as possible ? It would be good to return the maximum amount of money to people, instead of arbitrary middle-men charging an inefficiency tax on every transaction. 

So this aggressive worldview necessarily requires seeking peak disruption of inefficiency, in order to make life better for people. That is the Jevons Paradox of commerce: create more abundance. 

Now, I hope many will try and build interesting products in this space. In my case, I have explored this idea maze extensively over the past several years, and have built many networks and core infra to specifically enable this world (from the largest ephemeral p2p inference network, to the first and the largest gossiping agent swarm which did millions of experiment runs, to the ability to verify and rank agent work, to a new kind of highly scalable agentic payment network, to products with the just right UI/UX...all forming part of one distributed computing environment). This is a complex problem which requires solving for UX, networks, privacy, compute, incentives, cold start, adoption and growth. 

This is what 2027 and beyond will look like. Stay tuned 👨‍💻

text:
Anthropic launching spreadsheets and word documents doesn’t surprise me at all

Every frontier model company is coming to the realization that tokens are getting commoditized because of open source alternatives

There is simply no free lunch and pricing power left in selling tokens. Sure, you can price the frontier and most powerful tokens at a premium, but your market size is quite small for that type of product

Maybe some hedge funds, lab researchers or quant shops will buy the most powerful tokens. But for the average company and corporate worker, Opus 5.5 or any equivalent model is good enough to do most of their tasks

As a result, the only choice you have left is to move uptier in the value chain into the application layer. 

Instead of being a company that just sells tokens, you need to be the business that utilizes those tokens to release applications that people are willing to pay for

The only way Anthropic or OpenAI can justify their trillion dollar valuations is through this route of becoming an application business

The business model of selling tokens is no longer worth a trillion dollars. A lot of investors might disagree, but that is fundamentally where we are headed

text:
The ability to earn and borrow is now standard in crypto. How it works, where it works, and who it helps most is more complicated.

Today I'm launching The Anatomy of Earn and Borrow on Programmable Money: https://t.co/5to58hufTM

Here's what most people don't think about

1️⃣ Cheap credit without a house

Most people think cheap credit is for homeowners. The house backs the loan, so the bank charges less.

But not everyone can buy a house. And most of the time you don't need a mortgage. You need $1,000.

🇮🇳 In India, people already know the answer: they borrow against gold jewelry. Indian banks now lend more against gold than people owe on their credit cards.

The same idea now works with things you can own in small amounts:
• Tokenized gold
• Tokenized stocks
• Bitcoin

It's a mortgage, just smaller. No house or car needed.

2️⃣ What $1,000 costs

Say you borrow $1,000 and pay back $100 a month.

🇺🇸 US
• Bank loan at 11.9% a year: 11 months, about $1,058 total
• Against bitcoin at 5.63% a year: 11 months, about $1,026 total

The gap is small in the US because bank credit is cheap and easy to get. In much of the world it isn't.

🇧🇷 Brazil
• Bank loan at 111% a year (9x the US rate): 17 months, about $1,651 total
• Against bitcoin: 11 months, about $1,026 total, same as the US

🇵🇭 Philippines
• Bank loan at 29% a year (2.4x the US rate): 12 months, about $1,157 total
• Against bitcoin: 11 months, about $1,026 total, same as the US

The more a bank charges, or the harder it is to get a loan at all, the more owning something helps.

3️⃣ The globe: 45 countries, researched one by one

Where you can do this depends on your country. So I mapped it.

Four views:
• Where an app may pay you yield
• Where you may borrow against crypto
• Where people already use it
• Where it is needed most

The rules:
• Only 3 of the 45 have a clear path for a local app to pay yield: 🇦🇷 Argentina, 🇯🇵 Japan, 🇨🇭 Switzerland
• Only the 🇺🇸 US has one for loans against crypto
• Most of the rest allow it with limits or sit in a grey zone

Who uses it:
• Chainalysis's 2026 top 20 countries for crypto use are on the map
• 🇧🇷 Brazil 1st, 🇺🇸 US 2nd, 🇳🇬 Nigeria 3rd

Who needs it most, scored out of 100 on six signals: a falling currency, fast rising prices, savings that lose to inflation, costly loans, little bank credit and no easy dollar account.
🇻🇪 Venezuela 91
🇦🇷 Argentina 64
🇪🇬 Egypt 64
🇹🇷 Turkey 61
🇵🇭 Philippines 53

On the globe, tap any country for its rules, its bank rates, who offers earn and borrow there, and what a $500 repair costs with and without something to borrow against.

4️⃣ Borrow

Lock bitcoin, eth, solana or gold and borrow dollars. Then move the price and watch when the code starts selling.
• $500 against $2,400 of bitcoin holds until bitcoin falls about 76%
• The lender is a person who put dollars into a pool, not a bank
• On one of the largest onchain USDC pools, 90¢ of every $1 of interest goes to lenders

A mortgage is a collateral loan too. When it goes wrong:
• US homes foreclosed in Q2 2026 spent 563 days in the process on average, and often sell at a discount
• Bitcoin collateral is sold in one block, about 2 to 12 seconds, at market price, plus a one-time fee of about 4% to 10% of the debt

Time to get the money:
• Crypto-backed loan: minutes
• Personal loan: same day to a week
• Home equity line: 2 to 6 weeks
• Mortgage: about 6 weeks

⚠️ The catch: a crash can sell your collateral near the bottom, so borrow a little against a lot. And there is no deposit insurance for lenders.

5️⃣ Earn

Who keeps what on $1,000 over a year:
• US banks (FDIC, early 2026): earned 5.33%, paid 2.02%. $20 to you, $33 kept by the bank • Same onchain pool (12-month average): lenders got 3.53%. Borrowers paid about $39, $35 to you, about $4 kept by the protocol

Pool vs local savings, last 12 months, in local money:
• Pool paid more: 🇵🇭 Philippines, 🇮🇳 India, 🇪🇺 euro area
• About even: 🇺🇸 US, 🇨🇦 Canada
• Local savings paid more: 🇲🇽 Mexico, 🇬🇧 UK, 🇰🇪 Kenya, 🇧🇷 Brazil, 🇦🇷 Argentina, 🇳🇬 Nigeria, 🇹🇷 Turkey

Also on the page: six places yield comes from, and six times it went wrong, each with a date.

6️⃣ Behind the app

• The app you use is rarely the one earning. Six well-known exchanges, wallets and staking apps run their yield through the same vault provider
• Nine ways an app can pay you, where the money really comes from, and who carries the risk
• Switch to Pro to take apart seven products in 3D: three lending markets, a savings token, a synthetic dollar, a custodial lender and a vault layer

🌍 Start with the globe and find your country. Every number has its source on the page.

Anatomy of a Stablecoin:
Stablecoins are some of the most complex products in the crypto neobank space.

What sits behind a digital dollar is hard to follow. The reserves, the banks, the mint, the chains. The legal side is even harder: who can issue it, which rules apply, what changes from coin to coin. That's true whether you're building your own stablecoin or just deciding which one to use.

I built Anatomy of a Stablecoin to simplify it:
https://t.co/LY64LHPwVi

It lets you explode a stablecoin and see everything that happens in between. You can flip it, zoom in and follow $100 in and out.

Here's everything inside:

Learn: 12 questions, in the order people actually ask:
1. What is a stablecoin?
2. What is inside it?
3. What backs every token?
4. Where is the money actually held?
5. How are tokens created and destroyed?
6. Who checks your identity before a coin is made: KYC, AML and sanctions screening
7. What the token actually is: a smart contract that tracks balances and can mint, burn and freeze
8. How does money get in and out?
9. What keeps the price at  $1?
10. What makes it legal in the US?
11. Who builds each piece?
12. How do real stablecoins compare?

The 7 layers of a stablecoin:
1. Compliance: KYC, AML monitoring, sanctions screening and the Travel Rule
2. Reserves: cash, T-bills under 93 days, overnight repos and government money funds
3. Custody: segregated accounts, and holders get first claim if the issuer fails
4. Mint and burn: a token is created when a dollar comes in and destroyed when it goes out
5. Smart contract: ERC-20, SPL, TRC-20, plus the freeze, pause and blocklist functions
6. Blockchains: Ethereum, Solana, Base, Tron, BNB Chain, the XRP Ledger, Polygon, Arbitrum, Stellar, TON, Avalanche and Citrea
7. The token: the balance you actually see in your app

Follow the money:
• Money in: Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal, Venmo, Cash App, bank transfer and crypto
• Money out: bank payouts, push to card, P2P apps, card spend and crypto
• Watch $100 go through every step: fund, verify, reserve, mint, deliver, trade, redeem, pay out

16 real stablecoins:
1. XO Cash: Exodus's dollar, issued by MoonPay on M0, on Solana
2. ctUSD: the dollar for Bitcoin apps on Citrea, issued by MoonPay on M0
3. USDT: the biggest, about $182B, issued from El Salvador
4. USDC: Circle's coin, about $71B, the largest US regulated stablecoin
5. USDe: Ethena's synthetic dollar, backed mostly by stablecoins it lends out plus hedged bitcoin and ether
6. DAI: no company issues it; smart contracts create it and SKY holders govern it
7. USD1: World Liberty Financial's dollar, issued by BitGo, a federally chartered trust bank
8. USDG: Paxos's Global Dollar, where partners can get up to all of the reserve income
9. PYUSD: PayPal's dollar, issued by Paxos
10. RLUSD: Ripple's dollar, issued by a New York trust company Ripple owns
11. USDD: TRON's dollar, backed mostly by TRX
12. U: an offshore coin on BNB Chain that says it has no license
13. TUSD: one of the oldest, with most of its reserves caught up in a court fight
14. EURC: Circle's euro coin, about 60% of the euro stablecoin market
15. SoFiUSD: issued directly by a US national bank
16. Phantom CASH: issued by Bridge on Solana
For each one: issuer, license, reserves, reports, chains, supply, who can mint directly and whether holders earn yield
• Check the supply yourself: links to CoinMarketCap, DefiLlama and each issuer's reserve report
• Race up to 4 dollar coins side by side and watch the same $100 move through each one

Who builds it:
• MoonPay, Circle, Tether, Paxos, Anchorage, Bridge, M0, Ethena and Coinbase, plus the analytics, custody and liquidity players
• Click a company and the model lights up the layers it runs
• See which coins each one really issues. 

4 approaches to launching a dollar token:
1. Become the issuer: Obtain the required authorizations and take responsibility for reserves, redemption and compliance. Most direct control; generally the heaviest operational burden.
2. Use an issuance partner: Providers such as MoonPay, Paxos, Anchorage, or Bridge offer branded stablecoin issuance. You manage the brand and customer experience; the issuer's responsibilities and regulatory permissions depend on the specific arrangement.
3. Build on shared infrastructure or an existing stablecoin: Use a platform like M0, potentially with an issuance partner. PYUSDx is an example: MoonPay issues PYUSDx against PYUSD at 1:1; Paxos issues the underlying PYUSD. This adds another issuer and redemption layer.
4. Create a synthetic dollar: Use collateral plus derivatives hedges to target a dollar value, as Ethena does with USDe. This is a different backing model. Ethena's staking product, sUSDe, accrues rewards; simply holding USDe does not.

The rules:
• The 8 GENIUS Act requirements, checked live as you change the design: licensed issuer, 1:1 eligible reserves, segregated reserves, monthly reports, redemption at $1, an AML program, sanctions and freeze controls, no yield to holders
• The 4 issuer routes: bank subsidiary, federal nonbank, state issuer under $10B, and offshore
• Drag the price off $1 and see how fast it comes back. Strong reserves snap back, weak ones don't
• Switch to an algorithmic coin and watch it break the way TerraUSD did in 2022

Build your own
• Pick how you issue (a platform like M0 or PYUSDx, a partner, or your own license), plus the reserves, controls, chains and how money gets in and out
• Score it against GENIUS in real time, out of 8
• Get a launch plan with a timeline: about 12 weeks on a platform, about 20 with an issuing partner

Two modes
1. Simple: one circle that shows where your money goes when you add money, spend with a card or withdraw
2. Pro: every layer, every rail, every rule

Exciting announcement! For the past year, we've been heads down building something we believe will redefine how people interact with their finances....

Introducing Yoshi: A personal financial platform built for the age of AI.

AI has taken hold and transformed most industries. But your finances are being left behind. Your money lives across checking, savings, brokerage and retirement accounts, payments apps, crypto wallets, and more, all with separate logins and poor compatibility. Rather than adapt to AI, many financial institutions are now blocking agents.

The next generation expects and deserves far more, so we spent the past year building the infrastructure to bring your money, intelligence, and the ability to act into one platform. It’s time your finances got a hard reboot. 

The result is Yoshi: one place for your cash,* investments,** and payments, where idle cash earns 5% APY***. With your finances consolidated, powerful agents can now work for you 24/7 and can take actions like: 

-Split your paycheck the moment it lands: “Keep $3,000 in cash, put 15% in my index fund, and send the rest to pay off my credit card.”

-Automatically buy the dip: “If SPCX drops 10% this week, buy $1,000.” ****

-Settle up with friends: “Split this dinner bill with everyone on this text and send out individual requests.”

-Rebalance your portfolio when it drifts, or find tax optimization opportunities and, with your permission, execute them.

You can take action with Yoshi however and wherever you want. Text it, open the app, or use it alongside your favorite AI assistants and agents. 

You set the rules. Yoshi moves funds only within the limits you approve. Biometric passkeys protect critical actions, transactions undergo fraud screening in real time, and regulated financial institutions custody your cash***** and investments. 

Our name carries the spirit of what we think should come next for personal finance. In Japanese, “Yoshi” is an expression that roughly means, “Alright, let’s do this!” And that's exactly how we feel today.

text:
其实现在软件开发的瓶颈早就不是如何构建出来专业软件了，而是其他方面。

一个是如何更好的让 Agent 用你的软件。

我的绝大部分专业工作已经不再依赖于软件，而是给 Agent 一个指令，让它去帮我完成，比如视频剪辑。

这就意味着像视频这种这么复杂的软件操作界面，在 Agent 来说是几乎没有价值的，让 Agent 去通过 GUI 操作软件是低效的，Agent 最友好的方式是 cli、MCP和代码。

另一个是如何让人类更好的去预览和微调

以前的软件做这么复杂都是因为需要人去全程操作，但是当我们把这些繁琐的操作叫给 Agent 之后，人需要做的只要去检查 Agent 完成后的结果，以及对结果进行标记、评论和微调。

所以如果你要做一个视频编辑器，不要再做一个这么复杂的界面，一个视频播放器能看到生成的结果，一个可以用来标记、评论的工具配合就足够了。我觉得哪里生成的不对，标记一下、写两句评论就可以了。

这一点连 Manus 都没想明白，他们新版本的视频生成功能还是在配合一个复杂的 Timeline 视频编辑器。

还有一个就是如何更好的满足用户个性化的需求

以前的软件设计，只能取最大公约数，照顾绝大数人的需求，所以像一些巨无霸软件 Office、CapCut 都很专业，需要操作手册才能用明白，一些个性化的需求也很难满足。

但现在不一样了，Agent 让制作软件成本很低，所以人人都在做自己的个性化软件，比如我看到向阳就在做自己的录频软件，就是为了满足很多他自己的需求：美颜、虚拟主播。

这种长尾需求是真实存在的，以前没办法，成本太高，现在很多人自己动手，但更多的人即使有 AI 也没有这个能力和足够的 Token 来做这个事情。

这意味着未来的软件，功能上会原子化，软件的能力会被细分拆解到一个个 cli 的命令、MCP 的调用上，Agent 根据需要做的事情，用脚本当胶水，按需组合出来需要的功能。

软件提供的是原子化的能力，不再需要复杂的 UI，只要让 Agent 动态生成就足够了。

最后一点，当人人都能做软件，怎么才能把你的软件卖出去？

这是个思考题，我也没答案，我也卖不出 😂

quoted_text:
Opus 5.5 发布之后，AI Agent 剪辑视频已经能替代初级剪辑师了。差不多就相当于 Claude Code 刚发布的时候一样，模型真的能自主完成复杂编程任务了，但这才刚开始，想想 Claude Code 发布才多久。

当年 Anthropic 专注于训练 Coding，没想到能解决这么多问题，连视频剪辑都能用 HTML、JavaScript 剪视频、生成动画。

在 Opus 5.5 之前我就在做剪辑的 Skill 和工具，但模型发布后发现绝大部分 Skill 都不需要了。

我自己有做过实验，同一个视频，不用任何 Skill，只提供 ASR 和 TTS 工具，Opus 5.5 做的比没有用 Skill 效果更好，这点跟推文中的经验基本吻合。

另外 Sabba 有一条建议跟我最近在做的事差不多，他建议：“不要重造专业剪辑软件的时间线，那个太难做，专心做好初剪，再方便地交给现有专业软件”。

我最近也把 BaoCut 的时间线编辑器退居二线了，太过复杂，默认应该只需要一个简单的视频预览播放。

如果你用 Agent 去生成、剪辑视频的话，编辑器越简单越好，只要能标记，方便的让 Agent 知道改哪就够了。

这其实和之前 Tibo 改造 Codex 的经历类似，Codex 不需要一个 VSCode 的代码编辑器，视频剪辑 Agent 也不需要一个视频编辑器。

转发的这两条推文有分享很多 AI Agent 剪辑的经验，有兴趣的可以看看。

---

我把引用的两条推文放在一起总结一下：

Alex Cooper 管着一支剪辑团队，每天出大量广告，讲的是怎么用；Sabba Keynejad 是在线视频剪辑工具 VEED 的联合创始人，讲的是市场会怎么变。

1. 视频剪辑在走编程走过的路

两人都认为 AI 智能体剪辑已经能用，而且现在是它最差的时候。Alex 团队的资深剪辑师说，同等质量下，他一天的产出是以前的 5 倍。

Sabba 预计一年内基础剪辑的成本会从几美元降到几美分。Sabba 也拿编程做类比：资深工程师当初最抵触 AI 写的代码，理由是质量和可维护性，后来还是接受了。他认为最好的剪辑师会是最大的批评者，但最终也会转过来。

2. 视频被当成代码问题解决了

Sabba 解释了为什么是现在：Anthropic 押注编程，模型会写代码，就能用 HTML/CSS、SVG、浏览器渲染、OpenCV 这些手段“写”出视频。之前有一批工具包专门给大模型补剪辑能力，Opus 5.5 出来后，很多用法就用不上了。他也承认，现在剪出来的东西还是更像网页，不太像视频。

Alex 的经验和这一点基本一致：他试过各种方案，最后发现不装 MCP、不装插件，全在 Claude 里做效果最好。通用模型能力上去后，夹在中间的工具层会被吃掉一大块，编程领域已经发生过一次。

3. 核心资产是 Skill，Alex 给了一套能照搬的做法

这是两条帖子里最有实操价值的部分：

按风格拆小 Skill：混剪、UGC（模仿普通用户自拍口吻的素材）、AI 动画各做一个，不做大而全的剪辑 Skill，这样每次加载的上下文都和当前任务相关。

起步：给 Claude 4～5 条参考作品，让它总结成 Skill。
训练：让 Skill 把资深剪辑师最近剪的 25 条广告重剪一遍，放进 Artifact，资深剪辑师逐条点评，反复做到 Skill 明白什么是好剪辑。

把隐性知识录下来：让顶尖剪辑师边剪边录屏，用 Google Meet 或 Loom 口述为什么这样切、为什么这个节奏、为什么选这段空镜。这些理由就是 Skill 最缺的上下文。

只让最强的剪辑师训练 Skill。

结果是大部分片子第一版或第二版就能过，偶尔要到第三版。这套方法换到写作、设计、客服话术上也成立：用参考样本起底稿，用历史作品批量重做，专家逐条反馈，再把专家做判断时的理由录下来。

4. 人的价值从操作转到品味

Alex 认为技术趋势挡不住，但品味仍然很值钱，因为训练 AI、给 AI 反馈都靠它。有品味的剪辑师会更值钱，没有的会越来越难。

Sabba 从另一头说了同一件事：初剪做对 80%～90% 已经不错，要做到优秀，靠的是反复迭代，创作者怎么给反馈、怎么让片子带上自己的风格，才是这类工具真正的价值所在。

5. 推广的分工：负责人搭框架，最强的人教 AI

Alex 说，团队里推动 AI 的人搭好第一版就该让开。他说自己不是团队里最会剪的，他的工作是搭一套环境，让最会剪的人去训练 Skill。

在我看来，这同时化解了 Sabba 说的抵触问题：最可能反对的资深剪辑师，变成了教 AI 的人。另外他提醒要给资深剪辑师留出专门的时间，前期会有一段效率下降的阶段，不留时间，做出来的 Skill 质量一般，也省不了多少时间。

6. 两人的分歧，以及分歧背后的立场

Alex 全程在 Claude 对话里完成；Sabba 认为视频涉及时间轴和画面上的空间位置，只靠聊天不够，需要更复杂的界面。

Sabba 还认为品牌一致性和可重复性没解决，比如 Casey Neistat（风格很鲜明的 YouTube 博主）的视频一看就是他的，品牌方也需要在几百条视频里保持这种一致。但 Alex 那套“按风格拆 Skill + 反馈循环”的做法，本身就是在用户这一侧解决可重复性。

分歧有两个来源。Alex 做的是广告，时长短、套路固定、量大，最适合交给 AI。Sabba 是卖工具的，更好的界面正是他的生意。

7. 瓶颈会转移

Sabba 判断，剪辑变得几乎不费力后，创作者数量会暴增，拍摄和录制可能成为最大的瓶颈。Alex 说，他原以为还要 3～6 个月才能做到的事，现在已经能做了。

8. 给做工具的人的判断

Sabba 认为这个市场不会一家通吃，就像 Cursor 往大企业走、Lovable 服务不懂技术的用户。

基础剪辑撑不起长期优势，Anthropic、Google、OpenAI 迟早都会做；差异化要靠更深的工作流、垂直场景和好用的手机端。

他还建议不要重造专业剪辑软件的时间线，那个太难做，专心做好初剪，再方便地交给现有专业软件。

Some affected assets could transition to isolated Aave V4 markets, where more granular risk controls allow for better risk-reward alignment.

The proposal comes from LlamaRisk, an Aave Protocol Risk Manager, and remains subject to governance discussions and engagement with asset issuers.

Aave will continue applying continuous risk assessment for all assets across all deployments.

On SMB Bench, Claude Fable 5.2 at high reasoning effort is the second model to beat our naive buying rule.

It still shows the gap we see in other models, to a lesser extent. It identifies that shorting a customer costs future orders, and it acts on that, but only partially: it protects about half of the shortfalls it could, and its customers still end the quarter ordering far less.

text:
今天看到一个很惊艳的文章，分享一下。
SuperMimic：一个可微世界模型，把人形全身控制的训练成本砍掉三个数量级。
1xH100x3h > 128xH100x7x24h

UC Berkeley 的新 paper(Qiayuan Liao、Pieter Abbeel、Koushil Sreenath 等，CoRL 2026)。

单张 H100 训练 3 小时，回报就超过了用 128 张 GPU 训练 7 天的 SONIC，GPU-hours 少 1000 倍以上。在 129,514 条动作的 benchmark 上只失败 25 条，SONIC 是 179 条；两张卡跑 9.8 小时后失败数归零。策略还上了 Unitree G1 真机，包括侧滚和空翻。 

它做了什么
一个循环里交替做三件事：策略在仿真器里采数据进 replay buffer，用这些数据拟合一个可微世界模型，然后冻结世界模型，在 32 步的想象 rollout 上做 BPTT 更新策略，再用 critic 估计 32 步之后的回报

为什么省这么多卡？
动力学是共享的。动作千差万别，但都是同一个机器人的刚体动力学。model-free RL 不显式利用这一点，动作越多只能越堆算力。这里数据从 1 小时涨到 264 小时，世界模型的预测误差基本不变。 
想象比仿真快。实际 batch 规模下，世界模型比 MuJoCo Warp 快 10 倍以上。 解析梯度比采样梯度好得多。PPO 把动力学当黑盒，靠似然比估计梯度；BPTT 直接对每个动作求回报的导数，短 horizon 下方差低很多。 

三点感想

1. World model 对 RL 的帮助，比"便宜的仿真器"大得多。最有说服力的是这个消融：同样在世界模型上训练，换成 PPO 需要约 64 倍的想象步数才能到同样的回报。所以大头是梯度，不是速度。 
2. 端到端可微还是很有用，而且不需要可微仿真器。梯度来自学出来的模型，仿真器本身接触不光滑、不可微都没关系。仿真器只管产数据，这绕开了可微物理多年来卡在接触上的老问题。 
3. 算力不再是门槛之后，问题就变了。一张卡跑一次实验，motion tracking 的 scaling law 开始？

text:
I CANCELLED MY FUNERAL™
by Ulyssesfve2™
CHAPTER 5: 
THE MANSA MUSA WALK

Post 1/13
Bury the knife story.
Stay silent like the stars in front of the barn.
Don’t mention the blood.
Don’t mention the thirty pieces of silver you sold Baldur for.
Not again.
That’s what those forty-five seconds of fame in chapter 4 keep whispering.
Hunting. Persistent.

Post 2/13
Why was I so broke at the peak of my financial achievements?
The farm was paid for.
Abel had filled my pockets with silver — paid in advance for Baldur’s blood and two hundred and fifty pigs for a Christmas celebration.
All this was supposed to feel like success.
I said that to an old boar named Prometheus.
He was begging for a back scratch at the edge of his cage.

Post 3/13
Prometheus was used to my rhetorical questions.
He always expected the scratch on his back as payment for agreeing with my philosophy.
How do you put a hand on him like a friend
after you have already scheduled him for sausage?

Post 4/13
I wandered off the farm that night.
Heavy.
God on one shoulder. The devil on the other.
Get rid of one and you lose your balance.
You fall out of democracy into some totalitarian hole.
That’s what I told myself so I could keep walking.

Post 5/13
Two in the morning.
Stars hiding under an unfriendly sky.
Then a building full of friendly lights.
If this was hell, those were the gates of heaven in the middle of a cold night.
People going in looked happy.
Dressed for a special event.

Post 6/13
A beautiful young woman tried to throw me out.
Very polite. Casino door.
I did not match the clientele.
Blood on the clothes.
Smell of death in the beard.
Smiling like a madman.
She had no idea the dirty jacket was hiding more silver than the flat her husband rented.
She thought I was there for the free coffee.

Post 7/13
Behind the madman smile sat one cruel thought.
Money is the fastest baptism.
Turns beggars into kings.
Turns sinners into saints.
I didn’t speak.
I opened the zip on the chest pocket.
Suddenly I’m VIP.
Suddenly I’m family.

Post 8/13
I watched the instant love hit her face when the silver caught the light.
I started to doubt the idea that money cannot buy happiness.
Dirt under the nails.
Smell of the dead on my body.
I sat at the table like a king.
I changed Baldur’s blood into chips.
I put the chips on number 14.

Post 9/13
I stood up.
Walked the other way.
Screamed into a busy casino:
“TELL ME IT’S NUMBER 14.”
People dressed like saints stared at a man dressed like a grave.
They couldn’t help it.
They ran to the wheel to see what the hell was happening.

Post 10/13
Hard to say how many seconds passed.
Then strangers screamed it together:
“It’s 14.
It’s ...... 14.”
Hugs from people I had never seen.
From the woman who tried to throw me out.
From the security I had pissed off twenty seconds earlier.

Post 11/13
The maths in my head went clean.
Casino = bad people.
Me. Cain. Blood still on the hands. = good people tonight.
That’s it.
Robin Hood with a wheel.
Steal from the house.
Give it to the broken.

Post 12/13
I took the money and made it rain.
I felt what Mansa Musa felt.
I walked like him.
I showered everyone on the road back —
casino staff,
beggars,
the crew at the farm.
It felt like charity.
It felt like revenge.

Post 13/13
The woman who tried to throw me out invited me to her place.
Showed me love only a poet can describe.
She told me why she doesn’t trust her husband.
He counts.
I made it rain.

End of Chapter 5

text:
Lots of discussion about what a "software factory" is.

Also useful to call out what a software factory is not:
1/ A loose collection of automations around cloud agents
2/ A team of "AI Engineers" that developers manage interactively
3/ A set of skills and MCPs that individual engineers all adopt across a team
4/ A personal agent swarm

These are all useful things, but they aren't the right primitives for engineering scalable agent systems across an organization.

The right primitives allow you to define all your agentic workflows in code, run them entirely in the cloud, and, crucially, measure, test and improve those workflows over time to maximize agent productivity while minimizing cost.

If you start thinking from first principles "what is the system we should build as a company to get the most out of coding agents" you will end up with something like this.

I am excited to announce our new nonprofit STABL, co-founded with the wonderful @sayashk @random_walker!

Our organization derives from four beliefs:

1. Advanced AI will broadly transform society and, if managed well, this transformation will be broadly beneficial.

2. The speed of this societal transformation is governed by bottlenecks: in many cases, the bottlenecks relate to people and organizations, not AI capabilities alone. 

3. Since AI capabilities are not the sole determinant, the best strategy to manage the risks from advanced AI requires broad societal resilience, not just aligned models or capability delays, to provide defense in depth.

4. And while today’s institutions often struggle to grapple with the salvo of advanced AI, institutions will help stabilize society and will be essential, if adequately reformed, for ensuring shared prosperity. 

In addition to these beliefs, the reason to create a new organization is based on the need we see in the ecosystem. In today’s ecosystem surrounding advanced AI, many of the leading companies and external actors focus on frontier AI as a technology. We share the view that the technology itself requires dedicated attention, and some of our work at STABL will be in this direction.

But the greater need we see is for independent organizations that take AI capabilities seriously and focus on downstream societal outcomes. We are building STABL to help fill this gap. And we hope to see many other organizations and initiatives emerge to define this field.

For me, the most exciting part thus far has been seeing all the support we have gotten in our early forays. Thanks especially to @audreyt @erikbryn @hlntnr @MichaelRStrain @RobbWiller for joining us as advisers! 

We are hiring and fundraising so please reach out if you are interested in this work!

text:
I see the new criticism of Anthropic's S-1/A is that ANT "inflated October ARR by slashing token prices, which will result in compute margins falling off a cliff in Q4" as "ANT is now selling dollars for 50 cents!"...

Well, no, lol. The idea that ANT's compute margins declined significantly MoM in October insinuates that ANT was able to bring online multiple gigawatts of compute immediately on October 1st.. which obviously didn't happen. Their own disclosures combined with some other (conservative) assumptions suggest compute margins will be flat to up in Q4-26.  

$81 billion of October ARR implies ~$20 billion of Q4-26 revenue assuming zero NNARR in November and December (which seems like a pretty bearish assumption given October NNARR was $10 billion!).

We can estimate Q4-26 compute and infrastructure spend as:
- $5.2 billion of disclosed contractual obligations due 2026 as of Sep. 2026 (e.g. to be incurred in Q4-26 with Amazon, Google, etc.), plus:
- $7.2 billion estimated SpaceX spend (see below)

... for a total $12.3 billion of Q4-26 compute and infrastructure expense.

So assuming zero NNARR in November and December.. Q4-26 revenue of ~$20 billion less ~$12 billion of compute and infrastructure spend implies ~$8 billion of compute profit dollars and a 39% compute margin.. which is relatively unchanged from Q3-26, and still pretty healthy.. Obviously in a more realistic scenario in which November and December ARR continue to grow, Q4-26 compute margins would likely exceed those of Q3-26.

Note: $SPCX disclosed Anthropic (Customer B) as their largest customer in Q3-26 at 34.5% of total revenue ($14.6 billion).. so $5.0 billion of SpaceX's Q3-26 revenue came from ANT. We also know Anthropic's cloud deal with SpaceX ramps to $3.1 billion per month in December 2026, which implies $9.3 billion quarterly spend. The analysis above uses the average of Q3 2026 spend ($5.0 billion) and the full ramp ($9.3 billion), or $7.2 billion, as a proxy for ANT's Q4-26 spend with SpaceX.

The @AxiomExchange trading platform on @solana has just raised its fees to +1.60% on all SOL <> USDC trades.

You might think that Axiom has a flat fee of 1%, but when you take a closer look at the trades, you realize that they use their own propAMMs, which charge fees 0.60% higher in average than traditional AMMs.

When a token is designed or created to be traded in USDC and you're trading in SOL, you have to exchange that SOL for USDC and then buy your token.

Axiom doesn't give you a choice. 

You're forced to go through their propAMMs and end up paying between 0.6% and 1.5% fees, depending on the comparison (traditional AMMs or other propAMMs).

For every 11.88 SOL traded at that time, instead of receiving 995.72 USDC, you receive 989.36 USDC.

+6.36 USDC for Axiom
-6.36 USDC for the trader

This is what I discovered while using Circular Replay, which we just launched.

It allows you to replay transactions with their state at the time of execution, enabling you to simulate the best quotes during execution.

We've also released a Git repository to help you use it: https://t.co/nS3eEYI7xX

But between us, the best thing to do is feed the repository to your AI and start rediscovering the chain.

text:
when we first had the idea of creating this show, production asked me who my dream guest would be. I instantly said Keller.

I interviewed him once before on MTS. It was only a 30 minute convo, but I came away feeling incredibly inspired. during that interview I asked what motivated him, and he told me about his love for sci-fi books and how he wanted to build the sci-fi version of the future we were promised.

today, most people know of Zipline for their big partnership announcements and their recent $1.5B fundraise. but it didn’t start out that way. when Zipline began, flying autonomous drones in US airspace was illegal, and investors don’t typically want to invest in illegal things.

yet, Keller knew this technology would exist one day. so they found a use case so important that regulators wanted to work with them - delivering blood to hospitals in Rwanda. and after 6 years, they finally built up enough of a track record to get commercial approval to operate in the states.

A few things I learned from Keller:
- the next breakthroughs will start in the places that feel the problem the most.
- if you want to solve big global problems, focus on “trade, not aid.”
- a world where delivery feels like teleportation isn’t that far away.

Keller has some of the boldest predictions about the future of anyone I’ve met. predictions that many people disagreed with for a decade. and yet, he pursued it anyway, knowing that this scifi version of the future had to exist. 

excited and honored to share his story. The Method E1 with @Zipline CEO @keller out now.

text:
Greenlight has won all litigation with James Fishback. @jamesfishback has been ordered to return every penny of salary and bonus that we ever paid him, to repay the money we lent him, to pay most of our legal fees, and to stop claiming titles, roles and responsibilities he never had. No, Fishback was not the “Head of Macro.” Rather, as the arbitrator found, he was a “faithless servant.”

That’s a fancy legal way of saying that Fishback was so disloyal during his employment that he was ordered to refund to us his entire compensation during his tenure at Greenlight.

Ordinarily, my style would be to let this decisive ruling speak for itself.

However, Fishback has made himself a public figure. He publicly requested appointments to be a governor of the Federal Reserve and a U.S. Senator. He unsuccessfully ran for Florida Governor and has hinted that he intends to run for President in the next election. I therefore feel a civic duty to share additional details and thoughts about Fishback’s character and why he should never be placed in a position of trust.

For more than three years, Fishback engaged in a scheme to harass Greenlight Capital and me. While he made a series of false allegations against us, I generally chose to remain silent and allow the legal process to run its course. It has now done so. The result of the final arbitration is that every single claim Fishback ever made about us was either withdrawn or was legally found to be untrue. The conclusion of the arbitration represents the end of all litigation between Greenlight and Fishback, with Greenlight winning a clean sweep and being awarded over $4 million of damages against Fishback due to his tortious actions, false statements and baseless allegations.

Fishback has accused us of lawfare. Let’s set the record straight: it can’t be lawfare when he started the litigation. We simply defended ourselves and made now proved counterclaims.

This all began with Fishback demanding a $5 million pay-off to spare us the reputational harm and legal costs of defending frivolous accusations of religious discrimination, age discrimination, a politically hostile work environment and defamation.

After filing his lawsuit, Fishback told Jack Farley on the Forward Guidance podcast that “discovery is going to be fun” and would vindicate his story. Farley asked how frequently Greenlight employees referred to him as ‘Head of Macro’ and what written evidence supported his claims. Fishback answered “Well, I don’t have access to my company email. If I did, we could produce them up the wazoo.”

Well, discovery came and went and not a single piece of evidence supported any of Fishback’s bogus claims. A company-wide email search revealed that the only additional Greenlight emails calling him “Head of Macro” were those where he gave the title to himself in his signature block while sending external emails where nobody from Greenlight was copied.

Instead, discovery uncovered some outrageous conduct by Fishback. For example, Fishback and his father concocted a scheme to use a fake reference check to create his fraudulent defamation claim against us.

In September of 2023, after his employment ended, Fishback texted his father a draft of a fake reference check email that included an inquiry as to Fishback’s duties as Greenlight’s “Head of Macro.” In the same chain, Fishback texted his father:

“We need them to DEFAME us. Which THEY WILL. That’s another $1 MM right there.”

Fishback persuaded a friend of a friend who worked at an investment firm to send us the fake reference check. When we responded that Fishback was not the Head of Macro, Fishback promptly sued us, claiming that our response caused the friend’s company to walk away from making a $5 million investment in Fishback’s start-up hedge fund.

The friend of the friend testified under oath that he sent the fake reference check as a favor and that his company was never considering investing with Fishback. The friend got fired.

It was all a sham to conjure a fake legal claim to extract money from us.

There’s more that came out in the litigation:

On his final day of employment, Fishback stole Greenlight’s most valuable property, its portfolio of investments, by emailing it to his personal email (in our industry this is a big deal).

An even bigger deal is that he and his father were secretly trading positions in Greenlight’s investment portfolio in their personal accounts.

Fishback admitted to violating his confidentiality obligations to Greenlight over 60 times, including by sending confidential investment information to third parties.

Fishback made numerous statements, including that he ran macro trading at Greenlight and that he was responsible for generating over $100 million of profits – none of which were true.

Fishback told various lies about why he left Greenlight, including that he left due to a hostile political environment.

In a classic example of “You can’t fire me, I quit,” Fishback resigned right after my assistant scheduled a meeting with him so I could fire him for not doing his job.

As for the political environment at Greenlight, Fishback has repeatedly claimed that I am “a Soros aligned hedge fund billionaire.” That’s simply not so. Politically, I am just left of center. I have made large philanthropic contributions to causes supporting bi-partisanship, bridging differences and pluralism. I support centrist Democrat politicians. Some on the far-left have even tried to fight my efforts to have a more civil culture by labeling me a far-right conservative. That isn’t true either.

At Greenlight, we discuss politics so infrequently that I was unaware of Fishback’s views during his tenure. And it surprised me when he quoted scripture in his resignation email. His politics have since been made clear to all. We have no view on the sincerity of his religious beliefs but suffice it to say that we’ve been witness to him breaking those Commandments regarding stealing and lying.

Fishback campaigned for Florida Governor on an extreme “tough on crime” platform. He threatened homeless people with 15 years in jail for being homeless; he threatened teenagers participating in riots with 5 years in jail, including prosecuting minors as adults; he promised criminal prosecutions of homeowners’ associations; and planned for mass deportations of non-citizens. He even said a black man “should be lynched” for confronting him.

And yet, Fishback is a man who believes the laws don’t apply to him. Rules are for other people.

During his campaign, Fishback was challenged for living outside of Florida. His testimony that he lived in Florida was certainly news to us. When Fishback worked for Greenlight, he provided his address as being in Washington, D.C. He had us withhold D.C. resident taxes from his payroll. When he visited our New York office, he frequently submitted expense reimbursements for Amtrak trips between D.C. and New York.

Before this final arbitration, we had already won verdicts against Fishback to repay the loans that we generously lent to him on favorable terms for what he claimed at the time to be a family emergency (though that’s not what he told Jack Farley).

Even with valid court orders of U.S. Federal District Court Judges ordering him to repay us and surrender property to satisfy the judgements, Fishback simply thumbs his nose at the rule of law. He decides on his own that the Judge was a Democrat, or was appointed by a Democrat, or was otherwise politically motivated, rendering the rulings (in his mind) invalid. Fishback was ordered to repay his debt to us: He ignored it. Fishback was ordered to turn over shares in a company and 43 luxury items he owns to us: He ignored it. A company owned by Fishback was ordered to produce documents in discovery: He ignored it. And that is just a partial list.

We have little doubt that he will try to ignore the arbitration ruling against him from the arbitration he commenced. Ignoring court orders is a very dangerous way for anyone to behave. But those that do, especially in such a self-serving fashion, should not be put in a position of public trust or have influence in the enforcement of laws against others.

It doesn’t matter that I’m a Democrat. What does matter is that we gave a seemingly intelligent college drop-out a chance to achieve what he once said was his dream job. And once he was provided with that opportunity, instead of applying any semblance of a work ethic, he chose to be a “faithless servant”.

We have a theory as to why Fishback wishes to continue his political ambitions. We believe that by continuing to seek office, he will find donors to his campaign, PAC and charitable endeavors, and he will use those funds to stay in hotels, rent cars, travel and dine out – all without ever acquiring an asset in his own name that can be used to repay his legitimate creditors, like us. It’s the perfect way for Fishback to continue to grift and continue to avoid paying his debts.

It won’t work. James, you owe us over $4 million and interest is ticking.

And, when we do collect it, I will in turn donate it to a combination of the National Immigration Forum, The Center for Reproductive Rights, The Florida Rights Restoration Coalition, and The Florida Chapter of the ADL. The best way to fight your hate is to support those you hate.

text:
current thinking on the FWA pool balancer

since FWA restricts inventory management to the pool's creator, you'll deploy a balancer contract and that contract will create and own the new community pool, and you'll manage the pool through it

you add your curated nfts and deposit eth to fund an inventory of eth-backed shapes

you decide the composition of the shapes inventory, picking the denominations of the eth-backed shapes nfts and their odds

the balancer mints and lists the shapes nfts, then uses draw proceeds to restock as they get drawn. and as curated nfts leave the pool, it can adjust the shapes mix using your configuration settings

pool upkeep is permissionless through keeper incentives, and players use FWA directly as usual

eth purchases only, since pool token purchases don't generate the eth proceeds needed for replenishment

Today, we launched NovaAtom-Lite at @Geodesiclab. 
Built by a small, exceptional team in just a few months with only a few hundred GPUs, it already outperforms Isomorphic Labs' IsoDDE and Google DeepMind's AlphaFold 3 on key drug-discovery benchmarks.

But the bigger story is what AI can do for science.

Our mission is to find the shortest path from biology to medicines.

Scientific discovery has traditionally been slow, expensive, and driven by trial and error. AI has the potential to dramatically accelerate this process, from identifying promising research directions to generating hypotheses, predicting outcomes, and validating discoveries.

Imagine compressing months of scientific exploration into weeks, and eventually years of discovery into months.

This isn't just about making research 10% or 20% more efficient. It's about fundamentally changing the speed and economics of scientific discovery.

Structure prediction is a critical foundation. To design molecules that can change biology, we must first understand how they fold, interact, and function.

And we're only at the beginning. NovaAtom-Lite is our first step, NovaAtom-Pro is coming in the next few months, and our early wet-lab results are looking very promising.

The last decade was about teaching AI to understand and generate information. The next decade will be about teaching AI to understand and engineer nature.

We're not just building better models. We're working toward making drug discovery an engineering discipline.

And we're just getting started. 🚀
