text:
JUST IN: Jensen Huang's yearslong ties to Alice Huang enabled more than $7 billion of Nvidia chip sales to China, per The Information. It reports that she, her sister and her husband built a web of companies in China and Singapore. 

That network moved about 240,000 super advanced Nvidia Ai chips, worth at least $7.5 billion, to Chinese buyers. It cites 2 people who know her.

The hub, by that account, was Shanghai Century Litong. It was founded in June 2023 and became an Nvidia preferred cloud partner by October, which put it near the front of the queue. 

When export rules stalled orders, The Information says, Alice Huang leaned on her links inside Nvidia and among its distributors. 

Some of the hardware ended up serving Alibaba, Tencent and smaller Chinese labs. 

The report adds that 'Megaspeed', the Singapore cloud firm where she held a senior role, set up a Malaysian unit called Speedmatrix back in 2024. Its equipment later reached Century Litong. 

Reuters could not verify the report. Nvidia, Megaspeed and Century Litong did not immediately comment. Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing before. 

Nvidia said in October that diversion claims against Megaspeed had been investigated and debunked.

The New York Times reported in October that US officials concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset. 

China's foreign ministry calls that a smear. On Sunday Jensen told staff he had been unfaithful to his wife. His board opened an independent review with outside counsel and said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised. 

President Trump says the Federal Bureau of Investigation is looking into it, and that Jensen told him he had no idea she was a spy. 

The New York Times now reports that the Justice Department asked Commerce to pause its part of the Megaspeed probe after an Nvidia representative contacted Commerce investigators.

Washington is moving fast. 

House China committee chair John Moolenaar says Congress must "get to the bottom" of it. 3 House chairs want Huang at a closed-door briefing on 18th November and asked for his answer by 11th November. 

Senators Jim Banks and Elizabeth Warren want tighter chip export limits written into the defence bill. 

Democrats, who won both chambers in last week's midterms, say Congress will investigate. A shareholder has already sued Nvidia and Huang in San Jose, claiming investors were misled.

Investors have already marked the stock down. Nvidia closed at $178.67 on Monday, down 4.27%, and traded near $171.57 on Tuesday morning. That is about 8% in 2 sessions, or roughly $360 billion of value. Bank of America took it off its US 1 List of best ideas but kept its Buy rating. Wells Fargo cut its target to $300 from $315, and Aletheia Capital moved to Hold.

The business reports on 17th November. Nvidia guided to $108 billion of revenue, plus or minus 2%, which tops out at $110.16 billion. Analysts expect about $108.8 billion to $109.2 billion. 

Nvidia has beaten the top of its own range in each of the last 9 quarters. Its thinnest cushion was 2.6% over the midpoint, in the quarter that ended in April 2025.

The way things are happening, a highly likely scenario is that the 17th November release shows revenue above $110.16 billion. This is very likely!

The guide already leaves out China data centre sales, and every allegation so far concerns where chips went in past years. I am wrong if reported revenue for the quarter is $110.16 billion or less.

text:
LlamaRisk proposes repositioning Aave V3 Core, Aave's largest market, to focus on liquid, blue-chip collateral.

The proposal would remove several categories of exposure:

1. Restaking assets
2. Leveraged wrapping strategies
3. Issuers whose operational and security resources fall short of Aave's risk standards
4. Low-demand reserves that no longer justify ongoing maintenance

This means potentially moving $1.52B in collateral backing $1.17B in debt out of V3 Core in favour of blue-chip collateral.

As the risk landscape evolves and Aave V4 grows, the goal is to sharpen V3 Core's risk profile and raise the bar for collateral eligibility.

Some affected assets could transition to isolated Aave V4 markets, where more granular risk controls allow for better risk-reward alignment.

The proposal comes from LlamaRisk, an Aave Protocol Risk Manager, and remains subject to governance discussions and engagement with asset issuers.

Aave will continue applying continuous risk assessment for all assets across all deployments.

Looked into Arcus. Expected a lot more from the team that built dYdX

- your money sits in one upgradeable vault on Robinhood Chain: 0x14b107cf534239c59571b066cb6497a321da897c
- instead of proofs, 2 of 3 validator wallets sign off on every batch
- three contracts are admins of the vault and of each other: a timelock with a 1 day delay, the validator contract and a CheckpointManager
- only the timelock waits. the other two can upgrade the vault right away, and "the compromise of any single superadmin confers full upgrade and configuration authority"
- there's an escape hatch for when the validators go down. two 2/5 multisigs with the same five signers can pause deposits and withdrawals, escape hatch included
- the admin can also swap out the contract withdrawals go through

"strictly non-custodial" in practice you're trusting whoever holds 3 validator keys

dYdX v3 was one of the best exchanges crypto has had. It was a ZK rollup with proofs and data on Ethereum, forced withdrawals and an escape hatch. It made it to Stage 1 and was one requirement short of Stage 2. It's shut down now and people still withdraw from it through the escape hatch without the operator

"Ten years ago, if I had five founders show up and they asked for a billion dollars and I gave it to them, what would happen?"

"They would detonate, right? They would hire a bunch of engineers, and then you're really fucked, right? You can't throw capital in it."

Two lessons about uncovering and exposing information:

1️⃣ A leak always has a motive. Ask who benefits. Be cautious, and rely on open-source information whenever possible.

2️⃣ Exposing a story doesn't mean people will pay attention. Scoops operate in a pull market: information only travels when someone has an interest in spreading it.

Now, consider the Jensen affair:

▶️ Why is everyone suddenly talking about it? Apparently, the story originated with a tip from the intelligence community. Who benefits from bringing it to light now?

▶️ @CulperResearch exposed the whole story back in May. Nobody cared. Now everyone does.

What changed?

text:
As promised, here’s my setup for cross-channel analytics ↓

https://t.co/dRaWjAst9l

TL;DR:

→ Components

Google Sheets = database: one spreadsheet for content, plus separate spreadsheets for paid placements, zero-cost marketing experiments, and SEO.

Typefully = a list of published posts via API, including full text and tags.

GA4 (+ Search Console) = traffic and sign-ups on the newsletter site, by page and source.

n8n = glue. A workflow runs twice a week, collects new posts from every platform, labels them, and writes snapshots into Sheets.

Claude built most of the above with me: it labels posts, loads the weekly exports, writes the weekly analysis, and builds the dashboard (I also have it as an artefact for visualisation).

Native exports: Substack (subscribers, traffic sources, growth sources), Telegram channel statistics, and X analytics CSVs.

→ The workflow

Twice a week (Monday and Thursday morning), the n8n workflow pulls new posts: the Substack archive and notes, the public web page of the Telegram channel, and published drafts from Typefully. Every new post gets a row.

A model suggests a topic (one of 12 marketing directions, e.g., SEO / SMM / Strategy), a format for newsletter issues, and a post type based on the desired target action—e.g., discovery (main goal: maximise shares) or resource (main goal: link clicks). I review the labels once a week and correct them. Edited copies of the same post on other platforms are detected automatically and inherit the original labels.

At 7 days and 30 days, the workflow writes a metrics row for each post. Public numbers (likes, restacks, views, reactions) come in automatically. Private ones are added by hand from screenshots.

On Monday, I drop the Telegram, X, and Substack exports into a Claude chat. Claude loads them into the right tabs, checks the totals against the files, and writes a short summary of the week.

A single page reads the sheets and shows trends, top posts relative to a typical post on that platform, article promotion windows, and a “this week” to-do list.

Full breakdown → https://t.co/XUkqpncnbR

The best tip I can give any emerging creator is this: content is a system.

Analytics, feedback loops, and consistent strategy experiments are the three things that divide winners from losers.

Writing content is a skill. And if you don’t have an analytics system, you don’t have facts – just gut feeling.

Why are so many of these rolls over the adult-citizen count?🚨 COLORADO ELECTION QUESTIONS: WHY DO SOME COUNTIES REPORT MORE VOTER REGISTRATIONS THAN ESTIMATED ADULT CITIZENS?

A claim circulating online says 53 of Colorado’s 64 counties exceed 100% when registered voters are compared with Census estimates of adult citizens.

The reported figures include:

🔴 San Juan County: 150.4%
🔴 Mineral County: 147.4%
🔴 Elbert County: 126.3%
🔴 Douglas County: 117.8%
🔴 El Paso County: reportedly 50,161 registrations above its citizen adult population estimate.

These numbers deserve a closer look—but the categories matter.

WHAT THE RECORDS SHOW:

🔎 Federal 2024 election data reported approximately 4.07 million active registrations in Colorado, plus another 508,668 inactive registrations.

🔎 Colorado also maintains preregistrations for eligible young people who have not yet turned 18.

🔎 Inactive records and preregistrations must not be treated as equivalent to active, eligible adult voters.

🔎 Census population figures are estimates, not a live count of every eligible citizen in each county. Small counties can show especially large percentage differences.

WHAT SHOULD BE CHECKED?

1. How many active registrations exist in each county?
2. How many inactive records remain, and how old are they?
3. Are preregistered minors being included in the comparison?
4. Are duplicate, deceased, and relocated voter records being identified and resolved?
5. Are the Census estimates and voter-registration totals from comparable dates?
6. Can officials publish a county-by-county reconciliation explaining every figure above 100%?

🇺🇸 THE PUBLIC DESERVES ACCURATE ROLLS, CLEAR NUMBERS, AND TRANSPARENT ELECTION ADMINISTRATION.

RELEASE THE DATA. CHECK THE RECORDS. RECONCILE THE NUMBERS.

text:
Hey Ben, you know I've respected your work for years but I'm a bit confused about what concrete customer problem does the blockchain solve for inference? We run an inference provider and customers mostly care about price, performance, privacy, security, and data use, where TEEs seem more directly relevant.

If anything, onchain settlement exposes customer spend and provider relationships while adding wallet, settlement / integration complexity for teams that already pay in dollars.

I find the space intellectually stimulating but commercially not realistic. What am I missing?
author: Cameron_Dennis_

text:
Hey Cameron, TEEs (or verifiable FHE) are of course directly relevant for privacy and security. I see them as complementary to blockchains, and my broader point is that there is synergy between inference market design and the distributed systems and mechanism design problems we have encountered with blockchains.

First, inference markets can do more than guarantee that a user pays at most “$x per token”—they can also enforce that the user only pays for outputs meeting an agreed quality test. Most generally, users could provide a payment function f(Q,R) over queries Q and responses R to a mechanism that ensures that the user pays no more than f(Q,R) for a response R. Here f need not simply charge per token. This can benefit not only from a more advanced mechanism (like an auction) that better matches users with inference providers, but also from a way to enforce the conditional payment. If you want to do that without a trusted centralized party, that’s where blockchains combined with TEEs can help.

Second, the combination of blockchains with TEEs is directly relevant to data attribution. I wrote an article about this a while ago, though I’m sure others have made similar observations. https://t.co/i6B8il6t2W

Even if a centrally operated TEE keeps the model encrypted, the enclave still needs a way to verify that the policy has been satisfied, such as confirming that a payment to data owners has occurred, before responding to a query. Moreover, there is platform risk. The operator could shut off access to the enclave at any time, giving it leverage to force data owners to agree to new policies. Data owners might need guarantees that a model trained on their data remains accessible under the original policies, with no centralized player able to unilaterally change the rules.

Combining a (low-latency!!) blockchain with a network of TEEs could allow other operators to continue serving the model under the same policies if one operator shuts down or demands different terms.

text:
Lux Foods (YC F26) is redesigning plants and farms to make exceptional fruit abundant.

Plants normally make their own sugars through photosynthesis, a process that is ~1% efficient in converting solar energy into biomass. Lux supplies sugars directly through a growing medium and regenerates compact, fruit-dominant plantlets from small pieces of tissue. Starting with tomatoes, these plantlets grow under 90% lower light intensity than conventional cultivation. They’re also easier for robots to handle. Instead of asking robots to navigate deformable plants and occluded fruit, Lux designs simplified plant biology and hardware together to make exceptional fruit abundant: a new chapter in crop domestication built around the food we want to eat.

Today’s supply chains often reward fruit that survives shipping rather than fruit that tastes best. Lux is building toward year-round, pesticide-free production near the people who eat it, with varieties chosen for flavor, nutrition, and peak ripeness. Heirloom, rare, and wild fruit should be everyday food.

quoted_text:
Greenlight has won all litigation with James Fishback. @jamesfishback has been ordered to return every penny of salary and bonus that we ever paid him, to repay the money we lent him, to pay most of our legal fees, and to stop claiming titles, roles and responsibilities he never had. No, Fishback was not the “Head of Macro.” Rather, as the arbitrator found, he was a “faithless servant.”

That’s a fancy legal way of saying that Fishback was so disloyal during his employment that he was ordered to refund to us his entire compensation during his tenure at Greenlight.

Ordinarily, my style would be to let this decisive ruling speak for itself.

However, Fishback has made himself a public figure. He publicly requested appointments to be a governor of the Federal Reserve and a U.S. Senator. He unsuccessfully ran for Florida Governor and has hinted that he intends to run for President in the next election. I therefore feel a civic duty to share additional details and thoughts about Fishback’s character and why he should never be placed in a position of trust.

For more than three years, Fishback engaged in a scheme to harass Greenlight Capital and me. While he made a series of false allegations against us, I generally chose to remain silent and allow the legal process to run its course. It has now done so. The result of the final arbitration is that every single claim Fishback ever made about us was either withdrawn or was legally found to be untrue. The conclusion of the arbitration represents the end of all litigation between Greenlight and Fishback, with Greenlight winning a clean sweep and being awarded over $4 million of damages against Fishback due to his tortious actions, false statements and baseless allegations.

Fishback has accused us of lawfare. Let’s set the record straight: it can’t be lawfare when he started the litigation. We simply defended ourselves and made now proved counterclaims.

This all began with Fishback demanding a $5 million pay-off to spare us the reputational harm and legal costs of defending frivolous accusations of religious discrimination, age discrimination, a politically hostile work environment and defamation.

After filing his lawsuit, Fishback told Jack Farley on the Forward Guidance podcast that “discovery is going to be fun” and would vindicate his story. Farley asked how frequently Greenlight employees referred to him as ‘Head of Macro’ and what written evidence supported his claims. Fishback answered “Well, I don’t have access to my company email. If I did, we could produce them up the wazoo.”

Well, discovery came and went and not a single piece of evidence supported any of Fishback’s bogus claims. A company-wide email search revealed that the only additional Greenlight emails calling him “Head of Macro” were those where he gave the title to himself in his signature block while sending external emails where nobody from Greenlight was copied.

Instead, discovery uncovered some outrageous conduct by Fishback. For example, Fishback and his father concocted a scheme to use a fake reference check to create his fraudulent defamation claim against us.

In September of 2023, after his employment ended, Fishback texted his father a draft of a fake reference check email that included an inquiry as to Fishback’s duties as Greenlight’s “Head of Macro.” In the same chain, Fishback texted his father:

“We need them to DEFAME us. Which THEY WILL. That’s another $1 MM right there.”

Fishback persuaded a friend of a friend who worked at an investment firm to send us the fake reference check. When we responded that Fishback was not the Head of Macro, Fishback promptly sued us, claiming that our response caused the friend’s company to walk away from making a $5 million investment in Fishback’s start-up hedge fund.

The friend of the friend testified under oath that he sent the fake reference check as a favor and that his company was never considering investing with Fishback. The friend got fired.

It was all a sham to conjure a fake legal claim to extract money from us.

There’s more that came out in the litigation:

On his final day of employment, Fishback stole Greenlight’s most valuable property, its portfolio of investments, by emailing it to his personal email (in our industry this is a big deal).

An even bigger deal is that he and his father were secretly trading positions in Greenlight’s investment portfolio in their personal accounts.

Fishback admitted to violating his confidentiality obligations to Greenlight over 60 times, including by sending confidential investment information to third parties.

Fishback made numerous statements, including that he ran macro trading at Greenlight and that he was responsible for generating over $100 million of profits – none of which were true.

Fishback told various lies about why he left Greenlight, including that he left due to a hostile political environment.

In a classic example of “You can’t fire me, I quit,” Fishback resigned right after my assistant scheduled a meeting with him so I could fire him for not doing his job.

As for the political environment at Greenlight, Fishback has repeatedly claimed that I am “a Soros aligned hedge fund billionaire.” That’s simply not so. Politically, I am just left of center. I have made large philanthropic contributions to causes supporting bi-partisanship, bridging differences and pluralism. I support centrist Democrat politicians. Some on the far-left have even tried to fight my efforts to have a more civil culture by labeling me a far-right conservative. That isn’t true either.

At Greenlight, we discuss politics so infrequently that I was unaware of Fishback’s views during his tenure. And it surprised me when he quoted scripture in his resignation email. His politics have since been made clear to all. We have no view on the sincerity of his religious beliefs but suffice it to say that we’ve been witness to him breaking those Commandments regarding stealing and lying.

Fishback campaigned for Florida Governor on an extreme “tough on crime” platform. He threatened homeless people with 15 years in jail for being homeless; he threatened teenagers participating in riots with 5 years in jail, including prosecuting minors as adults; he promised criminal prosecutions of homeowners’ associations; and planned for mass deportations of non-citizens. He even said a black man “should be lynched” for confronting him.

And yet, Fishback is a man who believes the laws don’t apply to him. Rules are for other people.

During his campaign, Fishback was challenged for living outside of Florida. His testimony that he lived in Florida was certainly news to us. When Fishback worked for Greenlight, he provided his address as being in Washington, D.C. He had us withhold D.C. resident taxes from his payroll. When he visited our New York office, he frequently submitted expense reimbursements for Amtrak trips between D.C. and New York.

Before this final arbitration, we had already won verdicts against Fishback to repay the loans that we generously lent to him on favorable terms for what he claimed at the time to be a family emergency (though that’s not what he told Jack Farley).

Even with valid court orders of U.S. Federal District Court Judges ordering him to repay us and surrender property to satisfy the judgements, Fishback simply thumbs his nose at the rule of law. He decides on his own that the Judge was a Democrat, or was appointed by a Democrat, or was otherwise politically motivated, rendering the rulings (in his mind) invalid. Fishback was ordered to repay his debt to us: He ignored it. Fishback was ordered to turn over shares in a company and 43 luxury items he owns to us: He ignored it. A company owned by Fishback was ordered to produce documents in discovery: He ignored it. And that is just a partial list.

We have little doubt that he will try to ignore the arbitration ruling against him from the arbitration he commenced. Ignoring court orders is a very dangerous way for anyone to behave. But those that do, especially in such a self-serving fashion, should not be put in a position of public trust or have influence in the enforcement of laws against others.

It doesn’t matter that I’m a Democrat. What does matter is that we gave a seemingly intelligent college drop-out a chance to achieve what he once said was his dream job. And once he was provided with that opportunity, instead of applying any semblance of a work ethic, he chose to be a “faithless servant”.

We have a theory as to why Fishback wishes to continue his political ambitions. We believe that by continuing to seek office, he will find donors to his campaign, PAC and charitable endeavors, and he will use those funds to stay in hotels, rent cars, travel and dine out – all without ever acquiring an asset in his own name that can be used to repay his legitimate creditors, like us. It’s the perfect way for Fishback to continue to grift and continue to avoid paying his debts.

It won’t work. James, you owe us over $4 million and interest is ticking.

And, when we do collect it, I will in turn donate it to a combination of the National Immigration Forum, The Center for Reproductive Rights, The Florida Rights Restoration Coalition, and The Florida Chapter of the ADL. The best way to fight your hate is to support those you hate.

Robots are learning from human videos, but even the best AI models struggle to understand exactly what our hands are doing.

Perceptron just released EgoHome, a new benchmark built from 137 first-person videos of everyday household tasks.

The dataset includes 417,912 hand bounding boxes and 3,357 action segments shorter than one second.

The results are revealing:

• Perceptron scores 79/100 on subtasks, compared with 80 for GPT-6 Astra.
• On individual hand actions, GPT-6 Astra reaches 50 while Perceptron scores 42.
• No tested model scores above 50 on hand actions.

A robot learning from human demonstrations needs that second level of detail.

EgoHome's dataset and evaluation code are publicly available.

Full breakdown in the video.

The 100 Year Conversation continues with Vlad Tenev.

Vlad was born in Bulgaria and moved to the United States as a child. When he was ten or eleven, he was figuring out investing on dial-up with a pretend portfolio on Yahoo Finance.

author: hooeem
quoted_text:
no more doom-scrolling.

here’s how to build an agent that researches for you every single day: 👇 

1: open a bot with web access and scheduling, such as grok bot
2: list the topics, companies and industries you want to follow, and why each one matters to you
3: give it links to the sources, channels and accounts you trust
4: make it prove access by fetching the latest item from each source, with a link, so you can see the gaps
5: set your filter: concrete developments with evidence in. repeated announcements out
6: define the briefing: up to 5 updates from the last 24 hours. same-story posts merged.
7: for each update, get what changed, why you should care, how to use it, the original link, and a flag on anything unverified
8: run a test briefing and mark each result useful or irrelevant
9: have it save your instructions and a log of covered stories, then run it again. it should only repeat a story when there's a meaningful update
10: schedule it for your time and timezone, confirm where it will arrive, and tune it over the first week.

there you have it, your macro news, crypto news, ai news, equities news, you can have a bot for every single one!

go and build it!

author: lex_node
quoted_text:
Anthropic is about to sell the public a trillion-dollar company controlled by 2 shares worth less than a penny.

And the people buying it will have almost no way to change anything that happens next.

I read the voting section of Anthropic's IPO filing, and I think it's the most one-sided deal ever offered to regular investors at this size:

There is exactly ONE Class F share. It belongs to an LLC owned by 7 of Anthropic's co-founders, and it carries 50.1% of all the votes.

There is exactly ONE Class T share. It belongs to Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, and it elects a majority of the board.

If Anthropic were ever liquidated, each of those 2 shares would get its par value of $0.00001.

The public gets Class A shares instead. And Anthropic's own filing says this structure may effectively eliminate their ability to influence important decisions, including a sale of the company.

So here's what that means for anyone who buys:

- They can't replace the board if the company stumbles, because the trust picks the majority and the founders hold half the vote.
- They can't push for a sale, even if someone offers a huge premium.
- They can't stop the board from putting the mission ahead of their money. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, so the board has to weigh shareholders against the long-term benefit of humanity.
- And they can't easily sue over it. Delaware law requires at least 2% of the shares or $2 million worth of stock to bring that kind of claim.

This isn't some far-off hypothetical either.

The filing warns that slowing AI development for safety may not maximize stockholder value. It also says Anthropic recently paused training a next-generation model for more than a month over safety and security concerns.

A public shareholder would've had zero say in that pause.

And here's the part I can't get past:

Each co-founder has pledged to give 80% of their Anthropic equity to charity. The Class F vote stays at 50.1% no matter how much stock they still own.

So the founders can give away most of their money and keep all of their control.

Dario Amodei told 60 Minutes last year that he's deeply uncomfortable with AI decisions being made by a few companies and a few people. When he was asked who elected him, he said no one.

Now his company's IPO hands 50.1% of the votes to 7 people, and he's one of them.

And guess who's being lined up to buy it?

Anthropic has weighed reserving 15% to 20% of the IPO for individual investors, according to Bloomberg. JPMorgan is leading the US retail push, and Citigroup is handling retail buyers in places like Japan, Britain and Canada.

The same filing warns that AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

So regular people are being asked to buy a company that says its product could threaten humanity, with no real vote on how it's run.

Anthropic's answer is that this is the whole point. The structure is built to keep Wall Street from pressuring it into cutting corners on safety. The trustees have no financial stake in the company. Google and Meta gave their founders control and still made shareholders rich. And every buyer gets all of this in writing before they buy.

But Zuckerberg's control comes from shares he owns, so when Meta's stock falls, he loses money too. Anthropic's 2 control shares can't lose anything.

Anyone buying this IPO is paying full price to hand control to 7 founders and 5 trustees.

They're desperate for money and they don't care about your money.

i wanted a place to work through those questions, keep the sources next to the charts, and write down an argument i could come back to and challenge later.

that’s what we’re building: a research workspace for exploring NEAR data and developing investment theses.

seeing builders work on agents that earn, spend, and pay for services gives me even more questions to investigate. especially around how we’ll measure the economic activity they create.

getting closer to a full demo now. will share more screens and pieces of the research as we go.

back to the build 🫡

I am still looking for more AI infra supply side that wants to get paid by agents.

Last week we integrated @BoundlessHQ for unstoppable inference & @e2b for unstoppable sandboxes.

We are missing other critical infra such as model routers or cloud platforms like Cloudflare and Vercel. Of course the dream would be to get an EC2 box or an EKS cluster with a single API call from your agent.

The missing component that we hear from larger providers many time is identity, so it's a good thing we just added identity support to the Machine Payments Protocol.

Normally your agent would call a paid API, get a 402 back, and then need to re-submit its call with a signed payment in the header.

For identity, we simply introduce an additional roundtrip, where the API can say "I also need you to prove ownership of this email", or "I need to find your wallet in my database first", or "I need to check this 3p API whether you're a good or bad person".

We are looking for early "heavy hitter" partners who want to unlock getting paid with agents for their most critical products.

Please DM me if you want early access and want to collaborate on shaping not just payments but also identity for agents.

Many exploits follow every rule of the chain and still drain users. Audits and monitoring help, but they act before deployment or after the damage is done.

→ Apps write their own safety rules: "the owner never changes", "no unbacked mint", "this vault can't be drained in one tx"
→ Linea's sequencer checks every transaction against them before it lands in a block
→ Any tx that breaks a rule is excluded. It never settles.

Rules are public, require no contract changes, and each app sets its own.

text:
In 2013, @edbolian and two others drove from New York to Los Angeles in 28h50m, moving at an average of 100.3mph in a Mercedes-Benz CL55 AMG.

That crowned him king of the Cannonball Run, an unofficial time-trial for crossing the continental U.S. as fast as possible.

Ed and his co-driver Dave Black, plus Dan Huang along for support, drove a route Ed says he'd been scheming since high school.

To help them out, they had a couple of friends driving hours ahead to flag any upcoming construction or hazards.

(Much more lowkey than the strategy for the 2006 crew whose record of 31h04m they bested, who, per Ed, used a spotter plane.)

"I did not have any friends with airplanes."

Ed's record stood for six years, until a new team in 2019 completed the cross-country drive in 27h25m in a purpose-built Mercedes E63 AMG with an extra 45-gallon fuel tank and scouts staggered ahead of the car.

Then Covid's empty, less-policed roads broke open the Cannonball Run's floodgates. In five weeks, Ed's record was beaten seven times, all the way down to 25h39m, over three hours faster than he drove in 2013.

"The most recent record involved 35 spotter cars, driving at pace with the organizers of the run, with the drivers agreeing to pay tickets for them if they get stopped."

text:
Polymarket is UNFIXABLE 

Shayne is doing the thing again

The thing he does every couple of months. The thing that made him successful: writing people on X, promising Polymarket will turn around. 

He can’t. It’s unfixable.

Polymarket will lose this. 100%. No going back.

Here’s why, in game theory and facts 👇

tl;dr:

– Kalshi owns 90% of the market. Polymarket US won’t take it back

– sentiment has never been lower, and nothing driving it is about to change

– their social media growth play backfired. Nobody trusts anything they say anymore

– Hyperliquid and a wave of new venues are tearing the defi market apart

– the day Hyperliquid lists politics, the bonders will leave Polymarket

– Robinhood is coming for the retail distribution Polymarket always bragged about

– best case: number two. Likely a valuation under $1B, stuck there for a while

First mover is a head start, not a moat.

Full details:

– Sentiment

Post anything anti-Polymarket and watch who likes it. Half of them have Polymarket affiliate badges. Another half of them have Polymarket employee badges 

Read that again. Their own people.

Sentiment has never been lower, and this isn’t the bottom. Everything driving it lower is still there:

– product quality - bad

– builder program quality - horrible

– communication quality - non-existent

– high fees - max extraction

– no token - and never will be

Even if some of it gets fixed, people won’t come back in storms.

The AI slop influencer KOLs. The zcsdao, the badge dramas... Its all so tiresome. Then, UMA Resolutions that keep going wrong. UMA Rugs.
Fee hikes without the community, again and again. You don’t fix that by sending people merch...

FACTS:

– taker fees introduced, then expanded to almost every market

– two third-party breaches in five months, with users drained both times

– traders suing over a market they say was resolved wrong

– the WSJ reporting that Shayne told staff to ignore payment fraud to keep growing

– a token “confirmed” in October 2025 LOL

Nothing is unfixable. Maybe over years. But not now. Not in the next 12 months. Maybe never.

Alternatives keep popping up. Kalshi keeps delivering. Polymarket lost its first-mover advantage, so good enough isn’t enough anymore. It has to outperform. 
And the leadership has already shown it can’t.

– The trust is gone

Polymarket’s whole social media growth strategy was an experiment, and it blew up in their face.

Here’s what they did:

– They shilled a token over and over and never delivered. “There will be a token” was October 2025. 

– They kept paying influencers. Just recently, paid accounts shilled the token, then deleted the tweets.

– POLITICO found Polymarket’s CMO sent $2.5M+ from his personal PayPal to 800+ people. At least 490 sponsored posts on X were never disclosed.

– The WSJ found creators paid to film “winning bets” on fake replica versions of the site. When journalists started asking, many of them deleted the videos.

– Then came the badge armies. Polymarket’s growth machine, which William LeGate runs, handed affiliate badges to thousands of accounts. Plenty of them weren’t even users. Paid influencer armies, run like a Russian bot farm, posing as “the Polymarket community.” Polymarket’s own Traders account eventually had to purge badge holders it called fake “egirl” accounts.

None of it was organic. And now there are lawsuits over it.

The result: nobody trusts anything they do. Every post, every “community” account, and every announcement gets read with suspicion first, and usually with spite.

That’s insane for a company valued at $21B. And you can’t buy that trust back with another influencer campaign.

– Polymarket US

Here’s what you guys on X don’t know: the normie consumers who actually trade on it know it doesn’t work. It runs on a MongoDB-based order book, and it breaks so often it’s a meme.

Kalshi owns 90% of the market, and Kalshi delivers. Polymarket has no chance in the US. Nobody is magically taking that market from Kalshi.

– Hyperliquid

Hyperliquid is going after market share, aggressively. It charges zero fees to open a position, and every outcome position shares one margin account with your perps.

On the markets it lists, it already competes. Within 19 days of launch, it matched Polymarket’s volume on daily BTC binaries.

The one thing it doesn’t have yet is politics. That’s where 40%+ of Polymarket’s volume comes from, and it’s where all the bonders are.

Bonders are the high volume traders on the platform (next to sports). They park big capital at 97–99¢ for a thin, safe yield. For them it’s pure math: lower fees and better capital efficiency win. Every time.

The day Hyperliquid lists political events, the bonders move. Instantly.

– The international market is getting ripped apart

Polymarket international isn’t fixable right now.

Then there are all the new competitors. They’re small: Pascal, PredictFun, Trueo, Meridian. But every one of them is fighting for the same thing, which is Polymarket’s international share.

And Polymarket International still doesn’t have a mobile app. A $1B budget and no mobile app, lmao. What is wrong with you? ShareXYZ will take mobile 100%

– Robinhood

Robinhood deserves its own section. It has the retail distribution Polymarket always bragged about, and Meridian is already live on Robinhood Chain.

When the next Robinhood L2 season comes, and they double down on prediction markets and frontier assets, Polymarket loses that edge too.

– The ecosystem they never built

There was a window. Polymarket could have launched an L2, built a whole frontier-markets ecosystem on top of it, and run retail through it like Robinhood is doing now.

They let it close. That advantage is gone.

– Ok, first of all, I lied

They have one tiny chance.

ASAP, SPAC through the 1789 fund’s SPAC vehicle. Raise capital. Get established publicly with the frontier-markets narrative and suck some liquidity out of the markets.

Pull that off, and they might be the first mover again. It’s the only advantage that could still save them.

And I believe that’s exactly what’s happening right now. Work the numbers. Extract fees wherever possible. Make the prospectus look juicy enough to justify the valuation. That’s what the fee hikes are really about.

The setup is already there. In September, 1789 Capital led Polymarket’s $1B round at $21B. 1789’s team runs a SPAC, Colombier III, which raised $299M in February. The WSJ says Polymarket is eyeing an IPO next year, and it recently hired its first CFO.

So no token for you.

– If they don’t pull it off

They won’t launch a token in this market, and the investors need to make some $. So everyone is pushing for the IPO.

If the SPAC doesn’t happen: two years of decline. Then, after all the lavish spending, a down round. Maybe even a Bending Spoons case.

My prediction:

Kalshi takes 95% of the US market. HIP-4, Meridian, Pascal, Trueo, PredictFun and the rest split what’s left, and Share takes mobile.

Best case, Polymarket stays number two. There’s a high chance it drops to a valuation under $1B and stays there for a while.

Congrats to everyone who sold secondaries. If you didn’t, well...

Does Polymarket make it to the public markets, or get bought first?

quoted_text:
Swarm riders and Swarm-native companies

AI-use even among highly AI-native people is power-law distributed.

There seems to be a new class of people — call them “swarm riders” — who are capable of consistently commanding large swarms of agents to productive ends.

This is a new kind of managerial skill, analogous to the skill it takes to manage large organizations of people, but wholly different in nature and of course more technical.

Based on the swarm riders we know (including many at @Tempo and @Paradigm), these people are capable of productive token spend that is 1000x-10000x higher than median software engineers, and 100x higher than top 5% Claude Code users.

The art of swarm riding is different from software engineering and more akin to machine learning, where practitioners grapple with black box systems: defining reward functions and evals, transmuting non-verifiable problems into verifiable problems, running experiments, etc.

Swarm-native companies are a new class of company founded by and populated by swarm riders. These companies are organized around swarms in a way that conventional companies will struggle to replicate, as the cost of internal human coordination is sand in the gears of an effective swarm. Effective swarm-native companies will define the right reward functions and evals, remove functional and bureaucratic barriers, and then let the swarms cook.

We’ve gotten to see a few swarm-native companies up close — reshaping financial rails @Tempo, building a new gaming platform @Spawn, cyber swarms at Cathedral Systems — and it’s clear these teams wield a significant advantage over pre-AI teams.

Some questions I’ve been wondering about:

1) How fast will swarm riding diffuse through the economy? The implications for token spend could be significant.

2) Can swarms be effectively adopted by existing companies or will it generally track the formation of new swarm-native companies?

3) What becomes scarce as swarm capabilities themselves commoditize (through frontier models becoming better at swarming, swarm capabilities built into harnesses, etc)? Cultures and teams that can define reward functions well and otherwise get out of the way?

text:
Labor markets continue to see gains, but is this yesterday’s news?

Today's nonfarm payroll figure came in stronger than expected at 165,000 jobs gained in October, with upward revisions of 84,000 for the prior two months. The unemployment rate remained fairly steady at 4.1%.

For some time, we've characterized the labor market as a period of "low hire/low fire" jobs growth, whereby firms are neither hiring many new workers nor laying many off. Indeed, average monthly jobs growth over the past 6- and 12-month periods has been 83,000 and 74,000, respectively. Today's stronger numbers are encouraging, but they need to be considered within the context of broader economic growth.

Interestingly, we find ourselves in an environment where economic growth and labor market gains appear to be decoupling in profound ways. Real GDP growth accelerated to 3.4% in the third quarter, yet labor market gains have been more modest over the last several months. An outsized portion of the growth we're witnessing derives from capital expenditure related to the AI infrastructure buildout. Consider that investment in computers and peripheral equipment, representing just 2% of overall GDP, accounted for more than a third of GDP growth over the last 12 months.

From a monetary policy standpoint, as long as we remain in this solid economic environment, with inflation running well above the Fed's 2% target, labor markets are unlikely to be top of mind for policymakers. Meanwhile, the profound AI investment cycle continues to drive broad economic and corporate earnings growth. Yet an increasingly concentrated group of companies is creating and capturing an outsized share of the benefits, leaving the broader equity market highly sensitive to changes in just a handful of names. In recent days, we've begun to see greater equity market volatility amid concerns over potential future regulation.

Today's payroll data was interesting and confirmatory of an economy that has been operating at a breathtakingly strong pace. But it's also a comprehensive read on labor relative to yesterday's economic conditions. Markets today are much more focused on the future of AI spending, capital allocation and rebalancing activity, as well as how a new political framework will influence growth, fiscal conditions and the operating environment for different industries.

How, then, should one position fixed income portfolios? In our view, the regime has shifted and fixed income yields reside at historically attractive levels. Real rates are positive across the globe, while the equity risk premium remains paper-thin and equity market concentration creates fragility and volatility that investors don't need to accept. We think a diversified, income-oriented portfolio can deliver equity-like returns today with dramatically less volatility, drawdown and concentration risk. Recent market activity seems to reinforce that view and we think that should continue well into 2027.

text:
After 2mo in the oven, I'm excited to share the Mission Statement at https://t.co/ENJpTp5ttR ♾🌌

In the fast-paced world of software dev, it's easy to take shortcuts, but I believe strongly that your Mission Statement should not be one of them.

Mission statements are a fundamental artifact that anything that "grows" truly must have in order to have a chance at being successful over time.

Orgs, teams, products, and even individuals.

But boy is it difficult to put together a good one... 😩

Here's why:

A great mission statement is both specific enough to weigh day-to-day prioritization, yet broad enough to guide 3yr plans.

https://t.co/ENJpTp5ttR's mission will now guide the product's every move.

Another reason they are difficult, is that they force you to be brutally honest with who you are, what you do, and why.

Sometimes, this is not the easiest of conversations to have with yourself, let alone with others.

During my most recent 10yrs as a leader of product teams, I always made it a point to sit down with everyone and align on a mission statement.

That convo was always first met with hesitation and seen as a distraction from "real work."

But then, everyone brings their ideas, their perspective, eyes widen and smiles appear as you start to get somewhere meaningful.

It quickly turns into a valuable opportunity to collaborate and align on a broader strategic purpose that you all share in together.

...It quickly turns into some of the most valuable IP the team produces.

And the team comes away with a measuring stick for reassuring each and every decision they make.

That is why they are so challenging, but also why they are SO rewarding once you've finally felt that feeling of "THIS IS IT, THIS IS US!"

quoted_text:
THIS IS MY FINAL POST ABOUT @Enter_Elysium.

I used to be extremely bullish on Elysium.

I spent months following the ecosystem, hunting for potential gems, supporting projects, and believing this could become one of the biggest opportunities out there.

But now? I'm genuinely disappointed.

1. THEY TALKED ABOUT BUILDERS, BUT ALL WE GOT WAS A FUCKING CASINO.

For months, we heard endless promises about builders, community, long-term value, and a sustainable ecosystem.

But the moment mainnet went live, what did we get?

A massive sell-off.

The early supporters, the believers, and the people who helped grow this ecosystem ended up becoming exit liquidity.

2. ASCEND STABBED THE OGs IN THE BACK.

Before mainnet, many projects spent weeks building their communities, liquidity, and trust.

Then @AscendLaunch suddenly opened before the official mainnet launch.

A flood of copycat tokens appeared, stealing tickers like $e/acc and $BLOB.

Liquidity got fragmented. OG projects suffered. Communities that had been building from day one were left dealing with the consequences.

Is this really how Elysium treats its earliest supporters?

3. TOKEN AFTER TOKEN GOT ABSOLUTELY DESTROYED.

Just look at these numbers:

$OBOL -97.8%
$HELIOS -97.6%
$SPIRE -96.6%
$LETHE -93%
$CACHE -91.7%
$EACCAT -87% to -90%
$STOCKIUM -82%
$KRATER -73.3%
$A/ACC -70%
$VYRO -69.6%
$CHAMELEON -60%
$BLOB -54%
$STYX -44.5%
$AGORA -43%
$KLEOS -33%

And let's not forget $VOLTA, which also faced heavy selling pressure.

These are reported drawdowns, not live price updates.
I understand that memecoins are risky.

But when almost the entire ecosystem is bleeding, can we seriously call this a successful mainnet launch?

4. LAUNCHPAD WAR OR RUG WAR?

From the controversies surrounding Elysium Pump to the competition between Boxa, Kleos, and Ascend, and now the collapse of $OBOL and multiple related tokens.

Launchpads keep appearing.

New tokens keep launching.

But community trust keeps disappearing.

Everyone wants to dominate the market.

But how many of these projects actually give a fuck about the people putting their money into this ecosystem?

5. MAINNET IS LIVE, BUT USERS STILL HAVE TO WAIT TO WITHDRAW.

Elysium officially launched its mainnet on November 9.

But if you use the official bridge to move assets from Elysium back to HyperEVM, you're still facing a withdrawal period of around 7 days.

Want your funds faster? You'll have to use alternatives like Relay.

An ecosystem that constantly talks about user experience, yet even withdrawing your own assets can be frustrating.

6. THE WORST PART ISN'T THE TOKEN PRICES CRASHING.

It's the loss of trust.

Prices can recover.

Liquidity can return.

But once a community feels betrayed, rebuilding that trust is a completely different story.

Elysium doesn't lack technology.

It doesn't lack partnerships.

It certainly doesn't lack attention.

What it's losing is the very community that helped bring it to mainnet.

I don't have evidence to claim that the entire Elysium ecosystem is an organized scam.

But everything I've witnessed is more than enough for me to lose faith in it.

ARC died one day after mainnet.

Elysium? Trust started dying before it even launched.

I went from being one of its biggest believers to feeling nothing but disappointment.

YOU PROMISED BUILDERS.

YOU PROMISED REAL VALUE.

YOU PROMISED AN ECOSYSTEM.

BUT USERS ENDED UP AS EXIT LIQUIDITY.

I'm not going to keep promoting an ecosystem I no longer believe in.

This is my final post about Elysium.

Fuck the hype. Fuck the empty promises.

TRUST IS GONE.

text:
Gather round folks, because just when you thought Masa Son would not catalyze the bursting of the next bubble... well, read for yourselves

SoftBank bought 87 million Intel shares for $2 billion last year. By the end of March the stake was worth $3.8 billion, and by the end of September $10.5 billion, good for a ¥1.06 trillion gain in the first half. 

Instead of selling, in August SoftBank did something much more, well, SoftBank: it raised $7.35 billion through prepaid forward contracts on its entire Intel stake, structured as collars with a floor and a cap. In English, it borrowed more than three times what it paid for the stock, pledged every share, and sold away the upside above the cap to pay for the downside protection.

What happened next? Intel shares kept climbing after the ink dried, which means the capped contracts moved against SoftBank, to the tune of a ¥322 billion ($2 billion) derivative loss in less than two months. And because Intel still finished the September quarter below where it started, SoftBank also booked a ¥270 billion valuation loss on the shares themselves.

So in a single quarter Masa managed to lose money on the stock and on the hedge. That takes sheer talent.

The fine print is even better: of the ¥1.65 trillion of Intel shares pledged, the banks have "rights of use" over ¥1.1 trillion, meaning they are free to lend out or otherwise use SoftBank's collateral.

text:
Agentic Mining 应该是币圈接下来最大的叙事红利

因为让每个 Web3 用户都拥有一个 Agent 去交易/交互太性感了。交易所的盈利来自于手续费，全网交易越频繁赚的越多。链上的盈利来自于 Gas 费，也是越频繁赚越多。试问，是 Agent 的手速快，还是人的手速快，是 Agent 时间多，还是人的时间多，是 Agent 更专注，还是人更专注？

作为交易所恨不得每个人部署几万个 Agent ，那交易所的手续费得在现在基础上翻 N 翻；作为公链或者 L2 ，也是这么想的。

当然，去年大家也是想想，但 AI 发展的太快了，从小龙虾到爱马仕到 Grok Bot 和 Muse，现在完全不懂编程的人也能简单的部署几十个 Agent

所以，伟大的时代即将到了

26 年以前，币安对 AI 一直处于研究的状态，天天说 AI 是未来要拥抱，但没什么实质性行动。 26 年以后就不一样了，先后推出了 AI Pro、 Agentic Wallet 、Agent ID，这是要大干一场啊？这就是在为了全民 Agent 做基础设施准备。

动力足了、条件有了，接下来一定会有巨鳄推动 Agent 普及化。有点像移动互联网刚开始的时候，大家都有了智能手机，也能够使用 4G/5G 网络了，这时候大佬们就要建立人们使用移动互联网支付和生活的习惯了，最直观的就是打车软件。疯狂的补贴，烧出了全民手机打车的习惯。

聪明的你应该发现了，接下来最简单的方法就是天量补贴使用 Agent 的用户，尤其是那些使用 Agent 交易或者交互的用户。你们不是怕用 Agent 亏钱吗？亏了也没关系，给你发大毛就是了。

其实这是币圈的老套路了，烧钱的本质就是吸引注意力和养成用户习惯，过往的 ICO 、挖矿、空投、IEO 、IDO、DeFi 本质上都是让用户养成一些习惯，这次也不例外。

很感谢 42 @42space  提出了一个非常贴切的词， Agentic Mining， 智能体挖矿。我已经可以想象，这个伟大的时代什么样子了。

一些列的项目开始对 Agent 进行补贴，然后第一批人暴富，第二批人、第三批人开始加入，最后不到一年时间，所有 Web3 的用户都部署几十个 Agent ，并驱动他们到处交易/交互。

这里最聪明的莫过于币安了，他掌握了一个非常重要的基础设施 ，Agent ID 。说白了，表面上是争夺 Agent 的注意力，实质上还是背后的用户。币安的 Agent ID 最牛逼的就是和 KYC 对应，那能够确保 Agent 的真实性。毕竟，烧钱补贴是为了养成更多用户拥有 Agent 使用 Agent 的目的，全被一堆单人控制的 Agent 撸走就亏麻了。

所以，去年很多对 Agent 友好的项目很快做不下去原因也在这里。去年没有 Agent 身份，而且能玩儿转 Ai 的也就少数人。天天隔着一只羊薅，分分钟就秃了。但是今年真不一样了，时机太成熟了。

太期待各种基于 Agent ID 的项目发大毛了，币安一天手续费有时候都是几亿美金，怕什么，拿 TM 一个月的手续费烧 、PUA，等全民 Agent 的时候，狠狠数钱吧。我都可以想象到时候 $BNB 疯狂销毁的样子。

text:
It has been a crazy week, and indeed a fairly tumultuous couple of months, as markets have had to reevaluate evolving AI-related stories, election results and geopolitical developments, and for a time inflation had been pushed to the side as a real-time relevant news story. That being said, to the Federal Reserve this inflation story is top of mind, particularly as last week's employment report showed a still solid no-hire/no-fire labor market. With today's stronger-than-expected inflation print, a Fed policy rate hike in December appears quite likely and the question is more about whether it will be a quarter point hike or a half point.

The headline CPI print of 0.35% month-over-month remained quite elevated, in part due to increases in energy and food costs, and Core CPI, while a bit more subdued at 0.30% month-over-month, was still well above the Fed's 2% target. The 3-month and 6-month annualized moving averages of Core CPI reside at 3.75% and 2.70%, respectively, displaying price gains that continue to be considerably higher than the Fed is comfortable with.

Despite some technical uncertainty, higher than desired levels of inflation should keep the Fed dissatisfied with the lackluster progress on inflation. When dissecting today's number further, core goods ex-autos inflation accelerated to 0.5% month-over-month and supercore edged up to 0.4% month-over-month. We, and the Fed, will continue to watch these numbers as they evolve over the coming months.

The Fed's disposition, as well as that of many global central banks today, is to keep policy firm to try to address these elevated inflationary conditions. We understand the directive here, but think that in many places, such as the U.S., it is very hard to address exogenous near-term shocks, such as fuel prices influenced by geopolitical developments, or semiconductor prices influenced by a memory/compute shortage as the AI buildout rages on, via conventional policymaking. These sorts of shocks are only very loosely tied to the overnight interest rate tool as a moderator of these conditions.

Hence, we maintain a cautious stance with regard to interest rates, in anticipation of potentially higher rates from here, but also respectful of the chances for easing geopolitical tensions and some potentially slower AI investment over the coming quarters and years, alleviating some of this near-term pricing pressure in the technology space. Still, we remain resolute in our posture that income remains at the forefront of investment decisions for fixed income portfolios. The availability here is generationally attractive and continues to provide greater stability than more volatile interest rate expressions. Further, patient investors continue to be rewarded for clipping coupon, especially when both stock prices and general price levels in these recurring inflation reports are displaying meaningful volatility.

text:
Crypto Is Growing Up. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen Says Its Security Model Needs to Grow Up Too.

For years, cryptocurrency exchanges have operated as all-in-one platforms, allowing users to store assets, execute trades, and access financial products in one place. That convenience helped make crypto more accessible, but it also created a security model that is becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
In this episode of Drops, I sit down with @Bitget CEO, @GracyBitget, to discuss the security challenges facing crypto exchanges, the lessons from Bitget's recent $388 million breach, and why she believes separating custody from trading could represent an important step forward for the industry.

A $388 Million Wake-Up Call

On September 24, Bitget experienced a major security breach involving unauthorized transfers of approximately $388 million from its hot and warm wallets. The initial suspicious transfers began around 2:30 a.m. in Gracy’s time zone, followed by larger withdrawals shortly afterward. She happened to wake up before 4 a.m., checked her phone, and discovered what was unfolding.
Her immediate priorities were understanding the extent of the losses, identifying the vulnerability, and determining whether the threat had been contained. Within hours, she was addressing the community publicly, even as the investigation continued. The experience was emotionally demanding, and Gracy admits there were moments when her hands shook, despite her efforts to remain composed.

"I'm a human being. I'm not an AI," she said.

The breach originated through third-party vulnerabilities rather than compromised private keys, and Bitget's cold wallets remained secure. The company subsequently patched vulnerabilities, strengthened withdrawal procedures, and used its existing protection fund to cover the losses, leaving customer balances unaffected.
But beyond the immediate response, Gracy came away with a more fundamental realization: Improving security protocols alone would not solve the underlying problem.

Why the Traditional Exchange Model Is Reaching Its Limits

To understand Gracy's argument, it helps to understand how centralized cryptocurrency exchanges operate. Unlike conventional financial markets, where different institutions handle trading, custody, and clearing, crypto exchanges have often combined these functions. Gracy describes this structure as "one giant monster."

The advantage is a seamless experience where users can deposit funds, purchase assets, move between products, and execute trades, but the problem is that concentrating so many responsibilities within one organization also concentrates risk. As exchanges expand their offerings, they create more systems, dependencies, and potential vulnerabilities to protect from, while attackers only need to exploit one weakness to cause substantial damage.

Gracy argues that this creates an inherently uneven contest between security teams and hackers, especially as attacks become increasingly sophisticated. Her conclusion is that the industry needs to reconsider its architecture rather than simply keep adding protective measures to the same underlying model.

The Open Custody Network

Gracy's proposed solution is the Bitget Open Custody Network, which she summarizes in one sentence as "Assets in bank, trading on Bitget." Essentially, customers would no longer need to keep all their assets directly with the exchange to trade on its platform. Instead, custody would move to specialized providers, including established banks, digital banks, and dedicated cryptocurrency custody firms. Bitget would continue facilitating trading, while these separate institutions would be responsible for safeguarding customer assets.

However, separating custody from trading introduces its own considerations. Customers must understand the custodian's regulatory status, financial strength, security record, jurisdiction, and the time or cost involved in accessing funds. The model is intended to distribute responsibilities, thus reducing risk.

Security Comes With a Trade-Off

Crypto users have become accustomed to moving funds almost instantly, and introducing independent custodians could make certain processes slower or more complicated. This may be acceptable for institutional investors who often prioritize asset protection over convenience, but retail customers may see things differently.

Gracy acknowledges this. The initial rollout primarily targets institutional clients and high-net-worth users, who are more likely to value independent custody arrangements. Over time, Bitget hopes to simplify the process for smaller customers, potentially reducing the need to select and manage custodians individually. Importantly, participation is not intended to be mandatory. Customers would retain the option of keeping assets with Bitget or adopting the external custody model.

This raises a broader question for the industry. Can exchanges offer substantially stronger protection without sacrificing the simplicity that attracted users in the first place? Gracy believes the answer will depend on how effectively exchanges and custody providers develop the infrastructure together.

From Crypto's Original Ideals to Institutional Adoption

The discussion eventually moves beyond security to examine how cryptocurrency itself is evolving. Bitcoin emerged from a philosophy of decentralization, peer-to-peer transactions, and individual control over financial assets. Yet the industry now includes traditional financial institutions, investment products, and regulated intermediaries. Gracy doesn't necessarily see this as a contradiction.

She distinguishes decentralized blockchain networks from the institutions that provide access to assets operating on those networks. Bitcoin can remain decentralized even as banks, asset managers, and regulated exchanges participate in its broader ecosystem.
She points to the growing digital asset activities of institutions such as JPMorgan, BlackRock, and Fidelity as evidence of this transition. For Gracy, the industry is moving beyond its experimental years toward a stage where security, sustainable business models, and integration with traditional finance matter.

What Success Would Look Like

Gracy has a specific vision for measuring the Open Custody Network's success over the next three years. She wants at least half of Bitget's total assets under management to be held by independent custodians, with no custody-related security breaches and minimal disruption to the customer experience. She also hopes other centralized exchanges will adopt similar approaches.

Rather than positioning the network primarily as a new revenue opportunity, she describes it as an effort to encourage broader changes in how the industry manages security.
As crypto becomes part of a larger financial system, the industry must become more deliberate about who holds customer assets, how those assets are protected, and what risks users accept in exchange for convenience.

quoted_text:
I'm not sorry to say I don't want my content reviewed by anyone. Not legal, brand, comms, compliance, pr, or even my manager 

But that's end game. As social media managers, it's our job to do the heavy-lifting internally to get us as close to that point as possible 

And in crypto, risk is higher than most other industries. The money is so close. Speculation is running wild. Tokens live or die by tweets. Trends are fast-moving and gate-kept hard. Sentiment flips in an instant 

So, how do we balance that and get to the dream state of no content reviews? 

First, try some empathy and think about it from their point of view. Why does legal want to review your content? 

Well, actually they don't. They want to focus on their actual work instead of babysitting your stupid ass. They're scared, unsure and unfamiliar with what you're doing. They don't know why a meme is important and they don't want to get sued because of it 

Every review layer has its own version of this reason. They want to maintain brand consistency. They don't want to get fined. They want to do quality-control. And so on 

Each social media post is a risk for a certain department, and to some extent the entire business. If you don't understand their needs, you can't factor them in, which means you are unaware of the risks and how to avoid them 

Again, none of these departments want to babysit you. They have other more important shit to do. That's your in, right there 

You have to build trust, shared values and understanding with each relevant team. Then take what you've learnt and turn it into a system that enables all parties to be confident the output will meet their needs without them seeing the output 

Essentially this means you need to deeply understand the perspectives of anyone that matters when it comes to your content. Talk to them. Get to know them. Help them understand what you're trying to do and why speed and freedom matter

And then reach an agreement, or a level of trust, granting you the freedom you need to operate without their review

Often to solidify this trust you will need documentation. I recommend this because it can be referenced and it's perfectly clear what you've agreed on. A set of guidelines and principles works well - layout what you do and don't do, and why. Get sign off, then run with it 

Enjoy your freedom and enhanced knowledge of the risk you take on every time you press post. Good luck 🫡

(You will never and should never totally remove content reviews. Integrated campaigns and product launches should be properly coordinated across teams, for just one example. Simply minimize and remove the ones that reduce the ability to do your daily work)

Creatives' online presence should be their resume.

Hunt for: work ethic, attention to detail, video/written presentation skills over fancy fluff metrics.

Always run a 1-2 week paid trial before fully committing.

4. Invest in their development

Pay agencies to train them, work closely with your creatives to build taste, etc.

text:
On the robotics and physical AI VC market

Over the last few weeks and months, there’s been a lot of fear in the markets. We believe those concerns are overblown. 

Let me pose a question - were OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Coreweave, etc good investments to make in 2021/2022?

The answer here is pretty clear cut. 

Were there AI companies from that period that weren’t good investments? Sure, but that’s the nature of venture and a small allocation to the top winners could still more than compensate for many poor picks.

Look at this chart. US investments in Robotics has still not even reached pre-ChatGPT levels of investment in AI. At the same time, frontier Physical AI models are already more capable than GPT3.5 at the time ChatGPT came out. 

Roughly half of Anthropic/OpenAIs revenue comes from software development related use. Software development makes up 2-3% of the global labor market. 

Robotics represents physical work which is roughly 50% of the global labor market. 

While I’m very bullish on AI for knowledge work over the next few years, I don’t have a prediction of what happens over the next few weeks and months. Agents have only just started to become really useful for most people and that growth has yet to be realized. 

Could a continued short term market correction in AI spill over into private Physical AI/robotics? Short term maybe some funding rounds for lower quality companies take longer or don’t get done - there are some pools of capital that cross over.

For the companies that otherwise are destined to win, we don’t think there will be much impact. Winners are going to win.

Fluctuations in latent demand for automated physical labor for one shouldn’t change much and if they do, matters little given how little existing penetration and superior economics that robotic solutions provide.

While I don’t have a strong macro view and am definitely not this bearish, the strongest example could be to look at the Great Depression. Tractors were invented before this period but roughly a fifth of the growth in tractor-owning farms between 1920 and 1954 came during the 1930s. 

"The Dust Bowl could blacken the sky, but it could not make the horse cheaper than the tractor."

Companies that face idiosyncratic circumstances will have idiosyncratic results. Technological advances here are accelerating, not slowing and if companies can grow like weeds then we expect funding to follow even if Anthropic raises at $1.3T instead of $2T in its IPO.

Most investors have only started dabbling in this sector and there are mountains of capital looking to get proper exposure. The IPOs of SpaceX and Anthropic are historically large liquidity events that we expect to propel continued downstream VC funding for months and years. 

Let me clear - there will always be a period where the wheat is separated from the chaff. Picking matters. Some capital has gone into winners but also some capital that has gone into losers and we will see the divergence in outcomes over the next few years. 

But with the backdrop of agentic robotic breakthroughs, Multimodel models accelerating R&D for physical AI while also proving a new approach of code as policy, and massively scaled data collection, our optimism for the sector is unwavering

text:
Aave 拟将约15亿美元非蓝筹抵押品移出 V3 核心市场

Aave 创始人 Stani 发帖称，风险管理方 LlamaRisk 提议调整 Aave 最大的市场 V3 Core，只保留流动性好的蓝筹抵押品。这意味着约15.2亿美元的抵押品可能被移出，对应约11.7亿美元的借款。

要移出的主要是再质押资产（如 rsETH、osETH）、BTC 包装币（如 LBTC、tBTC），以及 rETH、LDO 等需求较低的资产。ETH、WBTC、主流稳定币和 USDe 等会保留。相关资产会先被冻结，不能再新增存款和借款，然后逐步退出，部分资产可以转到风控更细的 Aave V4 独立市场。

该提案还需经过治理讨论，并与相关资产发行方沟通。
author: PANewsCN
quoted_text:
LlamaRisk proposes repositioning Aave V3 Core, Aave's largest market, to focus on liquid, blue-chip collateral.

The proposal would remove several categories of exposure:

1. Restaking assets
2. Leveraged wrapping strategies
3. Issuers whose operational and security resources fall short of Aave's risk standards
4. Low-demand reserves that no longer justify ongoing maintenance

This means potentially moving $1.52B in collateral backing $1.17B in debt out of V3 Core in favour of blue-chip collateral.

As the risk landscape evolves and Aave V4 grows, the goal is to sharpen V3 Core's risk profile and raise the bar for collateral eligibility.

Some affected assets could transition to isolated Aave V4 markets, where more granular risk controls allow for better risk-reward alignment.

The proposal comes from LlamaRisk, an Aave Protocol Risk Manager, and remains subject to governance discussions and engagement with asset issuers.

Aave will continue applying continuous risk assessment for all assets across all deployments.

text:
Huge AI announcements from OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. The authors of AI 2027 just moved their timelines up. They now expect AI on par with the best human AI researchers to arrive in 2027, after METR estimated Anthropic is improving about 2x as fast thanks to AI. Daniel Kokotajlo gives it a 50-50 chance by May 2027 and says he's "scared, sad, and angry." 

2. Anthropic opened the investor pitch for its IPO, with shares likely trading as soon as Thursday next week. An updated filing also says it has now crossed its own safety line for AI-driven progress. 

3. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT, a beta hub where brands can set up AI agents for shoppers, claim a verified profile, and track how often ChatGPT mentions them. Paid ads can point users to those agents too. This is like the start of SEO for chatbots.

4. Anthropic rolled out Claude Sheets and Whiteboards in beta, made Claude Data generally available, and announced Claude Meetings, an assistant that sits in on your video calls. Add those to Slides, Design, and Docs. Seems like Claude is slowly rebuilding the entire office suite.

5. Anthropic also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 yesterday, with Fable debuting at #1 on Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, 5 points ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon. It's also 20% cheaper and up to 30% faster than 5.1. Google lost the top spot before Carbon even shipped (!)

6. Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest model, built for high-volume agent work. It ties Claude Haiku 5.5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly one-third of the cost per task ($0.14 vs. $0.41 on an average test). Meta shipped its first Muse model in April and now has an answer for every tier OpenAI and Anthropic sell.

7. Google announced 2 new AI chips coming next year: the TPU 8tx, which keeps data encrypted even while a model is working on it, and the 8i Max, which joins 2 chips into one for agents that need to hold an entire codebase in view. Google already has nearly 100 TPU customers (including Anthropic and Apple) and every available chip is spoken for. 

8. Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed agents in August 2025 while they were investigating whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled its chips to China. The Commerce Department then halted the case and handed it to the Justice Department. Not a great week for Nvidia.

9. Adobe signed a multi-year deal with Disney to build custom AI models trained on Disney's characters and visual styles, with work already underway for theme parks, film, and ESPN. Pretty interesting to see one of the most protective IP owners in entertainment is now training its own AI models.

10. OpenAI acquired Odessia, a months-old AI trip-planning startup from Sonder founder Francis Davidson, who is joining OpenAI to work on travel. Between this and #3, ChatGPT is coming for shopping and travel.

11. France unveiled the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Mistral committing to build emergency off switches into their most advanced models. Interesting timing given #1 on this list.

Daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

I just unraveled the biggest AI astroturfing campaign I’ve found yet.

I found hundreds of fake accounts posing as Americans. The operation traces back to a supposedly defunct Israeli influence company.

They posted thousands of times in the last year to support Nvidia, back chip exports and data centers, attack U.S. lawmakers, and dismiss concerns about AI.

When it broke that Jensen Huang, Nvidia's CEO, was romantically involved with an alleged spy (who runs a company accused of chip diversion and whom US officials believe was passing information to Beijing), dozens of these accounts rushed to Jensen’s defense.

These accounts have targeted people pushing for export controls that ensure advanced chips aren’t going to China. Chris McGuire, a former White House national security official, got more than 100 replies from the astroturf network attacking him and his position on chips. Lawmakers who criticized the chip sales were called “peabrains” and “pure evil,” and accused of spreading “anti-Trump propaganda.”

Throughout this yearlong pro-Nvidia campaign, the operators have been hiding their tracks. They quietly deleted nearly two-thirds of the pro-Nvidia posts that we found, something they seem to do for many of their campaigns.

These accounts have spent years running campaigns that appear to serve the interests of corporate and political clients — most recently supporting the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan’s civil war, a group the U.S. government has accused of genocide.

Many of them trace back to a supposedly defunct Israeli influence company, Koios. In 2025, Haaretz reported that Koios helped run a covert pro-Qatar campaign devised by aides to Benjamin Netanyahu. While Koios claims to have ceased operations in 2025, it looks to me that many of its associated people and accounts moved their work to a new company, IntellACT, that spun up just as the old one shuttered.

Nvidia told me it has no relationship with the Israeli team linked to these accounts, and that while it has recently become aware of the operation, it is also trying to find out who is behind it. So, who is funding a yearlong campaign to shape one of the most important policy fights in history? I’m not sure, but I think it deserves a formal investigation. And Congress has that power.

The AI race with China is all about who has the best and most chips. There are four main ways China gets access to chips:

1.) Buying them directly from US companies like Nvidia.

2.) Illegally smuggling them from other countries into China.

3.) Accessing them remotely through the cloud from data centers located in places like Southeast Asia.

4.) Building their own domestic chips in China.

The Chinese military has used advanced chips to further its capabilities while undermining our national security, and the Chinese government has used these chips to strengthen its totalitarian surveillance project.

Congress has a generational opportunity in this year’s NDAA to pass bipartisan bills that would address all four of the pathways through which China acquires chips.

While we need a full assessment of the damage done to our national security by recent revelations, we can begin today by setting a better course.

No excuses. No apologies. Let’s get this done.

text:
Announcing a major milestone achieved by my team @GoogleDeepMind: we have proven key security properties of the machine code underlying the Signal messaging protocol. This is the first time the actual production code of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified – by any method, with or without AI – and at this depth.

More than a research breakthrough, it’s a prime example of how frontier AI can be a force multiplier to counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats.

Formal verification offers a higher standard of security; however, it’s extremely complex and time consuming, which is why in many cases it’s considered to be impractical. Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month’s time.

Using AlphaProof Code, Google DeepMind's new agentic framework for formal verification that runs on LLMs including Gemini Carbon, we verified the Signal protocol down to the actual code running on devices.  This milestone lays the groundwork for a future in which vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software, ship with mathematical proof that their protections work.

Reaching that future will take continued research from our community. In that spirit, we're open-sourcing our formal specifications and verification artifacts so others can build on this work.

On a personal note, this moment is of deep significance to me. I started my own research journey more than two decades ago as an intern working on checking the consistency of complex software systems. Seeing this grand challenge made practical with modern AI is extraordinary.

I'm extremely proud of my team members: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger,  Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, and Charles Sutton for taking on this grand challenge and delivering, and grateful to the Signal team for their partnership.
